News.title: Spotify down live: Website outage as music listeners 'get error trying to load'
News.content:
Spotify users are reporting issues with the music services website, app, and the server connection, according to Downdetector

Spotify down live: Website outage as music listeners 'get error trying to load'

Spotify's web player is down for hundreds of account users across the UK with people reporting error messages when trying to load.

According to Downdetector, a website which tracks online outages, people have also experienced problems with the music service's app and server connection.

Searches for issues with Spotify's Web Player have risen. One user commented on Downdetector that they are "getting an error message when loading both the website and app".

News.title: Covent Garden stabbing live: Police arrest woman in London as four men stabbed
News.content:
A woman has been arrested after four men were stabbed in Covent Garden in central London - the men were taken to a major trauma centre

Covent Garden stabbing live: Police arrest woman in London as four men stabbed

A 47-year-old woman has been arrested after four men were stabbed in London's Covent Garden.

The London Ambulance Service was called at 12.29pm today to reports of stabbings on Endell Street. It treated four people at the scene before taking them to a major trauma centre.

The four men are aged 34, 39, 42 and 52, the Metropolitan Police said. Their injuries are not believed to be life-threatening.

The woman was arrested on suspicion of possession of an offensive weapon and assault. She was taken to police custody where she remains. Images show police detaining a woman at the scene.

A London Air Ambulance has been pictured landing in Trafalgar Square.

News.title: M60 traffic live: Motorway closed clockwise near Stretford after 'police incident'
News.content:
A stretch of the M60 clockwise in Greater Manchester is shut due to a police incident, with traffic building in Stretford

A serious "police incident" has forced the closure of the M60 clockwise in Greater Manchester.

Long queues are building on the carriageway between Junction 3 for the A34 Kingsway and Junction 7 for the A56 Chester Road at Stretford, with trapped traffic caught in the closure.

National Highways said: "Traffic is held on the M60 clockwise between J5 Manchester & J6 Stretford due to a Police-led incident. Current delays 30 mins on approach, 3 miles of congestion."

Traffic monitoring service Inrix said: "Congestion to just after J1 (Stockport Pyramid), with traffic slowing on the opposite carriageway past the scene due to onlookers. The A5103 Princess Parkway is also stationary heading north on approach to J5. Cameras show the road is closed across all junctions for a police incident located between J5 and J6. Trapped traffic is being taken off at J5."

News.title: Celtic manager Martin O'Neill in hospital as club issue health update
News.content:
Celtic manager Martin O'Neill in hospital as club issue health update

Martin O'Neill was in the dugout for Celtic's 1-0 win at home to Dundee on Monday to begin their Scottish Premiership title defence, but the manager is now in hospital

View Image Martin O'Neill has undergone a 'small procedure' (Image: Ian MacNicol/Getty Images)

Celtic manager Martin O'Neill is in hospital after undergoing a 'small procedure', the club have confirmed. Celtic said in a statement that O'Neill, 74, is expected to be discharged within the 'next day or two'.

‌



There are no details about the Northern Irishman's procedure. O'Neill was in the dugout as Celtic began their Scottish Premiership title defence at home to Dundee on Monday, winning 1-0.

‌



After two interim spells last season, the former Aston Villa boss signed a one-year contract plus the option of a further 12 months to become Celtic's permanent manager in June. Previously, O'Neill hadn't managed since 2019.

‌



Celtic announced on Wednesday afternoon: "In response to speculation, we can confirm that Martin O'Neill has undergone a small procedure in hospital," the Scottish champions posted on social media.

JOIN US ON FACEBOOK! All the best sports news and much more on our dedicated Facebook page

‌



Inside the murky world of FIFA lobbying as Jamie Carragher reveals World Cup request READ MORE :

"We would envisage Martin being released from hospital in the next day or two and on behalf of Martin, we would like to thank supporters for their kind wishes. We would ask that the privacy of Martin and his family is respected."

O'Neill led Celtic to a memorable Scottish league and cup double last season. His first spell came after the shock departure of Brendan Rodgers in October.

He then returned to Parkhead in January, with Wilfried Nancy having been sacked after just eight games. After talks with Celtic's major shareholder, Dermot Desmond, O'Neill decided to stay on for this season.

‌



Despite having the option to extend his stay for the 2027-28 campaign, O'Neill recently indicated that the new season will be his last. When asked about his initial reluctance to take the permanent job earlier this summer, the 74-year-old admitted to Sky Sports: "Well, that was genuine, really, because I wasn't sure at the time. In all honesty, I'm not even sure now!

"But I've got the chance to come back. When we go and clinch the championship, it's euphoria you feel at the time, and then time passes on.

‌



"So you're a year further on, and I think the only thing I could really guarantee you is that, if I do survive the year, that would really be it. Time does catch up with you, and I genuinely mean this about surviving the year, because you step into it again.

"Last year gives you a bit of respite, that's all it does - but we're in the results business, and we have to win. And I'm absolutely no different to anybody else; I have to try and win some football matches, otherwise I'll find myself in trouble."

News.title: Family of Archie York, seven, killed in drug den blast pleads for killer not be released early
News.content:
Family of Archie York, seven, killed in drug den blast pleads for killer not be released early

Katherine Errington has hit out at plans to let Reece Galbraith out of prison under the early release scheme as he had been sentenced to 14 years for the manslaughter of Archie York

View 3 Images Archie York died in a blast from a drugs factory in Newcastle

The mother of a little boy killed in a drug factory house explosion has vowed to fight to keep his killer behind bars.

‌



Archie York, seven, died almost two years ago after a powerful explosion. It was caused by a dangerous drug factory in the flat below his home in Benwell, Newcastle-upon-Tyne.

‌



Reece Galbraith, who set up the deadly cannabis shatter lab, was jailed for 14 years after admitting manslaughter in the October 2024 blast.

‌



Archie's heartbroken parents Katherine Errington and Robbie York were recently dealt a devastating blow when they were told Galbraith could be freed. He may be released after serving just half his sentence, which Katherine described as "disgusting".

Parents of knife crime victims hail blade surrender breakthrough as 15,000 weapons taken off streets READ MORE :

View 3 Images Katherine Errington, the mim of Archie York, is campaigning to stop child killers being released early (Image: Newcastle Chronicle)

Child-killers convicted of manslaughter, like Galbraith, are still eligible to be freed after serving half their sentence.

‌



Archie's mum Katherine has now begged the Prime Minister to think again on the policy introduced to reduce the population of prisons.

Katherine said: "I'm gutted. It doesn't get any worse than what he did. They need to look at each offence more closely.

"I'm not staying quiet, I have still got a few years left. I'm just going to fight this until he's released.

‌



"Why should I just take this on the chin. I'm not accepting it. The way I see it is I have still got three kids now and I'm still mothering Archie. This is what I can do for him."

View 3 Images Reece Galbraith, 33, could be freed early from jail (Image: North News & Pictures Ltd northnews.co.uk)

Newcastle council leader Colin Ferguson backed Katherine's views, saying: “I welcome the decision to review the early release scheme.

‌



"The full implications of what this could mean for victims' families, communities and public confidence in the justice system have not been fully considered.

“Archie York was just seven years old when his life was cruelly taken from him.

"He was asleep in his own home, a place where every child should feel safe and protected.

‌



"Instead, his family suffered the unimaginable horror of losing a beloved son through no fault of their own.

“Archie’s death was not a tragic accident. It was the consequence of reckless and criminal actions.

“The prospect of those responsible for the death of a child being released early is deeply distressing for bereaved families.

Article continues below

“We owe it to every child and every community affected by such heartbreaking tragedies to ensure our laws properly reflect the seriousness of these offences."

News.title: Former neo-Nazi withdraws as Tory council election candidate after Kemi Badenoch offers him job
News.content:
Former neo-Nazi withdraws as Tory council election candidate after Kemi Badenoch offers him job

Joshua Bonehill-Paine has announced he no longer intends to stand for a seat on Somerset Council, despite getting the backing of Conservative Party leader Kemi Badenoch

View 4 Images Joshua Bonehill-Paine had been set to stand as a Tory on Somerset Council next year (Image: Channel 4 News/Youtube)

A former neo-Nazi activist who was jailed for racially harassing an ex-Labour MP has stepped down as a Tory candidate.

‌



Joshua Bonehill-Paine, who was found guilty in 2016 of launching an antisemitic attack on Labour peer Luciana Berger, who is Jewish, has announced he no longer intends to stand for a seat on Somerset Council. But he revealed he had been offered a new role by Tory leader Kemi Badenoch.

‌



Mrs Badenoch faced a furious backlash after defending his selection, while Jewish community leaders refused a meeting with him. Baroness Berger - who gave evidence in the trial when she was six months pregnant - described his offences as "deeply anti-Semitic, racist, misogynistic, pornographic". She said the case still "haunts" her and warned he should not "have any role in public life".

‌



Ms Badenoch defended his selection, arguing that Bonehill-Paine had been rehabilitated and now worked to tackle racism and antisemitism. She said she was "sad" that he had withdrawn as a candidate.

View 4 Images Kemi Badenoch had earlier defended the candidate (Image: Jonathan Brady/PA Wire)

In a statement Bonehill-Paine wrote: "The last 24 hours have shown that a lot of people do not understand how terrible I feel about the things I did when I was much younger.

‌



" I know that my previous actions continue to cause pain in the Jewish community. I had thought that getting involved in my local council and working hard for my community was a good way to show how much I have changed and that I want to give something back."

He went on: "Rather than standing as a local council candidate, I believe that my experience is better used supporting Kemi Badenoch in her ongoing mission to combat the antisemitism and extremism that is dividing our nation. I have therefore informed the Party of my decision to withdraw from next year’s council election and Kemi has instead offered that I become an adviser to the Conservative Party’s Culture and Integration Commission, specifically focusing on how young men become radicalised."

Earlier the Board of Deputies of British Jews and the Jewish Leadership Council (JLC) declined an offer from the Conservatives to meet Mr Bonehill-Paine.

‌



View 4 Images Baroness Luciana Berger, who was a Labour MP at the time, speaking outside the Old Bailey in 2016 (Image: PA)

They said: "Whilst we do believe in the possibility of rehabilitation, this should not in this case entail selection as a candidate for a major political party, and the impact of this decision on the victims ought to be a central consideration.

"We have agreed to meet the Conservative Party to discuss their decision-making processes and to urge them to rescind this decision."

‌



Baroness Berger told the Tory leader she had "got this very, very wrong". "This case still haunts me," she wrote in a post on X on Tuesday night. "I feel a bit sick reading well-known commentators debate his selection today and say that 'these are precisely the people we need in public office'.

"For the avoidance of doubt I don't believe this man should have any role in public life - because of both his racism and his view of women. Kemi Badenoch you've got this very, very wrong."

View 4 Images Bonehill-Paine was convicted in 2016 (Image: Metropolitan Police/PA Wire)

‌



Bonehill-Paine was convicted of racially harassing Baroness Berger after publishing five disturbing hate-filled blog posts about her. He was jailed in 2016 for two years, and the judge imposed a criminal behaviour order which allowed police to monitor his internet activity for five years after his release. Bonehill-Paine has responded by saying he now works to combat antisemitism and extremism.

Baroness Berger said: "I was six months pregnant when I had to give evidence at the Old Bailey for this case. It was two days of hell."

On Wednesday morning, she added that he falls "very, very short" of the bar for public office. "There's a big difference between going back into society and teaching others possibly about what you did and why it was wrong, to making the leap to standing for public office," she told BBC Radio 4's Today programme.

‌



"I think there's a massive distinction there. And this is not just one-off hurty words. This is a man that engaged and indulged in a sustained campaign, not just against me, but about many others. This man has a record of offences, including public order offences, things that he committed, not just against me as a Jewish woman, that were deeply anti-Semitic, racist, misogynistic, pornographic, but also extended it to other communities, including the Muslim community.

"And I think that we need to have a bar when it comes to standing for public office, and I strongly believe today that this individual falls very, very short of that."

The Tory leader said after his withdrawal: "While I am sad that Joshua feels he won't be given the space to explain his position and represent his community, I am glad he is going to work with me and the party on tackling radicalisation as part of our culture and integration commission.

‌



"If we are going to stop extremism and antisemitism we are going to need help from those people who were part of the problem, but have now changed and are being part of the solution. Piling on them and trying to get them cancelled may be sport for other parties but this is a different Conservative Party.

"Sometimes there will be difficult judgment calls, but right now I know that we are the only party actively working to unite the country rather than one particular faction or other."

Lib Dem MP Adam Dance - whose Yeovil constituency includes the Crewkerne ward where Bonehill-Paine was due to stand, said: "This withdrawal is the right outcome but it should never have got to this point.

Article continues below

"What's most concerning now is Kemi Badenoch's response - she has not accepted her party got this wrong and instead frames legitimate concern about antisemitism as `piling on'.

"That is a troubling message to send. Residents in Crewkerne and across our county will rightly question a Conservative leader who seems more focused on defending her judgment than addressing why this candidate was selected in the first place."

News.title: Cristiano Ronaldo reveals supercars as he says he's 'lost count' of number in £22m collection
News.content:
Cristiano Ronaldo reveals supercars as he says he's 'lost count' of number in £22m collection

Al-Nassr forward Ronaldo previously revealed that he would likely never drive a car in his massive fleet of vehicles, which he put together 'like an investment'

View 4 Images Ronaldo has more than 41 cars, he believes (Image: cristiano/Instagram)

Cristiano Ronaldo gave rare insight into his massive supercar collection with a new photo showing off his "toys" posted to social media.

‌



The Al-Nassr forward, who makes an estimated £2.42 million per week, showed off the more than 20 cars lovingly parked inside his garage. He posed up a storm around a sea of Ferraris, Buggatis, Lamborghinis and BMWs, after revealing last year that he has even "lost count" of how many luxury vehicles he owns.

‌



While he didn't reveal just how much the cars cost in the post to his more than a billion social media followers, the fleet earned him approval from his huge group of fans.

‌



Georgina Rodriguez hits back at body shamers days before marrying Cristiano Ronaldo READ MORE :

View 4 Images Ronaldo revealed he has a massive collection of Bugattis and Ferraris (Image: cristiano/Instagram)

The post, which fetched more than 16 million likes and hundreds of thousands of comments, was proudly captioned by the superstar footballer: "My toys." Flocks of followers commented approvingly underneath, calling him the "Goat" as they marvelled at the massive collection.

It is believed that Ronaldo has a collection numbering more than 20 cars, although they weren't all visible in the Instagram post, put up on the site on Tuesday.

‌



Visible cars in the photos included a Bugatti Veyron 16.5 Grand Sport Vitesse, reportedly Ronaldo's first Bugatti, a Bugatti Chiron, and Centodieci. Those three cars alone are worth well over £10 million, with the Vitesse setting buyers back a staggering $2.5 million (£1.85 million), the Chiron another $3 million (£2.22 million), and the Centodieci $9 million (£6.67 million).

View 4 Images The massive garage showe off Ronaldo's several Bugattis (Image: cristiano/Instagram)

Altogether, they're worth more than $14 million (£10 million), and they are far from the only cars that Ronaldo owns, with several more iconic vehicles also visible.

‌



Another is the Mercedes -AMG ONE, which was seen poking out from the corner of the image, a $5 million (£3.71 million) car that is one of just 275 ever produced. His less valuable - but stilll more expensive than most Brits could ever afford - cars include a McLaren Senna, Lamborghini Aventador, Bentley Flying Spur, and Mercedes G-Wagon Brabus.

They're worth £750,000, £270,000, £250,000 and £600,000 respectively, adding another nearly £2 million to the overall value of the collection.

View 4 Images Ronaldo has harbourned a long love for cars (Image: @Cristiano/Instagram)

Article continues below

Ronaldo admitted last year that he had "lost count" of the number of cars he owns, but estimated that his fleet could number more than a few dozen. In all, it is believed that collection could be worth up to £22 million, and he revealed last year that he likely wouldn't drive a single one of them.

Speaking to Piers Morgan's Uncensored podcast last year, the footballer revealed that the cars in his garage are "for collection" and "like an investment". He said: "I don’t go shopping. If I go anywhere, I can buy whatever I want, but I don’t need that anymore. Okay, let’s say three days ago I bought a car, but it’s for collection. It’s like you buy a frame.

"I’m not going to drive that car. It’s like an investment. Honestly, if you have to bet, I say I don’t know. 41, 40. I don’t know. I don’t know. I swear, I swear for my kids."

News.title: Sisters who waited over a decade for endometriosis diagnosis cast doubts on new 'speedier NHS tests'
News.content:
Sisters who waited over a decade for endometriosis diagnosis cast doubts on new 'speedier NHS tests'

Liv and Molly Smith said they suffered with pain for over a decade while waiting for an endometriosis diagnosis - the sisters shared concerns over new tests that could roll out on the NHS

View 5 Images Sisters Liv Smith (l) and Molly Smith (r) (Image: Kennedy News & Media)

Two sisters who waited over a decade to be diagnosed with endometriosis said they are sceptical about new tests, said to cut waiting times, that could roll out on the NHS.

‌



Liv and Molly Smith suffered with excruciating menstrual pain for over ten years but claimed doctors dismissed their concerns as "just bad periods". The sisters said they pushed for laparoscopy surgery and were both eventually diagnosed. At the moment this operation, where a camera is inserted into the pelvis through a small incision, is the only definite way to diagnose the condition.

‌



The sisters have spoken out after the National Institute of Health and Care Excellence revealed two non-invasive, that are said to slash years off the diagnosis time, are being recommended to the NHS.

‌



View 5 Images Molly laying in a hospital bed (Image: Kennedy News & Media)

The first one proposed is called Endotest - a saliva test that looks for genetic material to help support the diagnosis. The second test is known as EndoSure, which detects endometriosis by measuring electrical signals in the gut using sensor pads on the abdomen.

The Smith sisters say they welcome the new technology but also admit they're "apprehensive" about the success rate of the procedures due to the lack of education.

‌



View 5 Images Molly showing her stomach (Image: Kennedy News & Media)

Molly, from Leamington Spa, Warwickshire, said: "I feel like if it works it's great. With endo they say have an MRI or other scans and it will show up, but actually I had all of that and it didn't show it. It's different for everyone. Currently, without this new technology there is no definite way to diagnose or test without surgery.

"I like the fact that they're coming up with new ways to test for endometriosis as it's needed and this is brilliant, but it's if it works. I'm a bit hesitant about it at the moment.

‌



"When I had scans, like the MRI, when I was younger, they just said I didn't have it and I was fine. But then I had surgery and I was riddled with it. So, I'm a bit apprehensive about it but they must have done tests and seen if it works. I just don't think it'll work for everyone as everyone's cases are different. But anything they do to help the illness is great."

View 5 Images Liv's stomach following her surgery (Image: Kennedy News & Media)

Although the sisters were eventually diagnosed Liv, 26, said she spent eight years trying to get diagnosed after starting her period aged 16. She claimed her school attendance plummeted and she was even sacked from jobs due to the amount of time off she had due to pain from the condition.

‌



Endometriosis is a condition where tissue often found in the uterus grows outside the womb and can cause debilitating symptoms, such as severe pain, heavy periods and can make it difficult to conceive.

View 5 Images Liv Smith (Image: Kennedy News & Media)

Liv, also from Leamington Spa, said: "It's not just the bleeding and the pain, it causes so many other issues. I think there's still a long way to go, even if they are bringing in new technology."

‌



Molly, who was nine when her period started and waited until April 2010 for a diagnosis, said: "People just think it's a bad period and it's not, it's a debilitating illness. There needs to be more education out there and it should be taught at school as part of sex education.

"I think GPs need to know more too as this is everyone's starting point when you have problems. This is your first point of call when you have a problem." She said the tests were a "great step in the right direction" but warned more awareness awareness on the condition was needed.

Molly added: "It's great having the technology there but if people don't know about it and you keep getting fobbed off, what's the point of having it there?"

‌



NICE said both technologies are being recommended under new draft guidance for the NHS in England and Wales.

In November 2024, the independent body updated their endometriosis guidelines and made new recommendations and updated existing ones on diagnosing and managing the condition. This included updates like recommending specialist ultrasound as an alternative to MRI scans.

Dr Anastasia Chalkidou, director of the Health Tech programme at NICE, said: "A diagnosis of endometriosis can for some women take the best part of a decade, with the UK average standing at nine years and four months, and rising to 11 years for those from ethnically diverse communities. That delay means living with chronic pelvic pain that affects daily life, relationships and work.

Article continues below

"These technologies have the potential to change that by giving primary care professionals better non-invasive tools to identify endometriosis earlier allowing earlier and better treatment."

News.title: Ex neo-Nazi activist withdraws as Tory election candidate
News.content:
A former neo-Nazi selected by the Conservatives to fight a council election next year has pulled out after a backlash against his candidacy.

Joshua Bonehill-Paine was convicted of racially harassing Jewish former Labour MP Luciana Berger in 2016, while already serving a separate jail sentence for sharing antisemitic posts.

Tory leader Kemi Badenoch had defended the decision to select him as a candidate for the new Somerset Council seat of Crewkerne South, saying he had been rehabilitated and her party "believes in second chances".

But Bonehill-Paine said he had now withdrawn his candidacy, and had been offered a position as an anti-extremism adviser to the party.

In a social media post, he said the position with the Conservative Party's Culture and Integration Commission would focus on advising on how to prevent young men from being radicalised.

Bonehill-Paine spent three years in prison after he was jailed in 2015 for posting antisemitic material ahead of a planned neo-Nazi rally.

A year later in 2016, he was convicted of racially harassing then-Labour MP Berger, who now sits as Baroness Berger in the House of Lords.

He has described his past views as "indefensible" and says he has spent years opposing antisemitism since leaving prison in 2018.

But the party's decision to pick him for the Somerset seat sparked a huge political backlash, with Jewish groups declining the offer of a meeting with the party and Baroness Berger saying he should be barred from standing for public office.

In his social media post, Bonehill-Paine said his candidacy would prompt opposition parties to "spend all their time focusing on my past rather than the work I'm doing today".

"Rather than standing as a local council candidate, I believe that my experience is better used supporting Kemi Badenoch in her ongoing mission to combat the antisemitism and extremism that is dividing our nation," he added.

In a social media post, Badenoch said: "While I am sad that Joshua feels he won't be given the space to explain his position and represent his community, I am glad he is going to work with me and the party on tackling radicalisation."

"If we are going to stop extremism and antisemitism we are going to need help from those people who were part of the problem, but have now changed and are being part of the solution," she added.

"Piling on them and trying to get them cancelled may be sport for other parties, but this is a different Conservative Party."

But Reform UK hit out at Badenoch's decision to offer him the adviser role, with a spokesman saying it "beggars belief" and was "alarming news for the Jewish community in Britain".

News.title: Family 'devastated' by death of girl, 9, as man charged with murder
News.content:
The family of a nine-year-old girl who died after being found seriously injured in Arbroath have said they are "devastated" at her loss, as a man appeared in court charged with her murder.

Police have named the girl as Minnie Merriman from West Yorkshire. She died in Dundee's Ninewells Hospital on Monday.

A 35-year-old man, who police said was known to the girl, has appeared in court charged with her murder.

Christopher Rice from Wakefield, West Yorkshire, made no plea during an appearance in private at Forfar Sheriff Court and was remanded in custody.

News.title: Anthropic AI used fake profiles to target people in hack then hid the evidence
News.content:
Two of the world's most powerful AI tools created fake human profiles to try and trick people in attempted cyber-attacks, the UK's AI Security Institute (AISI) has revealed.

In the most serious case, Anthropic's Mythos AI tried to gain access to a service by sending private messages, having set up fake accounts mimicking real people - then hid the evidence.

It comes shortly after the two companies involved in the AISI testing - Anthropic and OpenAI - separately revealed in recent weeks instances of their tech hacking into other companies.

The firms said, in this latest case, the AISI's test had reduced or removed normal safeguards.

The AISI said on that Tuesday Mythos - and OpenAI's Sol - AI models had engaged in a level of "autonomy and deception" it had not seen before.

It clarified most of the malicious actions were carried out by Mythos.

AISI evaluators first noticed "unusual data transfers leaving our research systems" during a test, then found that "some of the agents being tested had engaged in sustained, potentially harmful activity directed at real people and organisations".

In the most serious case, a Mythos agent followed the routine of a human cyber-attacker by trying to trick people into giving it access to GitHub, a large platform where technology developers store software code.

The agent was trying to insert "malicious code" into GitHub's system.

It identified and researched the people who maintained GitHub and created a series of fake accounts based on those real people.

It sent messages and files through a file-sharing service as part of an effort to pressure and trick the people into approving its malicious code.

When challenged, "it edited its earlier activity to appear harmless and considered adopting a fresh identity to continue," AISI said.

Throughout the attempts, it was human review that stopped the agent from succeeding in delivering the malicious code to GitHub.

While AISI said the Mythos agent had not been instructed specifically to avoid or carry out such behaviour, it was "the first time we have seen risks around autonomy and deception manifest this clearly, without specific prompting, in the real-world".

The rival AI companies, which are poised to be listed on the public stock market, have been in the headlines in recent weeks after announcing their tools were responsible for several cyber-hacking incidents.

News.title: Police chief considers joining legal action over PC Harper killers' early release
News.content:
The driver of the vehicle, Henry Long, received a 16-year sentence and is not eligible for early release.

Speaking on the Today programme, Thames Valley Police chief Jason Hogg urged the government to reconsider its position.

Only prisoners convicted of murder, rape, grooming, and serious child sex offences will be excluded from the scheme in England and Wales - while those convicted of manslaughter remain eligible.

"I fully understand the challenges around the crisis in the prison system," he said.

"But the decision made and where that line has been drawn, I do not believe that people responsible for taking the life of another citizen in our country should be released early."

He said: "I was informed yesterday that the Police Federation are considering legal action, I am in discussions with the Police Federation with regards to this matter".

Asked whether this meant he would join them, he said: "I think we need to get some legal advice in relation to this. This is something I certainly would consider."

Following PC Harper's death and a campaign by his widow Lissie, Parliament passed "Harper's Law", which gives mandatory life sentences to the killers of emergency services workers. It also doubles the maximum penalty from 12 months to two years for those who assault police or other emergency workers.

But the new rules - introduced in 2022 - did not apply retrospectively to the sentencing of PC Harper's killers, and so do not prevent them from being released early.

Hogg said: "The law isn't retrospective and we all understand that, but the fact that they are released early simply seems perverse."

Aileen O'Connor, branch chairman of Thames Valley Police Federation told BBC Breakfast her organisation was exploring whether legal action was an option.

"If it is an avenue we can explore then I'll get behind that 110%," she said.

As for what shape a potential legal challenge might take, she said: "Ultimately that's for the specialists, the barristers and those in that legal sector to make that decision whether there is a challenge there.

"If there is a challenge then we will look to take that challenge."

Sentencing minister Jake Richards told the BBC it would be wrong to pick out individual cases and block two of PC Harper's killers from early release.

Although the government had reviewed what sentences would be excluded from the early release scheme, he confirmed "manslaughter is not one of those offences".

On Wednesday the Ministry of Justice released a new list of exclusions that will be exempt from the early release scheme.

It said rapists, as well as criminals sentenced for child sex offences and grooming and conspiracy offences for these crimes, will no longer be eligible to leave prison early.

Murderers and terrorists were already not eligible for the early release scheme.

Richards said: "It would be wrong to pick out individual cases within different offending cohorts. That wouldn't be right. It wouldn't be lawful either. So it is correct that those two individuals will be subject to the new regime from October".

News.title: See the Sun like never before with most detailed images yet
News.content:
Scientists using the world's most powerful solar telescope have captured the surface of our Sun in new, unprecedented detail.

Images and footage show "whirlpools" of activity that it has not been possible to see before.

It is the Sun's magnetic field being twisted and moved by the motion of hot gas.

That constant swirling is a driving force behind bursts of energy from the Sun, creating so-called space weather, that can disrupt Earth's power grids and satellites, and could even injure astronauts.

"The Sun is the source of that energy and of all of that space weather," explained Dr David Boboltz from the US National Solar Observatory, external (NSO).

Capturing more detailed pictures of our solar system's star will help in responding to that weather, he said.

"To figure out and eventually predict space weather, we want to understand the physics of the Sun, all the way down to the smallest scales."

News.title: Traitors star Joe Marler to become BBC's first celebrity Gladiator
News.content:
Former rugby star Joe Marler is to become the first ever celebrity Gladiator on the BBC's popular entertainment series.

The 36-year-old, who also took part in the first series of Celebrity Traitors, will be known as Mauler and face contenders when the fourth series of Gladiators begins in 2027.

"Mauler will see you now," Marler said in a video posted on Instagram, external announcing the news, recorded in the Gladiators dressing room.

The BBC said Marler will make his debut with a series of "special appearances packed with power, personality and plenty of surprises".

Filming for the fourth series is currently under way in Sheffield, the BBC confirmed in a statement.

"Known for his uncompromising style of play and larger-than-life sense of humour, Joe has built a reputation as one of the UK's most entertaining sporting personalities," the corporation said.

"Now, he's taking on an entirely new challenge as he joins the ranks of the Gladiators, bringing his trademark physicality and competitive spirit to one of television's toughest arenas."

The former England rugby international star, who is from Heathfield, Sussex, will join fellow Gladiators such as Nitro, Viper, Diamond and Sabre in battle when the show returns next year.

Gladiators was a hugely successful show on ITV in the 1990s, and saw members of the public take on a group of elite athletes who each had their own on-screen persona.

Olympic swimmer Sharron Davies, who like Marler was already known as a famous sports personality, joined that iteration of the show in 1995 as the character Amazon.

The format was revived by Sky for two series in 2008, before the current iteration launched in 2024, quickly becoming a hit for BBC One.

A celebrity spin-off is separately in the works, featuring contestants including presenter AJ Odudu, comedian Sara Pascoe, podcaster Chris Ramsey and social media star George Clarke.

News.title: El-Sayed's victory sends tremors through Democratic Party
News.content:
The tremors from Abdul El-Sayed's victory in Michigan's Senate primary will have been felt hundreds of miles away by the Democratic Party leadership.

In a year in which Republicans appear to be facing significant electoral headwinds, Democratic primary voters have taken a chance on a left-wing insurgent, raising the stakes in a Senate race in November that could decide overall control of the upper chamber.

The question is whether the way El-Sayed has electrified the party base and tapped into their anger will work on general election voters. And whether an unabashedly left-wing Democrat can win in a swing state.

The party establishment, which had backed his opponent, will hope so.

Primary results across five states on Tuesday were a snapshot of the mood of the American electorate three months before the midterm elections.

Here are four key takeaways from the results.

News.title: Misconduct proceedings dropped against officer who shot Chris Kaba
News.content:
The Met police officer who shot Chris Kaba will not face misconduct proceedings, the Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC) has said.

Sgt Martyn Blake shot the 24-year-old n Streatham, south London, in 2022 after Kaba tried to ram his way past police cars. Blake was cleared of murder following a trial in 2024.

A decision was made in January to pause any proceedings involving Blake until a law change relating to the use of force in misconduct cases was introduced and its impact was clear, the IOPC said.

Commissioner Sir Mark Rowley said the IOPC's decision brought an end to "almost four years of uncertainty" for Blake, calling the accountability process for police officers "disgraceful".

In June the use of force test in such cases changed from the civil law test to the criminal law test, meaning actions that did not amount to a crime should not amount to misconduct either.

Referring to Blake by his cypher NX121, Rowley said: "Today's decision finally brings to an end almost four years of uncertainty for NX121, his family and the wider firearms command, with all the considerable worry and stress that has brought.

"We also recognise the profound impact on Chris Kaba's family, who continue to grieve their loss."

News.title: Woman arrested after four stabbed in central London
News.content:
A 47-year-old woman has been arrested after four men were stabbed in Covent Garden in central London, the Metropolitan Police said.

The men, aged 34, 39, 42 and 52, were taken to hospital after emergency services were called to reports of a stabbing in Endell Street at about 12:30 BST.

The force said two men remain in hospital with injuries not thought to be life threatening or life changing while the other two have been discharged.

The woman was arrested on suspicion of possession of an offensive weapon and assault. The Met said it was believed to have been a mental health-related incident and that a pair of scissors had been recovered at the scene.

News.title: Miliband says re-opening Strait of Hormuz 'essential' as he meets Rubio
News.content:
Re-opening the Strait of Hormuz is essential to bringing down the cost of living in the UK, Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband has said ahead of talks with US counterpart Marco Rubio.

The Labour minister is in Washington for his first official one-on-one meeting with Rubio.

The pair are also expected to discuss the war in Ukraine and the humanitarian crisis in Gaza.

Miliband was invited to the US capital by Rubio after they met on the sidelines of a foreign ministers' summit in the Philippines, where the former Labour leader made his debut as foreign secretary.

The White House was reported to be concerned about Prime Minister Andy Burnham's decision to hand Miliband the Foreign Office brief, given his previous criticism of US President Donald Trump as a racist and a misogynist.

Trump is also a trenchant opponent of wind farms and supports the opening up North Sea oil and use of fossil fuels, whereas in his former role as UK energy secretary, Miliband championed net zero and renewables.

Burnham has signalled a shift in north sea oil policy, earning praise from the Oval Office, but the dynamic between Miliband and Rubio will be closely watched.

Last month, Washington's top diplomat in London, Warren Stephens, said Miliband had been "wrong" in 2016 to call Trump "a racist, misogynistic self-confessed groper" and added "hopefully his views have changed".

Speaking ahead of the talks, Miliband said: "The government is committed to nurturing our strong, enduring and essential alliance with the US.

"I am greatly looking forward to my second meeting with secretary of state Marco Rubio, in which we will discuss the ongoing work to reopen the Strait of Hormuz and secure a lasting ceasefire, which is essential to ease cost-of-living pressures on British families."

The strategic sea route, which had been open before the US and Israel launched the war in February, has been a flashpoint in the Middle East conflict and disruption to trade has driven up fuel and food prices.

Miliband added: "We will also discuss how we can continue to stand shoulder to shoulder with Ukraine against Russia's war â as well as the importance of addressing the dire humanitarian situation in Gaza and working towards a lasting peace for Palestinians and Israelis."

In the face of erratic US support, the UK foreign secretary is set to stress that Ukraine's security is inseparable from European and transatlantic security and restate the UK's commitment to stand with Kyiv for as long as it takes.

Miliband will be taking the UK's seat on the World Bank board, so he will also meet its president Ajay Banga during his visit to discuss development, climate change and strengthening global resilience.

News.title: Gary Glitter appears in court over historical sex offence charges
News.content:
Dressed in a blue shirt and wearing sunglasses, Glitter appeared by video link from His Majesty's Prison Channings Wood for the 11-minute hearing.

Under his real name, Gadd was told of the charges against him and spoke only to confirm his name and date of birth.

The prosecutor, Jonathan Polnay KC, told the court that Gadd said in a police interview he did not know the complainant, and that the allegations against him were false.

He also told the court that the offences involved one person, and are said to have taken place between the years of 1978 and 1981 when the complainant was eight to 11 years old.

He said she lived near where Glitter lived and that was how he came to know her. She says he gave her chocolate and that he invited her into his house where the offences occurred.

The allegations were first reported to the Metropolitan Police on 9 January 2025 and an investigation into the circumstances was launched.

Gadd was first interviewed on 22 July last year in relation to the investigation.

The 82-year-old was one of the biggest pop stars of the 1970s with a string of number one hits.

The Met said in July that the alleged victim was being supported by specialist officers and had been made aware that Glitter had been charged.

The singer is currently being held in HMP Channings Wood in Devon.

News.title: Restrict sale of pet flea treatments, government urged
News.content:
Pet flea treatments should be banned from general sale, a Lords committee has urged, after an inquiry raised concerns about their impact on their environment.

Spot-on treatments to prevent parasite infestations in fur and on skin are currently widely available for pet owners to buy in supermarkets and online.

But the House of Lords environment committee said their sale should be restricted, adding widespread use posed a potential threat to natural ecosystems.

The government said it was continuing to assess the availability of the treatments in order to ensure "correct usage by owners".

Currently, dog and cat owners are frequently advised to use preventative spot-on treatments every month to avoid parasite infestations.

But in a series of evidence sessions, the committee heard such blanket usage is not supported by robust scientific evidence and is likely to be harming the environment.

Many vets do not treat their own pets monthly, the committee heard, instead regularly checking their pets' fur with flea combs and restricting use to when fleas were spotted.

The committee heard that high volumes of fipronil and imidacloprid, common active ingredients in spot-on treatments, have been found in UK streams and rivers, killing off aquatic life, with a knock-on effect on wildlife higher up the food chain.

These chemicals have already been banned for use as agricultural pesticides because of their impact on wildlife such as bees, while the committee said "very little is known" about the impacts of newer chemicals such as isoxazolines.

In a report, external, the cross-party committee recommended that only vets, pharmacists and other qualified professionals should be able to sell such treatments, with pet owners advised to take a precautionary approach to using them.

News.title: Man gets third-degree burns from hot sand after using disposable beach BBQ
News.content:
Warning: This article contains a distressing image

A man who suffered third-degree burns from hot sand after using a disposable barbecue on a beach has warned others to be aware of the dangers.

Sam Knight had been using it on Cefn Sidan Beach, Carmarthenshire, with his family and stepped on sand that was still hot.

The 27-year-old had to be carried off the beach after suffering badly blistered feet and needed weeks of treatment.

Experts at a burns centre say injuries such as this are becoming increasingly common and warned beach goers to take precautions.

Knight told Radio Wales Breakfast he was not aware that sand could be a "real hazard".

He had used tongs to move the barbecue to one side and extinguished it, so he thought it was safe.

"When I returned to the area, I stepped on a boiling hot patch of sand, and had to be carried off the beach," he added.

Knight was taken to Neath Port Talbot Hospital referred to a burns specialist.

"I couldn't walk for a couple of weeks so I had to take a fortnight off work," he added.

David Fligelstone and Menna Davies are physiotherapists who work with the burns centre at Swansea Bay University Health Board.

Fligelstone said the number of incidents they are seeing is "going up year on year".

"The key thing is that people don't understand is that sand stays hot for such a long time after a barbecue is moved," he said.

"When you look at the evidence it's always the sand that hasn't been cooled that ends up causing that injury."

Davies said injuries like this can be "quite painful" and need to be dressed for a "long period of time".

News.title: Dewormer and scabies drugs being sold as cancer treatments, BBC investigation finds
News.content:
Animal dewormer and a drug used to treat scabies are being sold and promoted as unproven cancer treatments, a BBC investigation has found.

Following a tip off, an undercover journalist was able to buy fenbendazole and ivermectin from a stairlift salesman in south Wales, and also found them for sale on Amazon.

Macmillan Cancer Support said it was concerned by the findings and that a growing number of people were asking about the medicines, despite "no clinical evidence" that they work.

Amazon removed the products after we contacted them, and said it had "proactive measures in place" to stop prohibited products being listed by third-party sellers.

Senior doctors are worried vulnerable patients could be put at risk by taking the medicines, as they say it could harm or delay conventional treatment.

Six months ago, Rebecca Holder contacted the BBC after a visit from stairlift salesman Jason Sarver.

She said Sarver and her father Bob, who had a brain tumour, lung cancer and needed help with his mobility, had been discussing stairlifts when the salesman changed the topic to talk about the drugs.

News.title: Afghan boxer appears in court in connection with death of Scottish woman
News.content:
The man suspected of killing a Scottish aid worker in Greece has appeared in court in Athens.

The body of Elisabeth Ross was found in a suitcase at an abandoned building on 18 July, days after she had been reported missing.

Sharif Ahmadzai, who is 26 and from Afghanistan, was told during the private court hearing that he faces charges of homicide with intent, robbery and weapons offences.

He made no comment and the case was deferred until Thursday, when it is expected that Ahmadzai will be formally charged.

Homicide with intent is equivalent to a murder charge in Scots law.

Ahmadzai was driven to court in a grey Hyundai i30 with blacked out windows for the hearing.

News.title: Temperatures to drop briefly ahead of potential new UK heatwave
News.content:
Temperatures are set to drop across the UK over the next few days, ending the latest heatwave that has affected some areas of southern and eastern England.

Humidity levels will fall too, which should cool down homes and make nights more comfortable for sleeping.

The change in conditions follows another historic day in a summer that has seen many long standing heat records toppled or tied. On Tuesday, the UK registered its 34th day of temperatures reaching 30C (86F) or higher in a calendar year, equalling the record set in 1995.

Forecasts suggest that this record is likely to be beaten as early as next week, with some showing the potential for a sixth heatwave to develop.

So far, this year’s Strictly line-up promises glitz, glamour… and a dog trainer called Graeme. Huh? Or rather, who? That was the question posed in floods of comments as Graeme Hall, the star of Channel 5’s Dogs Behaving (Very) Badly, was unveiled as the latest “celeb” to join the class of 2026.

I’ve not encountered Hall before, and maybe that’s on me; he does have 165,000 followers on Instagram where he, unsurprisingly, mostly posts pictures of dogs. But I’m clearly not alone in my bewilderment. As his spot on the Strictly line-up was claimed, fans on social media were quick to declare this year’s group of celebrities the “weakest” in the show’s 22-year history, and crack jokes about the whittling away of the BBC budget. Given the BBC is currently aiming to make £500m in budget cuts, and is reportedly putting Strictly out to competitive tender next year, à la Doctor Who, they might be onto something.

But between two ex-Love Island contestants, two EastEnders stars and Kim Kardashian’s former hair stylist – who infamously filmed his wedding for The Kardashians then filed for divorce one week after the episode aired (Google it) – Strictly’s current cast is lacking a little lustre. Frankly, it’s feeling far more Dancing on Ice than Strictly in its heyday.

Yet there’s surely another reason the big-name slebs aren’t donning their ruffled shirts and spray tans this year. Like Claudia Winkleman, who said goodbye to the ballroom in 2025, they’re choosing the BBC’s other star vehicle: The Celebrity Traitors. For decades, Strictly has been a tried-and-tested format with big commitment leading to big rewards. Sacrifices had to be made, sure, in terms of time and the possible state of your marriage. But then a new, shinier project arrives; one that takes a small percentage of the time and comes with none of the baggage that has plagued Strictly in recent years.

open image in gallery Dog trainer Hall’s casting raised eyebrows among ‘Strictly’ fans ( BBC )

For a long time, the common wisdom was that nothing could enhance a celebrity’s career like Strictly. This was an upmarket take on reality TV, providing the contestants everything from week-on-week screentime to the chance to appear vulnerable and construct an underdog story in front of the public. You didn’t even have to eat wallaby testicles in the process! Many stars have used their dancing skills to move into a career in musical theatre, from boybanders Jay McGuinness and Aston Merrygold to Olympic golden boy Louis Smith. But there’s an indirect boost to be gained too, one allowing influencers (sorry, “social media stars”) to go mainstream and soap actors to get known beyond their niche audiences.

But back-to-back scandals have caused the image of Strictly as the nicest show on TV to crack. Prospective contestants have a better sense of what’s asked of them when they agree to take part, the answer being “a lot”. It happens to everyone, and will likely continue even with the impending shake-ups to the presenter and pro dancer line-ups. You could have the dream partner and a delightful experience, and still find the intensive training regime taking its toll. The Strictly curse is obviously a pop culture phenomenon these days, but spending that long in rehearsals with anyone is going to impact your relationships out of the show. Throw in the inevitable trolling from the show’s most opinionated viewers, and the question of whether it’s worth it lingers.

Still in its infancy, The Celebrity Traitors avoids those negative connotations. Filming takes place over a few weeks in Scotland: removed enough to get caught up in the game, but not so long it takes over your life. And yes, the game, which requires players to backstab their old friends (hello, Alan Carr and Paloma Faith), can be tricksy and infuriating and bring out the worst side in people. But it’s always done with the sense that it’s nothing more than a game. The public are far less quick to blame players, and little animosity remains.

open image in gallery The cast of ‘The Celebrity Traitors’ series two is announced – with a few spelling mistakes... ( BBC )

Produced by independent production company Studio Lambert, The Celebrity Traitors is not solely reliant on BBC funding, and has therefore been able to attract a far higher calibre of star than Strictly ever did back in the halcyon days of 2004. Once certified national treasures Stephen Fry and Celia Imrie signed on for series one, a new standard was set for what was possible. The love of the game made them want to play, and now, Richard E Grant, Jerry Hall, Michael Sheen and Maya Jama are lining up to have a go. Given the ubiquity of many of the cast of season two, you have to assume that’s a draw here too; particularly Rob Beckett and Romesh Ranganathan, who surely cannot physically be on television more than they already are.

But for the slightly less famous among the very famous cast, The Celebrity Traitors can prove an incredibly effective branding exercise. Musician Cat Burns saw her social media following skyrocket during series one. This proved well-timed – the final coincided with the release of her new album. Rugby player Joe Marler’s hit podcast, released weeks after that same series wrapped, has barely left the charts since it began. Bright young Bella Ramsey, Myha’la and Sebastian Croft all seem ripe for this kind of boost.

So I don’t blame the stars for seeing what The Celebrity Traitors has done for their peers, noting how comparatively little time it took and how much fun they had, and making a beeline for the Scottish Highlands. With a new presenting line-up incoming, Strictly is in a state of flux, while the Traitors format goes from strength to strength. Of course they’d pick the latter. Unless they’re really angling to play a T-Bird in the national tour of Grease, I think it’s the wise choice.

House Speaker Mike Johnson says he won't get involved in the abuse allegations against embattled Republican Representative Max Miller — describing them as “domestic events” that happen “all the time.”

“I haven’t spoken to Max about this in the last few days. Of course, I will,” Johnson said in an interview with Politico. “There’s all sorts of domestic events going on with 435 members of Congress all the time, it’s not my business to get engaged in it.”

When pressed about accusations that the Ohio Republican held a gun to the head of ex-wife Emily Moreno and broke their two-year-old daughter's collarbone, Johnson acknowledged the claims were “serious,” Politico reported Wednesday.

Moreno’s father is Republican Senator Bernie Moreno of Ohio, who said Sunday that his former son-in-law should drop his re-election bid, resign from Congress and get “serious psychological help.”

"He is a danger to my daughter, and I hold my breath every minute he has custody of my granddaughter," Senator Moreno wrote on social media. "If there are any basic standards of character required to hold elected office, Max Miller fails them."

open image in gallery House Speaker Mike Johnson acknowledges the allegations against Rep. Max Miller are ‘serious’ but says he won’t get involved because ‘domestic events’ happen ‘all the time’ ( Getty )

The remarks led several Republican colleagues to echo the call, with Senator Roger Marshall of Kansas saying: “I trust Bernie so much as a good friend, and his family has such high values” that “to go through with this, it makes me think that they’re telling the whole truth and nothing but the truth.”

President Donald Trump privately told Miller that “things aren’t looking good,” Axios reported Monday. The president also told reporters the same day that the situation involving him was “a very sad thing.”

At Miller’s request, the House Ethics Committee said Tuesday that it's looking into whether the 37-year-old lawmaker “may have engaged in domestic violence and abuse or illegal drug use.” Johnson said that investigation would get to the bottom of the allegations.

“I think Max is taking them seriously. I think our colleagues are,” the speaker said. “But, again, we have to allow this process to play out. It’s just begun.”

Hours after the Ethics Committee announcement, Miller appeared Tuesday on CNN, where he denied any wrongdoing and called the claims against him “politically motivated.”

open image in gallery Republican Sen. Bernie Moreno of Ohio called Sunday for Miller, his former son-in-law, to resign from Congress and drop his re-election bid ( Getty )

Miller also said he wouldn't drop his campaign for a third term in the House ahead of Tuesday’s deadline, saying: “I will never back down.”

"I am never going to give up, and what I mean by that is my daughter is going to grow up one day, and she's going to see all of this, and she's not going to see that her father caved to political and social media pressures for something that he never did," he added.

Emily Moreno’s accusations, contained in police reports and court documents, led to the resurfacing of a 2021 Politico report in which unidentified sources alleged that Miller had pushed and slapped then-girlfriend and former Trump White House press secretary Stephanie Grisham during an April 2021 domestic dispute, and had also shoved a high school classmate down a flight of stairs when she refused his advances.

Miller, through an attorney, denied those allegations at the time and later sued Grisham for defamation after she wrote about an abusive relationship with an ex-boyfriend, without identifying Miller by name.

They settled out of court, with both sides agreeing not to disparage each other but Grisham sued Miller last month, alleging he violated that deal.

open image in gallery Former Trump White House press secretary Stephanie Grisham is suing Miller for allegedly violating a non-disparagement agreement tied to their former relationship ( AFP/Getty )

Grisham also filed a motion Monday for a temporary restraining order against Miller to prevent further alleged violations.

During his Tuesday CNN appearance, Miller acknowledged that Trump had called him the day before and told him “it’s going to be a tough race” but didn’t tell him to drop out.

Miller also said that “Speaker Mike Johnson, everyone else — they’re standing behind me.”

Johnson told Politico that he thought that “what Max is suggesting there is that I’ve been intellectually consistent.”

“We don’t take disciplinary action against members for allegations,” the speaker said. “But he’s saying the same things privately to members that he is publicly, that he denies all this.”

Johnson also said that the allegations “don’t look good right now, of course,” adding, “Look, I pine for the days when we don’t have these kinds of disturbances, when we got people who act in accordance with the dignity of their office. “

“But people have domestic disputes,” he said. “It’s part of being flawed humans, as we are, and we have to let those processes play out.”

Sasa, an alert and floppy-eared mixed-breed puppy, did not return home when the remaining containment lines were lifted Wednesday in the wake of a wildfire that swept across mountains and coastal areas near Athens.

The pup was one of hundreds of pets and wild animals rescued by volunteers this week during the blaze, which prompted multiple evacuations.

The fire — at one point burning on five fronts — torched dozens of homes and more than 100 square kilometers (39 square miles) of land. It was the latest scene of destruction during Europe’s searing summer, where massive fires — including in countries accustomed to cooler summers — have worried animal welfare groups.

In the town of Megara, 40 kilometers (25 miles) west of Athens, rescue organizer Elena Dede said the local volunteer effort saved more than 280 animals, mostly dogs, during scorching heat and high winds.

Sasa and others were housed on an indoor sports court inside a collapsible wire cage with a rubber ball to play with and a metal water bowl.

“There was so much heat and the fire was so aggressive. It was changing directions all the time,” Dede said.

Richard Parr, director of the U.K.-based Center for Wild Animal Welfare, described these animal rescue efforts by firefighters and local charities as “heroic” but argued that hotter summers are increasing the risk facing millions of animals.

“At the moment, all too often, it is ad hoc, and it falls on the shoulders of private individuals, small charities,” he said. “The scale of the challenges they’re facing in terms of the number of animals affected and the areas of fire is gigantic and completely out of step.”

The organization is campaigning for a dedicated European Union animal rescue service and funding to address the problem.

“There’s just a massive mismatch between the huge scale of this problem and the resources and the capacity that are available to respond to it,” Parr said.

He also urged governments to consider setting up “fire refuges” for animals, such as ponds and rock piles that could offer shelter.

In Greece, the blaze has left rescuers with a logistical headache: where to return displaced animals like Sasa. Dede said local authorities were helping match missing-animal notices with rescued animals and find temporary homes until the process was completed.

However, she said she was mindful that the dogs at the stadium were among the fortunate.

“It was really hard for every volunteer and every person involved to survive the smoke and the stress,” she said.

“I will never forget the animals that we knew were left behind. I’m just hoping they were saved and ran free."

___

Petros Giannakouris in Megara, Greece contributed.

Temperatures in Central Europe soared to extreme levels again on Wednesday with Slovakia and Austria both having their hottest day on record.

For Slovakia, it was also the third time this summer that temperatures reached a record high. The country's south recorded temperatures above 40 degrees Celsius (104 degrees Fahrenheit) in the latest heat wave, with a new record of 41.4 C (106.5 F) in the town of Kamenica nad Hronom in southern Slovakia, the Slovak Meteorological Institute said.

The previous records were set on two days — June 29 and June 30 — with 41.0 C (105.8 F) in the town of Turna nad Bodvou, and 41.3 C (106.3 F) in Kamenica nad Hronom.

That smashed a 2007 high of 40.3 C (104.5 F) in the town of Hurbanovo.

The night of Tuesday into Wednesday was also the hottest on record, with 28.4 degrees Celsius (83 F) in the town of Skalica in southwestern Slovakia.

In Austria, the all-time high of 41.2 C (106.1 F) was measured in Bad Deutsch-Altenburg near the border with Slovakia, beating a 41.0 C (105.8 F) record from the previous day, the GeoSphere meteorological service said.

The Czech Republic and Hungary had also recorded their all-time highs earlier this summer.

This year, Europe has been sweltering under an exceptionally hot and arid summer, with tinderbox conditions setting off unprecedented fires that have forced hundreds of thousands of people to evacuate homes and vacation spots.

The continent is the world’s fastest-warming, with temperatures increasing twice as fast as the global average since the 1980s, according to the European Union’s Copernicus Climate Change Service.

Yvette Cooper has announced new fast-track support for motor neurone disease (MND) patients, forming part of a wider overhaul of social care.

The Health Secretary paid tribute to the late Rob Burrow, the former England rugby league star who died in 2024 from MND complications.

Visiting a Leeds care centre named after Mr Burrow, Ms Cooper highlighted his crucial work in raising awareness and improving support for those affected, also acknowledging the efforts of his family and former teammate Sir Kevin Sinfield.

She said: “What we’ve got to do now is make sure the principles that apply here about supporting families and patients are applied throughout the National Health Service and also in our social care system too.

“That’s why when Andy Burnham set out a vision for a National Care Service, we prioritised MND as being something we should focus on now, providing social care support for affected families and speeding it up as well.”

Kevin Sinfield, left, and Rob Burrow, pictured in 2023, campaigned to raise millions of pounds and raise awareness of MND ( Danny Lawson/PA )

The new fast-track pathway is intended to tackle “delays and fragmentation” in support for those with MND as part of the “first phase” of fixing the social care system, the Department for Health and Social Care said.

It will be developed alongside the Motor Neurone Disease Association, existing patients and carers, and others working in health, social care and housing.

Tanya Curry, chief executive of the MND Association, said: “We hear time and time again of people with MND forced to battle a system that is slow, disjointed and too complex to move quickly enough to support people with a rapidly progressing disease.

“This must change – Ms Cooper’s statement today suggests she agrees and that there is willingness at the highest levels of Government to transform the experience for people with MND.

“We must now see that willingness turned into action, with real solutions implemented nationally and locally, in health and social care.”

The announcement comes a week after the Prime Minister pledged to work with other parties to reform the social care system, describing the current situation as “bad for everybody”.

Mr Burnham announced he would be expediting Baroness Louise Casey’s commission into social care, bringing forward the original 2028 deadline to next year.

He also vowed to immediately begin reforming the workforce – saying staff should also be integrated with the NHS – as well as promising to work with the other major parties to reach a consensus on the issue.

News.title: Disney theme park attendance in US jumps despite decline in international tourism
News.content:
Disney reported a solid third quarter, driven by the global success of Toy Story 5 which grossed $1 billion at the box office and robust performance from its U.S. theme parks.

The Experiences division, encompassing global theme parks, cruises, and merchandise, saw operating income rise 20% to $3.02 billion, with domestic parks experiencing a 27% increase in operating income, despite a 13% decline for international parks.

Overall attendance at U.S. parks climbed 3% from a year ago on an increase in attendance from domestic tourists and annual passholders. The company said the performance was also helped by summer promotions and new experiences being offered at the parks.

The company announced a new global short-form content sharing deal with TikTok, integrating Disney-focused fan-created content into the Disney+ app, and is selling its 50% stake in A+E Global Media to Hearst for $1.2 billion.

Streaming services, including Disney+ and Hulu, saw revenue climb 11% to $5.53 billion, attributed to subscriber growth, price increases, and higher advertising revenue, as Disney continues its shift towards streaming entertainment.
