World.title: Africa: Has Uganda Changed the Ebola Rulebook?
World.content:
Uganda says modern outbreak science has changed what investigators can know. Is it time to rethink the 42-day rule?

When Uganda's Ministry of Health announced on July 28, 2026, that the country had declared the end of its latest Ebola outbreak, something unusual happened. There was no public congratulatory statement from the World Health Organization's headquarters in Geneva. There was nothing from the WHO Africa Regional Office in Brazzaville, nor from the WHO country office in Kampala.

The silence was difficult to ignore. Yet Uganda itself had no doubts. "Today, Uganda is Ebola-free," Health Minister Dr Chris Baryomunsi announced at the Uganda Media Centre in Kampala, bringing to a close more than two months of heightened surveillance, border screening and public anxiety after Ebola crossed into Uganda from neighbouring Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC).

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

By the time the outbreak ended, Uganda had recorded 20 confirmed cases, including two deaths. For many countries, that would have been the end of the story. For Uganda, it became the beginning of another. The country's declaration did more than announce victory over its ninth Ebola outbreak. It also quietly questioned whether one of the world's oldest public health conventions--the 42-day rule used to declare the end of Ebola epidemics--still reflects the scientific tools available to outbreak investigators today.

It was a subtle argument, carefully worded and rooted in Uganda's own experience. Officials at the Ministry of Health were not suggesting that the long-established rule should be abandoned. Rather, they argued that rapid molecular diagnostics, genome sequencing, digital surveillance and real-time contact tracing now allow investigators to reconstruct transmission chains with a level of certainty that was unimaginable when the international guidance was developed. If that proposition eventually gains wider acceptance, it could reshape how countries determine when an Ebola outbreak has truly ended.

A different kind of outbreak

Uganda has become one of Africa's most experienced countries in responding to Ebola. Since the virus first appeared in the country in 2000, repeated outbreaks have shaped a public health system recognised for rapidly detecting infections, tracing contacts and interrupting transmission before epidemics spread widely.

But the 2026 episode differed fundamentally from the eight that came before it. This time, Ebola did not emerge inside Uganda. It arrived from eastern Congo. Fifteen infected Congolese crossed the border seeking treatment in Uganda after the Bundibugyo strain of Ebola began spreading rapidly through Ituri Province. Four Ugandan health workers unknowingly became infected while treating those patients before Ebola had been diagnosed, while a driver transporting one of the patients also contracted the virus.

Beyond those five secondary infections, transmission stopped. On paper, Uganda's outbreak remained remarkably small. Across the border, however, the situation was dramatically different. By late July, eastern Congo was battling the largest Bundibugyo Ebola outbreak ever recorded, with more than 3,200 confirmed infections and 1,400 deaths spread across five provinces, according to a status report published on July 26 by the WHO Africa Region Office.

Health authorities warned that transmission could continue expanding along transport routes linking eastern Congo with Uganda and South Sudan. Uganda's challenge therefore extended far beyond treating patients. It had to convince its own citizens and the outside world that the virus had not gained a foothold inside the country.

Containing fear

This year's outbreak quickly became as much an economic and political emergency as a medical one. Since the virus had entered from across one of East Africa's busiest borders, every crossing point, trading centre and transport corridor suddenly acquired new significance. The government responded swiftly. Entry points with the DRC were closed. Surveillance intensified across western Uganda. Restrictions were imposed on community gatherings in high-risk districts, while daily markets that sustain thousands of cross-border traders were temporarily suspended.

Then came perhaps the most difficult decision. President Yoweri Museveni postponed the annual Uganda Martyrs Day celebrations at Namugongo, one of Africa's largest religious pilgrimages. Every June 3, tens of thousands of worshippers, including hundreds from eastern Congo, travel to the shrine. By the time the announcement was made, many Congolese pilgrims had already begun their journey.

Health Minister Chris Baryomunsi later defended the decision, arguing that allowing the pilgrimage to proceed could have created a "super spreader event". "Probably today the story would be different," he reflected.

Although Uganda contained the outbreak, the economic consequences spread much further. Western governments issued travel advisories. Some Gulf countries temporarily suspended travel from Uganda. Hotels reported cancellations, tour operators lost bookings and airlines adjusted services during what is normally one of the country's busiest tourism seasons.

Inside government, frustration steadily grew. Speaking in June during a joint virtual briefing with the WHO and the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), Permanent Secretary Dr Diana Atwine suggested Uganda was paying a price for being transparent.

"We feel that we, as a country, have been a victim of transparency and effectiveness in dealing with epidemics," she said. "The more we communicate, the more we are blocked, the more we are locked out, the more our citizens are stopped from travelling."

Her remarks captured a dilemma that has become increasingly familiar since COVID-19. Countries are encouraged to report outbreaks quickly and openly. Yet doing so can also trigger travel restrictions, disrupt trade and damage tourism long before scientists understand the true scale of the threat. That helps explain why Uganda's declaration carried significance beyond epidemiology. Ending the outbreak was not simply about stopping transmission. It was also about restoring confidence, reopening borders and signalling that Uganda remained safe for business and tourism.

42-day global benchmark

But, long before Uganda suggested that advances in science could reshape how Ebola outbreaks are assessed, the world had learned a difficult lesson: the virus does not always follow predictable patterns.

The now-famous 42-day rule emerged from those hard experiences. Because Ebola can take up to 21 days to develop after infection, international health experts adopted a waiting period of two complete incubation cycles before declaring an outbreak over. If no confirmed or probable case appears within that period after the last potential exposure, the chain of transmission is considered to have been broken.

The rule was forged during some of the deadliest Ebola epidemics in history, particularly the West African outbreak between 2014 and 2016, when countries that had celebrated the apparent end of transmission were later forced back into emergency response after fresh infections emerged weeks, and in some cases months, later.

Scientists eventually traced several of those flare-ups to survivors who continued carrying the virus long after recovery. Similar episodes were later documented in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, prompting the World Health Organization to strengthen its guidance on how outbreaks should be declared over.

In recommendations issued in 2020, WHO emphasised that declaring an Ebola outbreak over does not mean the virus has disappeared. Instead, it marks the transition into another phase of the response. Countries are advised to maintain enhanced surveillance for at least six months, continue programmes supporting Ebola survivors for at least 18 months and keep infection prevention measures in place because isolated flare-ups remain possible. WHO also encourages governments and the media to avoid describing countries as "Ebola-free," preferring language that says human-to-human transmission has been interrupted.

The distinction, health experts argue, helps avoid creating a false sense of security while reducing the risk of stigmatising survivors should isolated cases later reappear. Uganda says it fully observed those requirements. Officials confirmed that the outbreak was declared over only after the mandatory monitoring period had elapsed following the discharge of the last locally infected patient on June 16.

Interestingly, however, Dr. Baryomunsi had told the media on June 16 when the last Ebola patient was discharged from the Ebola Treatment Unit at Mulago National Referral Hospital, that Uganda had begun counting down the 42 days.

"Discharging the last patient does not mean that we are now Ebola-free," Dr Baryomunsi. "The international guidelines command us that when we discharge the last patient, then we start the countdown."

"The incubation period for Ebola disease is after 21 days, so we count two cycles of the intubation period. So, we start from now, the countdown, 21 days, then another 21 days, which makes it 42 days. So, if we don't register any positive case in that period, then Uganda will be declared Ebola-free."

Surveillance, Dr Baryomunsi insisted, would continue, border districts would remain on high alert and preparedness systems would stay in place while neighbouring eastern Congo continued battling its own epidemic. It remains unclear why the government then had a change of heart 12 days inside the countdown. Instead, when the government unilaterally declared the country Ebola-free, its experts chose to introduce a broader scientific proposition.

Has the science moved ahead?

Apparently, if the 42-day rule reflects decades of hard-earned experience, Ugandan health officials believe the science used to investigate Ebola outbreaks has moved on. Unlike the outbreaks that shaped international guidance, they argue, the 2026 epidemic began with something epidemiologists rarely enjoy: a clearly documented imported event.

The source of infection was identified. Investigators reconstructed every known chain of transmission. Every confirmed Ugandan case was linked to infected patients who had crossed the border from eastern Congo. All identified contacts completed follow-up without developing Ebola, while enhanced surveillance detected no evidence of undiagnosed community transmission.

For outbreak investigators, that level of certainty is unusual. In many epidemics, the greatest challenge lies in what cannot be seen. Patients may never be diagnosed. Contacts can be missed. The virus can continue spreading silently through communities before health authorities realise transmission is still occurring.

Technological advancement: A boon for Uganda?

Uganda argues that modern technology is changing that equation. Rapid molecular diagnostics now confirm infections within hours. Whole genome sequencing can establish how viruses from different patients are related. Digital surveillance systems allow contacts to be monitored in real time, while modern incident management systems combine laboratory findings with field investigations to produce a far more complete picture of an outbreak than was possible only a decade ago.

In its declaration ending the outbreak, the Ministry of Health argued that these advances provide "a level of epidemiological certainty that was not previously possible." The ministry stressed that the 42-day benchmark remains an essential safeguard where transmission is uncertain or ongoing. But it also suggested that, in exceptional circumstances, scientific evidence should carry greater weight alongside the passage of time..

Where an outbreak results from "a fully characterised imported event" and every chain of transmission has been conclusively mapped, officials argued, "a fixed time interval alone may no longer represent the only basis for determining that transmission has ended."

The argument is a careful one. Uganda, it appears, is not calling for the abandonment of the 42-day rule. Rather, it is asking whether advances in epidemiology should increasingly complement time-based criteria when determining that an outbreak has ended.

For now, international guidance remains unchanged. But Uganda's latest experience illustrates how improvements in science are beginning to challenge long-established public health practices. Whether that eventually leads to changes in global policy will depend not on one successful outbreak, but on evidence gathered from many more.

Victory comes with a warning

Even as Uganda celebrated, health officials repeatedly reminded the public that the danger had not disappeared. Across the country's western border, eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo remains in the grip of the largest Bundibugyo Ebola outbreak ever recorded. Thousands of infections have already been confirmed and transmission continues along transport corridors linking Ituri Province with Uganda and South Sudan.

That reality continues to shape Uganda's response after the declaration. Rather than scaling back operations, Kampala has shifted part of its attention into eastern Congo, supporting mobile laboratories, helping establish an 80-bed Ebola treatment unit and strengthening cross-border cooperation with Congolese health authorities.

Close 

"Although Uganda is now Ebola-free, our work does not stop here," Dr Chris Baryomunsi said as he announced the end of the outbreak. Surveillance, he said, will continue. Border districts will remain on high alert. Emergency preparedness systems will stay active because "the outbreak in the neighbouring DRC is still evolving."

In that respect, Uganda's approach closely mirrors WHO guidance. Although Kampala has suggested that advances in outbreak science should influence how exceptional outbreaks are assessed, it has not argued for weaker monitoring after an epidemic ends.

Instead, officials insist that surveillance, preparedness and cross-border cooperation remain essential long after transmission has been interrupted. That distinction is significant. Uganda did not declare the Great Lakes region free of Ebola. It declared that, based on the evidence gathered, human-to-human transmission inside Uganda had been interrupted. Whether that success endures will depend not only on what happens in Uganda's border districts but also on developments hundreds of kilometres away in Bunia and across Ituri Province.

A debate that has only begun

For now, life in Uganda is gradually returning to normal. Markets have reopened. Border communities are beginning to recover. Tourism operators hope international travel advisories will soon ease, restoring confidence in one of the countr"s most important economic sectors. Pilgrims who missed this year's Uganda Martyrs Day celebrations are already looking ahead to next year's commemoration.

History, however, may remember this outbreak for more than its modest size. Uganda has defeated Ebola before. This was, after all, its ninth outbreak. What made this one different was the question it raised. Can scientific advances eventually change one of global public health's longest-standing conventions? Or does a virus that has repeatedly humbled scientists still demand that caution remain the overriding principle?

The answers will not come from Uganda alone. International health guidance evolves slowly because changing global standards requires overwhelming evidence gathered across many outbreaks, countries and circumstances. Yet Uganda has opened a conversation that is unlikely to disappear.

As molecular diagnostics become faster, genome sequencing becomes routine and digital surveillance grows increasingly sophisticated, epidemiologists may eventually have to reconsider whether the calendar alone should remain the world's principal measure of certainty.

Until then, Uganda's latest Ebola outbreak stands as both a public health success and an invitation to debate. It demonstrates the value of decisive political leadership, transparent reporting, aggressive contact tracing and strong regional cooperation. It also highlights the economic costs that can accompany transparency in an interconnected world, where travel advisories and public perception often move faster than disease itself.

Perhaps that is the enduring legacy of Uganda's ninth Ebola outbreak. It reminds the world that defeating an epidemic is no longer simply about stopping a virus. It is also about understanding when science has advanced enough to challenge the rules that once defined victory. The outbreak may have ended on July 28. The debate it started has only just begun.

World.title: East Africa: Interpol Flags Kenya Among East Africa's Most Targeted Digital Economies
World.content:
Nairobi — Kenya's expanding digital economy is increasingly under threat from organised cybercriminals targeting mobile money services, telecommunications networks and government systems, according to the latest INTERPOL African Cyberthreat Assessment Report 2026.

The report paints a worrying picture of a rapidly evolving cyber threat landscape in East Africa, identifying Kenya as one of the region's most exposed countries due to its extensive use of mobile money and digital government services.

Among the key findings are more than 46,786 DDoS attacks against telecommunications networks in the first half of 2025, widespread intrusion attempts against government ICT systems and a sharp increase in phishing attacks.

INTERPOL also highlighted a 327 per cent rise in SIM-swap fraud investigations, with more than 123,000 fraudulent SIM cards detected and an estimated US$3.8 million stolen from mobile wallet users.

The international policing agency said criminals continue to exploit weaknesses in digital identity verification and inconsistent KYC procedures, enabling them to hijack phone numbers and access financial accounts.

It called on governments, regulators, financial institutions and telecommunications firms to strengthen cybersecurity frameworks and improve cross-border cooperation to counter increasingly sophisticated cybercrime.

World.title: Government-run grocery stores face renewed scrutiny after Chicago's experiment fizzles
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

The idea of government-run grocery stores is facing renewed scrutiny as Chicago abandons plans for a municipal supermarket, raising questions about whether taxpayer-funded markets can survive.

"Chicago's city-run grocery stores are on the brink of collapse after a Save A Lot terminated its licensing agreement with stores operated by Yellow Banana," Bryce Hill, director of Fiscal and Economic Analysis at Illinois Policy, told Fox News Digital on Tuesday.

"So the city spent $13.5 million on these stores, but now they're on the brink of closing. They were meant to address food security and availability in what the city deems food desks, but this outcome should really come as no surprise," Hill said.

EXPERTS SCORCH MAMDANI'S GROCERY PLAN AS AN 'ILLUSION' THAT WILL HAVE TAXPAYERS FOOTING THE BILL

Rob Karr, president & CEO of the Illinois Retail Merchants Association, told Fox News Digital Monday that the experiment is failing in multiple areas.

"So what we're seeing, particularly in New York and Seattle, are proposals to having the government actually artificially lowering prices by using their general revenue funds to make those groceries ‘more affordable,’ The state looked at that here in Illinois and dismissed it because it's inherently flawed," Karr said. "It has failed everywhere it has worked because it doesn't recognize the realities of the marketplace."

Chicago officials ultimately shifted away from opening a city-owned grocery store, opting instead to support privately operated neighborhood markets.

The Center Square reported Sunday that the closure of seven Save A Lot stores on Chicago's South and West sides has reignited questions about whether taxpayer-funded grocery initiatives can improve food access in low-income communities.

SNAP FOOD STAMP FRAUD HAS NEFARIOUS TERRORISM LINKS, TOP AGRICULTURE WATCHDOG WARNS CONGRESS

In the article, Nicole Huyer, a free-market policy analyst, said the closures underscore the shortcomings of government-backed solutions.

The outlet also reported that the stores, managed by retail platform Yellow Banana, closed after Save A Lot terminated its operating agreement with the company, pointing to financial challenges that included a significant decrease in SNAP purchases.

The Whole Foods in Chicago’s Englewood neighborhood, which closed in 2022, received a significant government subsidy, relying on an $11 million Tax Increment Financing (TIF) subsidy from the City of Chicago.

When it closed, local outlet WTTW reported that State Rep. Sonya Harper, D-CH, said in a statement that she was disappointed in the development, as the store had said its intention in opening to open was not about making a profit but about ensuring access to healthy food.

"I was proud to work with Whole Foods to bring a new location to Englewood because they claimed their decision was not based on profitability, but rather a desire to help provide access to healthy groceries for residents," Harper said in the statement.

STEVE FORBES: 4 WAYS TO FIX WHAT’S WRONG WITH NEW YORK CITY AND STOP THE EXODUS

Hill told Fox News Digital that the areas where government grocery stores are failing tend to not be friendly to business.

"Illinois and Chicago specifically is one of the toughest places to do business. So, Illinois has the second-highest property taxes in the nation," Hill said. "They're even higher in Chicago. Commercial property here is taxed at 250% more than residential property, which makes it tougher for businesses to operate."

"So, property taxes are out of control, which affect business margins as well," Hill added. "But on top of that, for consumers and for businesses, Chicago's total sales tax, which also applies to groceries, was just at an increase on August 1st. So the total sales rate in the city is now 10.5 percent. It's the second highest of any city in the nation. If the city's serious about helping businesses and residents in need, it should start there rather than wasting millions of dollars on projects that we know are going to fail."

Karr told Fox News Digital that cities should look at practical ways to make it easier for grocery stores to operate.

CHICAGO POL SAYS WALGREENS SHOULD BE CHARGED WITH 'FIRST-DEGREE CORPORATE ABANDONMENT' OVER CLOSURE OVER THEFT

"Instead of trying to use gimmicks, look at the real reasons why grocery stores are having a hard time staying open," Karr said.

"And frankly, the same applies to pharmacies," he added. "Although it's a little different because there's also pharmacy reimbursement at stake there. But when you look at grocery stores, what are your permitting processes? What are your licensing processes? What are your labor mandates? What's going on in your property tax? When you look at the city of Chicago and Cook County, we have the classification system where commercial and industrial carry two-thirds of the burden. That's a problem. You can't continue to pile those on and expect something to change."

Fox News Digital reached out to Yellow Banana and Whole Foods for comment.

World.title: Two brothers deliver storybook moment by homering in respective debuts on same day in incredible fashion
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

Aug. 4, 2026 is a day the Lombard family will remember for a long time.

Not one, but two brothers made their pro baseball debuts. George Lombard Jr. made his major league debut with the New York Yankees, while his younger brother, Jacob, made his professional debut in Low-A with the Miami Marlins organization.

Both brothers made debuts to remember, as they each blasted a home run with their new clubs.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE SPORTS COVERAGE ON FOXNEWS.COM

George Lombard Sr. and his wife, Judy, had flights booked to watch their youngest son, Jacob, make his pro debut in Jupiter. However, upon hearing news of Lombard Jr.’s promotion, Jacob insisted the family should see his older brother in the Bronx instead.

"We found out about 11:30 p.m. last night, so pretty late last night. And my mom was preparing, getting ready to drive up here to Jupiter. It's not too far of a drive from Miami, but my brother calls my dad, my mom and I on the FaceTime, like we kind of do every night, and he tells us the news and we were kind of all jaw-dropped," Jacob Lombard said during an appearance on ESPN’s "SportsCenter."

"My mom was freaking out. My dad is on the other side of the country in Seattle. I told my mom, ‘Don't even think about it. You're not coming over here to Jupiter. You're going to New York. All you guys are going to New York.’ I'm very happy that the whole family got to go out there and see him and they got to watch kind of my game play out."

George Lombard Sr. played in the major leagues for six seasons and is currently the Detroit Tigers bench coach. The team allowed him to leave and attend his son’s debut in person.

Jacob Lombard hit his home run first. In the top of the third inning, Lombard, in his second at-bat, pummeled a breaking ball into the visitors' bullpen for a solo home run for the Jupiter Hammerheads.

ZERO BS. JUST DAKICH. TAKE THE DON'T @ ME PODCAST ON THE ROAD. DOWNLOAD NOW!

The YES Network broadcast showed a jubilant George Lombard Sr. and Judy watching their youngest son’s home run on their phone and celebrating from their seats in Yankee Stadium.

George Lombard Jr.’s home run came in the fifth inning off St. Louis Cardinals starter Hunter Dobbins. Lombard Jr., also in his second at-bat, crushed an 0-2 breaking ball into the left-field seats, similar to where his younger brother hit his.

Beyond both brothers hitting home runs in their second at-bats of the game, there were other striking similarities to the blasts. Both home runs had 33-degree launch angles, and both had exit velocities about 100 mph. Jacob hit his home run at 99.9 mph, while George’s was 100.2 mph.

Jacob was able to watch his brother’s home run live, as the Hammerheads called a mound meeting and the Yankees’ game was on at the bar in the stadium. As he went to the mound, Lombard Jr. hit his home run, cementing a day for the ages.

"I'm screaming at third base like, 'I think he just hit home run. I think he just hit a home run.' And then the TV shows my parents hugging and I was like ‘Oh my, he just did that.’ So, it was pretty unbelievable."

YANKEES' GEORGE LOMBARD JR, REPLACING EMBATTLED ANTHONY VOLPE, MASHES HOME RUN FOR FIRST HIT IN MLB DEBUT

Both parents were emotional and proud of their sons.

"Just the fact that he's worked his whole life for this and that day had come, there was no words," Judy Lombard said in an interview on the YES Network. "For the first time in my life, I think, I didn't have words. I was just in shock."

"You don't ever get these days back," George Lombard Sr. said in an interview on the YES Network. "This was as emotional as any day we've had with our boys."

George Lombard Jr. said it was a day he won’t forget.

"It was really cool," the older Lombard said. "Being a close game, it was a big run. So it was probably a moment, a swing, a day I won’t forget."

The 21-year-old became the first Yankees shortstop to hit a home run in his debut. He was able to get the ball back when he met the fan who caught the ball after the game. Lombard Jr. traded a bat and signed hats for the fan in exchange for the ball.

TARIK SKUBAL'S DODGERS DEBUT ENDS IN DECISIVE 5-1 LOSS TO CUBS AS LA DROPS FIFTH STRAIGHT GAME

Lombard was the 14th player in franchise history to hit a home run in his big league debut and first since Jasson Domínguez went deep in his initial plate appearance against Justin Verlander in Houston on Sept. 1, 2023. The group also includes injured captain Aaron Judge (2016) and Hall of Famer Yogi Berra (1946).

At 21 years, 63 days old, Lombard became the sixth-youngest Yankees player since 1985 to make his debut and the second-youngest shortstop in that span. Derek Jeter debuted May 29, 1995, in Seattle at 20 years, 337 days.

Lombard Jr. also impressed with his defense, turning multiple slick double plays in the Yankees’ 2-0 win over the Cardinals.

"Obviously, a great first night for him," Yankees manager Aaron Boone said. "The home run was great. The defense was tremendous."

SIGN UP TO GET THE LATEST SPORTS NEWS

For Jacob Lombard, his brother’s major league debut is his goal.

"The whole goal is for me to also have that moment when, uh, you know, in a couple years. So, I'm excited. You know, they got to be there and I'm sure they're going to be at mine when mine comes," Lombard said.

If his minor league career is anything like his debut, it won’t be too long before the Marlins' 2026 first-round pick makes the major leagues, and the family can create another unforgettable memory.

World.title: Israeli President Herzog calls antisemitism a 'contamination of societies' as hate crimes surge
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

Israeli President Isaac Herzog issued a stern warning about the global spread of antisemitism in an exclusive interview with Fox News Digital at his Jerusalem residence.

"Antisemitism is an age-old plague which should be dealt with by everybody, by all societies. It's not an Israeli issue or only a Jewish issue," he said.

"It's a contamination of societies that starts with the Jew — never ends with them. It's the most dangerous phenomena that has to be dealt with aggressively, with no mercy, with full adjudication, and most importantly, with education," he added.

EXCLUSIVE: ISRAELI PRESIDENT HERZOG BLASTS MAMDANI, PRAISES TRUMP, SOUNDS ALARM ON IRAN

Herzog's warning comes as newly released New York City Police Department (NYPD) data show anti-Jewish incidents accounted for 56.9% of all confirmed hate crimes since the start of 2026, even though Jewish New Yorkers make up only about 10% of the city's population.

Herzog pointed to New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, whom he accused of spreading hate and compromising the lives of New Yorkers.

"Mamdani does not respect my nation's right for self-determination — the Jewish people's inherent right to have a nation of their own. And he's basically spreading blasphemy, hate, antisemitic rhetoric. He should understand that he's risking his own citizens, he’s risking their safety, well-being and life," Herzog told Fox News Digital.

In a video posted on social media on July 21, Mamdani called Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu "a war criminal" and "the architect of a horrific genocide against the Palestinian people."

Days later, Raul Morales, 51, allegedly yelled "Allahu Akbar" while stabbing two men on Manhattan's Upper West Side, including one who was visibly identifiable as Jewish.

SUSPECT ARRESTED AFTER ALLEGEDLY YELLING ‘ALLAHU AKBAR,' STABBING 2 MEN IN NYC ATTACK

"We've seen the stabbing just a few days ago ... just because somebody was dressed as an Orthodox Jew. This cannot be accepted in New York, which is a city that is dear to our heart, dear to Israelis, and dear to me personally," Herzog said.

More broadly, a report released last month by the J7 Large Communities' Task Force Against Antisemitism found that 20 people were killed in antisemitic attacks across seven countries outside Israel in 2025, marking the deadliest year for such violence in the Jewish diaspora since 1994.

The J7 comprises Jewish communities in the United States, Australia, Canada, Argentina, the United Kingdom, Germany and France.

According to the report, more than 23,000 antisemitic incidents were recorded across the J7 countries last year, representing a 97% increase in violent attacks and a 136% rise in overall incidents compared with 2022.

"Of course, Israel is doing its best, but it has to be an effort with governments all over the world, law enforcement agencies, educational systems and Jewish communities, which we care about a lot," Herzog said, in reference to confronting Jew-hatred.

Referencing a recent article by Prof. Niall Ferguson titled "The Death of History," he said, "How much TikTok or the social networks distort the facts of history? They negate the worst and greatest horror of humankind, the Holocaust. And that's why we have to stand up together and combat it," he told Fox News Digital.

Herzog stressed that misinformation spread through distorted and superficial channels makes it easy to smear Israel on social media, but that such narratives do not reflect reality.

There's a reason why Americans who visit our country, young Americans, fall in love with this country," he said.

Growing antisemitism, coupled with polarization within and between Jewish communities and a weakening sense of Jewish identity in some places, led Herzog to launch Voice of the People in April 2023. The initiative brings together a council of 150 emerging leaders — one-third from Israel, one-third from the United States and the remainder from around the world.

Leaders are selected through an algorithm from thousands of candidates and serve rotating terms of roughly two years, developing ideas to address challenges facing the Jewish world.

World.title: How 'Sopranos' star Vincent Pastore helped create the single greatest television season of all time
World.content:
Fans of the "Sopranos" are still reeling from the loss of beloved star Vincent Pastore over the weekend.

The veteran actor known for playing Salvatore "Big Pussy" Bonpensiero on the HBO crime drama was found dead in his Bronx home, and although he was only on the show for two seasons, his passing left a giant hole in the "Sopranos" community.

You can count me in as one of those fans who was particularly bummed to lose Pastore, because he contributed to what is perhaps the finest season of television that has ever been gifted to mankind.

RANKING THE MAJOR ANTAGONISTS OF 'THE SOPRANOS'

It's no secret that I love "The Sopranos," as a quick scroll through some of my work will yield a smattering of articles pontificating on every aspect of the show.

It's one of my favorite series of all time, and season two in particular represents what is, in my humble opinion, the apex of episodic television.

This is thanks in large part to Pastore's contributions as Tony Soprano's best friend and loyal soldier, Big Pussy.

Throughout most of season one, we are shown that Puss is Tony's confidant, even more so than his second-in-command, Silvio Dante.

Tony goes to Puss for advice about his son, among other things, showing the two have a connection that goes far beyond "the business."

But by the end of the first season, Puss is suspected to be an informant for the FBI, and before anyone from the Soprano crew can confirm their suspicions, he takes off for parts unknown, only setting off more alarm bells for Tony and company.

When he returns at the beginning of season two with an airtight alibi — going to Puerto Rico for acupuncture therapy to treat his ailing back — he has to re-earn the trust of his fellow crew members.

What makes Pussy's return unique, however, is that it is revealed early in the second season to the audience only that he's actually a rat, and the rest of the season is spent watching Tony subconsciously piecing together the evidence that his best friend is working with the feds to take him down.

It makes for riveting television the entire season, as we get several moments of tension as viewers know that Pussy has turned state's witness and could get whacked at any time.

Pussy's heel turn also gives us more insight into the FBI's inner workings, as the Bureau starts to become more of a main character thanks to the show focusing on his forced partnership with them.

This all culminates in the moment Tony finally figures it out, and the methods through which he arrives at the conclusion that his soldier is playing for the other team are some of the most creative and twisted in all of television.

In the penultimate episode of season two, Tony's biggest competition, Richie Aprile, gets taken out by his fiancée (Tony's sister Janice).

This happens right as Richie is about to make a move on Tony to take him out, so with one episode to wrap up the season, it appears as if all of Tony's worries are behind him.

Then we are reminded of the elephant — or in this case, rat — in the room.

After a late night meal at an Indian restaurant followed by a nightcap at the crew's favorite Italian restaurant, a season's worth of suspicions comes bubbling up for Tony in the form of a violent episode of food poisoning.

While deep in the throes of his intestinal Hell, Tony has a series of fever dreams that start out as subtle warnings and end up practically spelling it out for him.

"You know I've been working for the feds, right Ton'," a fish with Pussy's voice says to Tony.

It's so unique and brilliant, and I have no idea how the writers even came up with something like that, but it's easily my favorite hour of television ever made.

‘SOPRANOS’ STAR LORRAINE BRACCO SAYS SHE'S LOOKING FOR LOVE IN HER 70S

After that revelation, Tony and his crew take Pussy on a final, ill-fated boat ride where the compromised mobster cops to his crimes against the family before reminiscing on old times and sharing a final drink as Tony, Silvio, and Paulie draw their guns.

"You were like a brother to me. To all of us."

Before they have a chance to change their minds, the three heartbroken crew members unload their weapons into Pussy's chest and give him a burial at sea.

The episode and season end with a montage of all the destruction Tony and his crew have caused throughout the 13-episode run, interspersed with the mob boss enjoying the "fruits of his labor" at his daughter Meadow's high school graduation, blissfully unaware of (or unaffected by) the pain he's inflicted on his community.

The final shot lingers on the crashing waves of the North Jersey shoreline, reminding us of Pussy's ultimate fate, as the show fades to black while the haunting tones of The Rolling Stones' "Thru and Thru" play in the background.

It's perfect.

A perfect ending to a nearly perfect season of television.

And it's not just the Big Pussy storyline that makes season two must-watch TV, either.

The aforementioned Richie Aprile, played wonderfully by David Proval, makes for one of the most menacing villains of the series.

His back-and-forth with Tony throughout the season is equal parts hysterical and frightening, and he represents one of our protagonist's most formidable foes.

Season two also introduces another fan favorite to the cast in Furio Giunta, the native Italian who acts as Tony's enforcer and causes plenty of consternation between he and Pussy, as the latter (correctly) believes he is being replaced by the former.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE SPORTS COVERAGE ON FOXNEWS.COM

And I would be remiss if I didn't mention Tony's mother, Livia, who proves to be a bigger thorn in his side than even Richie at times throughout the show's run.

Nancy Marchand's turn as the morose, sociopathic matriarch of the Soprano family deserves special mention, particularly because she turned in such a masterful performance while battling the very cancer that would ultimately cost the actress her life shortly after season two wrapped.

"The Sopranos" would experience more highs throughout its six-ish season run, but none ever reached the zenith that was season two, in my opinion.

The writers are firing on all cylinders, the cast of characters is robust, and the plot lines are engaging enough to leave you begging for more at the end of each episode.

And none of it would have had the cultural impact it did if not for everyone's favorite FBI rat.

The world lost a legend in Vincent Pastore this past weekend, but his legacy lives on in perpetuity thanks to his turn as Salvatore Bonpensiero.

World.title: Progressive William Lawrence wins Democratic primary in one of the country’s biggest House races
World.content:
Democrat William Lawrence, a co-founder of the progressive Sunrise Movement, has won his party’s primary in Michigan’s 7th Congressional District, NBC News projects — a big victory for the insurgent left that also sets up a dramatic general election contrast with Republicans in a crucial battleground seat.

Voters in five states participated in primaries Tuesday, including several with major battleground districts up for grabs in November. And few are more hotly contested than this Michigan district, where Lawrence bested two prominent Democratic rivals with national security backgrounds after having differentiated himself as the more liberal candidate and as an aggressive critic of data centers.

Meanwhile, the battle between his two Democratic opponents, former Ambassador Bridget Brink and retired Navy SEAL Matt Maasdam, became increasingly bitter as the race drew to a close, and the two candidates ultimately appear to have split the more moderate wing of the party.

Lawrence will take on GOP Rep. Tom Barrett in one of the most tightly divided swing seats in the country. President Donald Trump carried the district by just 1 percentage point in 2024, and super PACs and other outside groups have reserved more ad spending there than in all but one other House race in the country.

Lawrence won support from an array of prominent progressives and outside groups, and a mysterious super PAC spent more than $1 million in the race’s final weeks to boost him and tear Maasdam down. The spending raised concerns among some Democrats that Republicans might be boosting Lawrence because they think he’ll be easier to beat in the general election.

Michigan voters are also cementing other key battleground House races Tuesday, albeit with less fanfare.

In Michigan’s 4th District, Republican Rep. Bill Huizenga will face off against Democratic state Sen. Sean McCann in the Kalamazoo-area district. Huizenga had Trump’s backing, while McCann was endorsed by top Democrats in the state like Gov. Gretchen Whitmer and Secretary of State Jocelyn Benson.

Republicans are still waiting to find out who will be their nominee against Democratic Rep. Kristen McDonald Rivet. And in the 10th District in suburban Detroit, which is being left open by GOP Rep. John James and his run for governor, Trump-endorsed military veteran Mike Bouchard will run against Democrat Christina Hines, a former special victims prosecutor.

In Virginia, the matchups are set in four districts expected to fit into the battleground puzzle in different ways this fall.

In the Norfolk area, Republican Rep. Jen Kiggans and Democratic former Rep. Elaine Luria head to a rematch of the 2022 2nd District election, which Kiggans won. In the Richmond-area 1st District, Republican Rep. Rob Wittman will face Henrico County Commonwealth’s Attorney Shannon Taylor in a district that could be competitive this fall — one that Trump won by 5 points in 2024.

Farther out on the battlefield, Democratic Rep. Eugene Vindman will face off against Republican Doug Ollivant, a retired Army lieutenant colonel, in the Fredericksburg-area 7th District, a race in which Vindman will start with a significant resource advantage. And Republican Rep. John McGuire will run against Democratic former Rep. Tom Perriello in a district Trump won by 12 points in 2024.

Missouri is home to one of Republicans’ best opportunities to gain a seat this fall after the GOP-controlled state Legislature redrew the congressional map to put Democratic Rep. Emanuel Cleaver into a seat Trump won by 18 points in 2024.

Republican Rick Brattin, a state senator backed by Gov. Mike Kehoe and the Club for Growth, is projected to win the nomination there, with Trump having weighed in for him in the race’s final days.

In Washington state, Republicans are targeting Democratic Rep. Marie Gluesenkamp Perez in a district Trump won by 3 points in 2024. She will face state Senate Republican leader John Braun, who has Trump’s endorsement, this fall.

Meanwhile, two Democratic incumbents faced serious primary challenges Tuesday. One, Rep. Wesley Bell of Missouri, is projected to win his primary, a rematch against former Rep. Cori Bush, whom he defeated in 2024. The other, Rep. Shri Thanedar of Michigan, is narrowly leading state Rep. Donavan McKinney in a race that has not yet been called.

Voters in a handful of safe seats are also picking nominees who are all but certain to win this fall.

In Michigan’s Oakland County, state Senate Democratic leader Jeremy Moss cruised to victory in Democratic Rep. Haley Stevens’ district, with Stevens running for the Senate.

In Missouri, Salem Radio Network host Chris Stigall won the Republican primary in the seat from which GOP Rep. Sam Graves is retiring.

And in Washington’s 4th District, Trump-backed Yakima County Commission member Amanda McKinney will move on to face retired Air Force Maj. John Duresky, a Democrat, in a red seat Trump won by about 20 points in 2024.

GOP Rep. Dan Newhouse, one of the last remaining House Republicans who voted to impeach Trump in 2021, is retiring.

World.title: Trump-backed John James wins Michigan’s GOP primary for governor
World.content:
Rep. John James has won Michigan’s Republican nomination for governor, NBC News projects.

James, who represents the Detroit suburbs, prevailed in the primary despite being vastly outspent by his opponent, wealthy businessman Perry Johnson.

President Donald Trump, despite harboring early concerns that a bid for higher office would put the two-term congressman’s competitive House district at risk, endorsed James and last week traveled to the state to campaign for him.

James, 45, will face Michigan Secretary of State Jocelyn Benson, the winner of Tuesday’s Democratic primary, this fall in one of the most fiercely contested battleground states. Term limits prevent Gov. Gretchen Whitmer, a Democrat, from seeking re-election.

An Army veteran who lost two Senate races before winning his House seat in 2022, James presented himself throughout the race as a capable public servant with applicable business experience, given his work with his family’s logistics company.

“This is an amazing state with all the great ingredients, but for the past seven-and-a-half years, under Gretchen Whitmer, we’ve been led to higher taxes, more crime on the roads — and frankly, the roads we have aren’t fixed yet,” James said during a televised debate last month, throwing back to Whitmer’s 2018 campaign vow to “fix the damn roads.”

“We’re going to work together to make sure that our children can read, to make sure that we put criminals in jail, and we hold those accountable who continue to let them back out,” James added. “And we’re going to be making sure that we come together to accomplish the mission of increasing hope and purpose with tested, positive leadership that has actually been tested from the battlefield to business to delivering for you right now.”

Johnson, 78, pounded the state with more than $31 million worth of ads, according to AdImpact, an ad-tracking firm. He drew on his work in quality control and improving business efficiencies while campaigning on a plan to eliminate the state’s income tax. Johnson also drew on his personal wealth, self-funding his run while declining political donations.

“In the state of Michigan, people are really tired of the politicians,” Johnson told NBC News in an interview last month. “I am an outsider. Nobody denies this fact. I’m the outsider of outsiders.”

James’ campaign spent a fraction on advertising — $2.8 million, according to AdImpact.

One potential factor in the results was the absence of former state Attorney General Mike Cox, who dropped out of the primary on July 17 and threw his support to James. Several polls had shown Cox grabbing a substantial share of the Republican vote and raised the possibility of an unpredictable three-way split that could have benefited Johnson.

Meanwhile, the general election challenge eased a bit for Democrats in May when former Detroit Mayor Mike Duggan ended his independent bid for governor. Duggan, a longtime Democrat, had expressed disappointment with both major political parties but caught attention — and grief — from Democrats who noted his reluctance to aggressively criticize Trump.

Michigan voters have not elected a Democrat to succeed a Democrat as governor in more than 65 years.

Benson deputy campaign manager Alyssa Bradley wrote in an email that the secretary of state “begins the general election with something no other candidate can claim: a record of delivering.”

An accompanying campaign memo took a parting shot at both Republican candidates for governor.

“John James and Perry Johnson spent this year lobbing personal attacks at each other and competing for Donald Trump’s attention, not talking to Michigan families about the cost of housing, healthcare, or keeping the lights on,” the memo read. “Both Republican candidates focused on election denying and Donald Trump, while Jocelyn has stayed focused on the issues affecting Michigan families every day.”

World.title: Rep. Wesley Bell defeats former Rep. Cori Bush in a Missouri Democratic primary rematch
World.content:
ST. LOUIS — Rep. Wesley Bell defeated former Rep. Cori Bush in a Democratic primary rematch, NBC News projects, in the latest chapter of a long-term fight over a deep-blue St. Louis-based district.

Bell overwhelmed Bush on the airwaves, fending off her push to make the race a referendum on his support for U.S. aid to Israel.

In total, Bell’s campaign and outside allies outspent Bush by a staggering 27-to-1 ratio, according to AdImpact, an ad-tracking service. United Democracy Project — the super PAC linked to the American Israel Public Affairs Committee, the pro-Israel advocacy group known as AIPAC — spent $2 million to support Bell, largely through negative ads attacking Bush. One such ad slammed Bush for being critical of former Vice President Kamala Harris.

It was a reference to Bush’s criticizing the Biden-Harris administration for supporting Israel amid what she deemed a genocide in Gaza. She endorsed Harris in the 2024 election.

As Bell cast his vote Tuesday, he criticized Bush for focusing on Israel and talking “over and over ... about an issue that is not impacting folks right here in St. Louis.”

“And while we take those issues seriously, you know, the M in Missouri doesn’t stand for Middle East,” Bell told NBC News. “It stands for Missouri.”

At a campaign stop later Tuesday, Bush hit back at Bell’s claims and said Missourians “are not happy” that he filled his “campaign coffers” with money from outside groups.

“Why are they meddling in our primaries?” she asked. “Why does he allow that?”

AIPAC loomed large in the race after it helped Bell oust Bush two years ago. United Democracy Project poured $9.3 million into ads in that primary, according to AdImpact, accounting for nearly half of the spending in the race.

Sidney Clark, a Democratic candidate for state representative currently serving in local government, said he supported Bell in 2024 but was voting for Bush this cycle because Bell, in his view, has “been paid for.”

“There are people out there who are using their money and financial influence to buy candidates, and I think that’s the wrong direction for our country,” Clark said after having voted at a St. Louis polling place.

Airest Wilson, another Democratic voter, told NBC News that candidates who take corporate money cross a red line for him — even if they are otherwise aligned with his political views.

“They don’t get that money for free,” he said. “You got to represent their interests. You can’t represent the constituents freely.”

“Cori, it took a lot of courage, but she rejected dark money. So that’s why I support Cori,” Wilson added.

This year, Bush ran two TV ads in the primary, each touching on multiple issues. But both linked Bell to AIPAC and cast him as more interested in sending money to Israel than Missourians, including those suffering from the aftermath of last year’s tornado.

Bell presented himself as a fighter against President Donald Trump, saying of Bush in one of his ads: “She fights Kamala Harris, Joe Biden and other Democrats.”

Bush said Tuesday that if she were to lose, it would not be a setback for the progressive movement.

“If there is a loss, then that just means that there is more work for us to do,” she said.

Asked whether she could see herself voting for Bell if he wins the primary, Bush told NBC News: “See myself voting for a Republican? Oh, I don’t think that’s on the ballot for me.”

World.title: Kansas voters reject GOP-backed measure to directly elect state Supreme Court justices
World.content:
Kansas voters have rejected a Republican-backed constitutional amendment that would have allowed them to directly elect state Supreme Court justices, The Associated Press projects.

In Kansas, the governor — who since 2019 has been Democrat Laura Kelly — has the power to appoint state Supreme Court justices, chosen from a list created by a nine-member nonpartisan commission. The measure on Tuesday’s ballot, which was referred by the GOP-controlled Legislature, proposed abolishing that system in favor of contests that would have more closely resembled partisan races for other elected offices.

The move came after the Kansas Supreme Court dealt conservatives some setbacks in recent years, including a 2019 ruling that the state constitution protected the right to an abortion. Voters sided with that decision three years later after the U.S. Supreme Court overturned Roe v. Wade.

Tuesday’s ballot measure campaign drew more than $12 million in spending on the airwaves, according to the tracking firm AdImpact, with opponents outspending supporters by more than 2-to-1.

Opponents of the initiative argued that Kansas voters already have some say in who their state Supreme Court justices are: After they are appointed, justices face retention votes from voters after one year and then every six years afterward.

Another core part of their message was keeping the judicial process separate from electoral politics to avoid partisan influences. In Wisconsin, for instance, recent state Supreme Court elections — which are nonpartisan in name only — have drawn tens of millions of dollars and attention from billionaire donors like Elon Musk.

“‘No’ stops judges from becoming politicians. ‘No’ prevents billionaires from buying seats on the court,” a narrator said in an ad from Kansas United for Impartial Courts, one of two major groups that opposed the ballot measure.

Supporters of the effort argued that voters should have more input in the process. According to the Brennan Center for Justice at New York University School of Law, voters in 21 states directly elect supreme court justices.

In a spot run by the biggest spender on the pro-amendment side — a group called Kansans for Democracy Inc. — a narrator criticizes the current commission system, ripping “elites” for getting to “decide who’s on the Kansas Supreme Court, behind closed doors, trading favors, rewarding friends.”

“The public can’t see it or control it. Voters like you completely cut out,” the narrator adds.

While none of the ads from either side mention abortion rights or other hot-button political issues that state supreme courts tend to rule on, Democratic operatives in Kansas told NBC News that the intent of the measure was clear.

They noted that as far back as 2019, state Attorney General Kris Kobach, formerly Kansas’ secretary of state, had called on the Legislature to advance a ballot measure to pave the way for the direct election of Supreme Court justices. In 2022, Kobach told The Wichita Eagle that such a move would allow, “slowly and quietly,” for anti-abortion justices to be placed on the court.

“This is about abortion,” Kansas Democratic Party Chair Jeanna Repass said in an interview ahead of Tuesday’s vote. “Plain and simple.”

Progressives also argued that Republicans chose to put the measure on the August primary ballot, rather than on the one for the November general election, to take advantage of lower voter turnout.

World.title: Missouri voters block GOP-led effort to raise bar to pass constitutional amendments
World.content:
Missouri voters blocked a Republican-led effort to raise the bar for passing citizen-led constitutional amendments, NBC News projects.

Under current state law, such ballot measures require a simple statewide majority for passage, a process that has been used in recent years to grant abortion rights, expand Medicaid and legalize marijuana.

But Amendment 4 would have required citizen-led ballot initiatives to win a majority in each of Missouri’s congressional districts, boundaries that are drawn by state lawmakers. Other ballot measures, like those referred from the Legislature, would not have been subject to this higher bar.

It would have created “the strictest passage threshold in the country for citizen-initiated ballot measures only,” according to Hannah Ledford, the deputy director of the Fairness Project, a group that supports citizen initiative processes. She added it could have left Missouri’s direct democracy process “functionally dead.”

Missouri is one of 26 states that allows voters to legislate directly by petitioning to place a constitutional amendment on the ballot.

The amendment was first proposed by Republican state Rep. Ed Lewis, after Missouri voters used the method to advance a spate of progressive priorities in a state where the GOP has full control of government. Many recent amendments would have failed under the stricter standard proposed by Amendment 4.

“This amendment is really an amendment to protect our Constitution,” Lewis said on a radio program earlier this month. “We have the absolute lowest and weakest process and that’s why we’ve had six initiative petitions passed in the last eight years that have really done real harm to our state and to our Constitution.”

The state’s Republican-controlled Legislature has repealed or limited some changes made through ballot initiatives, including repealing paid sick leave.

Opponents of the proposal heavily outspent its supporters, pouring more than $6 million into broadcast ads, according to data from the tracking firm AdImpact. The measure’s backers did not air any broadcast ads, AdImpact’s data shows.

The more-moneyed campaign against Amendment 5, a proposal to end income taxes and expand sales taxes, also included arguments against Amendment 4 in their ads.

The effort to change the constitutional amendment process also came after Republican lawmakers redrew the state’s congressional map last year to carve up the lone Democratic-held district. Earlier Tuesday, Missouri Secretary of State Denny Hoskins said that a referendum that sought to undo the new map would not appear on the state’s ballot, arguing the effort was unconstitutional.

Missouri isn’t the only state where Republicans have sought to make it more difficult for citizen-led constitutional amendments to pass. In November, North Dakota and South Dakota voters will decide whether to bump the threshold up from a statewide majority to 60%. And in Utah, there will be a similar measure on the fall ballot specifically related to tax increases.

World.title: Cyclosporiasis outbreak has expanded to six more states
World.content:
A massive cyclosporiasis outbreak linked to shredded iceberg lettuce has expanded to an additional six states, according to a source familiar with the matter.

The outbreak, caused by a microscopic parasite found in human feces, is responsible for hundreds of hospitalizations and two deaths since early May.

The newly linked states — Arkansas, Iowa, Missouri, Nebraska, New Hampshire and North Carolina — join Illinois, Indiana, Kansas, Kentucky, Michigan, Ohio, Oklahoma, Pennsylvania and West Virginia, said the source, who spoke on the condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to speak publicly. The Missouri Department of Health and Senior Services has reported 1,095 cases as of Sunday — nearly double the number of cases it reported last week.

The agency’s update marks a significant expansion in the outbreak of cyclosporiasis, a foodborne illness that often leads to watery, sometimes explosive, diarrhea.

The additional states, however, do not necessarily mean the outbreak is continuing to spread, said Dr. Stephen Ostroff, a former acting Food and Drug Administration commissioner.

The majority of the cases have been traced to lettuce at Taco Bell that was supplied by Taylor Farms and sourced from central Mexico. Last month, the produce giant issued a voluntary recall of all iceberg lettuce supplied from central Mexico, which the company said was distributed to restaurants and retail stores in 27 states.

The FDA hasn’t yet identified other potential sources beyond Taylor Farms.

The newly linked cases, Ostroff said, may involve people who ate the recalled lettuce weeks ago but were only recently diagnosed and reported to health officials.

“With an incubation period up to two weeks, there should no longer be people newly getting sick from that product,” Ostroff said. “But it takes a while for people to seek health care after onset, get tested and diagnosed, reported to state health departments and then to CDC.”

“Think of it like solving a jigsaw puzzle,” he added. “You have all these pieces sitting there, and the longer you work on it, the more likely it is you’ll figure out where each piece fits into the puzzle.”

More than 22,000 people have confirmed or suspected cyclosporiasis, and 517 people have been hospitalized in the multistate outbreak, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention said late Tuesday.

On Monday, health officials in Michigan — which has the most cyclosporiasis cases — confirmed the first deaths linked to this outbreak in the United States. Both people had underlying health conditions that may have been affected by the illness and dehydration, the officials said.

Ostroff said the key question about the newly added states is when their patients became sick.

The recalled Taylor Farms lettuce should no longer be available in the U.S., and its use-by dates ended Aug. 3, Ostroff said. If people were exposed after that, investigators may need to look for another source.

“We may have solved the Taylor Farms shredded lettuce piece, but that’s unlikely to explain everything we’re seeing,” he said.

World.title: John James wins Michigan Republican gubernatorial primary, CBS News projects
World.content:
U.S. Rep. John James, endorsed by President Trump, is projected to be the winner of Tuesday's Republican gubernatorial primary race in Michigan, according to CBS News.

As of 10:47 p.m., unofficial results showed that James was leading with 155,109 votes to businessman Perry Johnson's 111,942.

James will go head-to-head against Michigan Secretary of State Jocelyn Benson, who won the Democratic primary race.

The candidates

U.S. Rep. John James announced in April 2025 that he was running for governor.

James served as an aviation officer in the U.S. Army for eight years and was president of a supply chain and logistics solutions group. He lost U.S. Senate races in 2018 and 2020 to incumbents Debbie Stabenow and Gary Peters. He faced Democrat Carl Marlinga twice in the 2022 and 2024 elections, beating him in both.

His decision to run as governor leaves Michigan's 10th Congressional seat up for grabs. "But we all know that having a strong top of ticket is the greatest indicator that we'll have success for Republicans up and down the ticket," James said.

James has picked up a key endorsement from President Trump in the race, an announcement that led to former Michigan Attorney General Mike Cox dropping out of the primary. James also was endorsed by Rep. Aric Nesbitt, who suspended his campaign in June.

Johnson, a businessman who made his career in the American auto industry, announced in January 2026 that he is running for governor.

He ran in 2022 for the Michigan governor's seat, but was disqualified over invalid petition signatures. Johnson was also a 2024 presidential candidate, but failed to qualify for the GOP presidential debate series.

"My business experience brought quality and efficiency to help save the auto industry. We can deliver better services at lower cost by running state government with efficiency, accountability, and a results-driven mindset," he said.

Key issues

While in Congress, James focused on national security, energy independence, and supporting law enforcement.

An issue that he has recently taken on is the Canadian wildfire smoke that plagued Michigan this summer, resulting in several days of statewide air quality alerts. He is among a group of lawmakers who have called on Canadian officials to take action to limit the impact of wildfires.

If he becomes governor, he says he would put attention to protecting and preserving Michigan's water, land and air. "We absolutely need to make sure that we are resilient for extreme weather, and making sure that we're doing that in all seasons," he said.

Johnson's platform includes eliminating Michigan's state income tax. He said that by eliminating the state income tax, a typical family would keep about $4,747 a year. To make a budget work with such a dramatic drop in revenue, Johnson said he would audit state government spending to determine where the funding yields the intended returns and focus on efficiency. He also wants to reform property taxes.

Johnson is self-funding his campaign with his own wealth, but said he remembered his younger years living with little to no money. "When you've been there, and you've been in that kind of environment, you have an entirely different perspective," he said.

World.title: Benson wins Michigan Democratic gubernatorial primary, CBS News projects
World.content:
Michigan Secretary of State Jocelyn Benson is projected to be the winner of Tuesday's Democratic gubernatorial primary race, according to CBS News.

As of 9 p.m., unofficial results show that Benson was winning with 211,877 votes over Genesee County Sheriff Chris Swanson's 38,439 votes. At that time, 17% of the votes had been counted.

Benson would go head-to-head against Congressman John James, who won the Republican primary.

Democratic Governors Association Chair Andy Beshear released the following statement:

"Congratulations to Secretary of State Jocelyn Benson on becoming the Democratic nominee for governor in Michigan. Jocelyn understands the challenges families are facing, and she has been a fearless public servant who fixes broken systems and improves the lives of Michiganders. "As Secretary of State, she kept her promises and transformed one of Michigan's largest departments into one that saved people time, increased transparency, and defended our democracy against relentless attacks. As governor, Jocelyn will tackle corruption, lower the costs of health care, housing, and energy, and always stand up to Donald Trump when he threatens Michigan families and their freedoms. "She's already earned the trust of Michiganders by winning statewide twice, and the DGA will be all-in to make sure she wins this high-stakes race so she can keep standing up for the people of Michigan."

Democratic National Convention Chair Ken Martin released the following statement:

"Congratulations to Jocelyn Benson on earning the Democratic nomination to be the next governor of Michigan. As Michigan's Secretary of State, Jocelyn has dedicated her career to serving the people of Michigan, protecting the right to vote, and delivering results for families across the state. Her record of leadership has earned the trust of Michigan voters, and Democrats are united behind her as we work together to lower prices, protect healthcare, and build on our progress in order to keep Michigan moving forward."

The candidates

Benson was elected in 2018 and oversees the state's election processes and the motor vehicle department. She cited her achievements in that role, including decreasing wait times for in-person appointments and installing self-service motor vehicle stations across the state.

Benson's campaign promises include bringing accountability and transparency to state government, and working on behalf of the state's families with a "progressive vision for Michigan's future."

She has been critical of President Trump, who has repeatedly made claims of voter fraud during the 2020 election.

Benson has also faced lawsuits in recent months ahead of the election. In January 2026, four Black employees sued the Michigan Secretary of State, alleging racial discrimination in the workplace.

In May 2025, Michigan Attorney General Dana Nessel said Benson violated state law by hosting a campaign press conference in a state building's lobby. At the time, Benson said she didn't want people outside in the cold.

Swanson was elected sheriff of Michigan's fifth-largest county in 2020. His announcement that he would run for governor marked his full leap into politics after gaining national attention for marching with protesters following the death of George Floyd and speaking at the Democratic National Convention in 2024.

At the protest in Flint, Swanson removed his riot gear and marched alongside demonstrators.

Swanson attended Mott Community College in Flint and the University of Michigan, earning bachelor's and master's degrees in public administration, according to his website.

Key issues

The key issues highlighted in Benson's campaign include housing and affordability, healthcare, childcare, energy costs, and the development of renewable energy infrastructure. Benson also focuses on data centers, which have drawn attention in Southeast Michigan amid protests by several residents.

While Benson is not opposed to data centers coming to Michigan, she argues that they should bring jobs and low energy costs for residents, according to her website. She also pushed for public hearings on data centers to allow residents to express their concerns.

Swanson focuses on a cannabis protection plan, a pet protection plan and expanding the I.G.N.I.T.E. program in jails, according to his campaign website. The program, which he launched in Genesee County in 2020, aims to reduce reincarcerations through educational training. Swanson also pushes for funding to support school infrastructure such as bulletproof glass, metal detectors and single entry points to protect students and staff in the event of a school shooting.

Other issues that Swanson is prioritizing include reducing FOIA exemptions for government officials, economic growth and a seven-point education plan that consists of free breakfast and lunch for all Michigan students and addressing literacy.

World.title: McKinney defeats Thanedar in Michigan's 13th Congressional District primary
World.content:
State Rep. Donavan McKinney has defeated incumbent U.S. Rep. Shri Thanedar in Michigan's 13th Congressional District, CBS News projects.

The two Democrats both hold strong progressive policy viewpoints but differ in their backgrounds and values ahead of the Democratic primary.

Thanedar, who is finishing up his second term in Congress, was largely self-funding his campaign. He was elected to Congress in 2022 after winning the nine-way primary with 28.3% of the votes. McKinney, a member of the Democratic Socialists of America, ran on a platform centered on relatability and everyday people.

The candidates

Thanedar was first elected to Congress in 2022 and was reelected in 2024 after winning the Democratic primary against Mary Walters with 54.9% of the vote.

Thanedar represented Detroit in the Michigan House of Representatives from 2021 to 2023. He was born to a poor family in India and immigrated to the U.S. to pursue his Ph.D. in chemistry in 1979. Starting from nothing, he eventually worked his way up to serve as the CEO of numerous multi-million-dollar pharmaceutical development companies.

Thanedar is a vocal critic of President Trump, having introduced articles of impeachment against him in April 2025.

Thanedar's endorsements include those from his congressional colleagues, including House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries, U.S. Rep. Judy Chu and U.S. Rep. Bennie Thompson.

Throughout his political career, Thanedar has faced criticism for accepting corporate PAC money and spending taxpayer money on advertising. He renounced his Democratic Socialists of America membership in October 2023, citing their failure to condemn Hamas' terrorist attacks on Israel.

McKinney is a lifelong Detroiter who's running on a platform centered on relatability and focusing on everyday people. A product of Detroit Public Schools, McKinney graduated from the University of Michigan in 2014 before pursuing a career in organizing and public service.

McKinney has received high-profile endorsements from Congressional progressives, including U.S. Senator Bernie Sanders, U.S. Rep. Rashida Tlaib, U.S. Rep. Ilhan Omar and former U.S. Rep. Brenda Lawrence.

Key issues

The key issues highlighted in Thanedar's campaign include affordability, housing, universal healthcare and abolishing ICE. He has co-sponsored progressive legislation, including the Medicare for All Act, Raise the Wage Act and American Teacher Act, as well as pro-small business legislation such as the Investing in Main Street Act of 2023.

This is Thanedar's toughest primary yet, as opponents and colleagues criticize his lack of Detroit roots and his identity as a wealthy businessman who has spent millions on his campaign while representing Michigan's poorest district.

McKinney's campaign touches on restoring Black representation in Detroit and putting workers over corporations. His platform has goals of reducing income inequality through taxing the ultra-wealthy, transitioning to clean energy and investing in public schools. Like Thanedar, McKinney also supports Medicare for All.

Other issues McKinney is prioritizing include reducing corporate influence in politics, codifying abortion rights at the federal level and ending military aid to Israel.

World.title: Record-low Danube River levels threaten shutdown of Hungary's nuclear plant
World.content:
As the Danube River breaks new record lows across much of its nearly 1,800-mile stretch through eastern Europe, curiosities of the past — including woolly mammoth bones in Bulgaria, sunken Nazi warships in Serbia and unexploded WWII artillery in Hungary's capital — are emerging. But there's also an energy crisis unfolding for Hungary's nearly 10 million people.

The country's only nuclear power plant, known as Paks, is on the brink of completely shutting down. As of Wednesday morning, three of the plant's four reactors are not in operation, while one continues to operate at approximately 50% power.

On normal days, the 44-year-old Soviet-designed facility, which sits on the Danube about 60 miles south of Budapest, generates roughly 50% of the country's electricity.

But with a drought across southeast Europe now more than three months in, these are not normal days.

A view of the Paks Power Plant on July 31, 2026, in Dunaszentbenedek, Hungary. Janos Kummer / Getty Images

Unlike nuclear plants in the U.S., U.K., Germany and France — many of which sit on smaller rivers and rely on giant hourglass-shaped cooling towers to recirculate water — Paks was built to suck water in directly from the Danube, a river long assumed too mighty to run dry. Approaching the plant, there are no telltale dumb-bell silhouettes on the horizon signaling its presence.

"Several factors will determine whether Hungary's most important power plant can avoid a complete shutdown in the coming days," said Hungarian Prime Minister Péter Magyar, visiting the site Tuesday, attempting to balance reality while projecting optimism.

Just three months into office after his Tisza party ended Viktor Orbán's 16-year rule in a landslide election this spring, Magyar has called on all Hungarians to unite to conserve power.

Hardly any precipitation is forecast for at least the next 10 days and the Danube's water levels are expected to slip even lower.

"There are a few critical days left. Today and tomorrow are certainly that," Magyar said. "I ask everyone to continue the national unity that has developed in the country. Let's do what our country demands."

Magyar noted there is "light at the end of the tunnel," as forecasters predict a cold front moving in on Friday. The temperature in Budapest Wednesday and Thursday was expected to be above 100 degrees Fahrenheit.

The anxiety over Paks, Hungary's most critical piece of infrastructure, is the first real test of Magyar's young government.

This week, more than 300 government-linked buildings in Budapest have been ordered to turn off their lights, with the romantic spotlights on popular tourist hotspots like Buda Castle and the Chain Bridge staying dark after the late-summer sunsets.

To offset the loss of power generation, Hungary has nearly doubled its electricity imports from neighboring countries via the region's power grid, news site Euractiv reported. Hungary's electricity network is among Europe's most interconnected, letting the country easily buy power from its neighbors. Costs have not hit consumers yet as the new government absorbs the difference for now.

"The electricity market is stable, and supply is problem-free," the government said, while urging households to avoid running washing machines and tumble dryers between 5 and 10 p.m. to ease pressure on the grid.

Europe is the world's fastest-warming continent, warming more than twice as fast as the global average, according to Copernicus, the European Union's Earth observation and climate monitoring group.

The continent has warmed by around 4.5 degrees Fahrenheit compared to pre-industrial levels, with the fastest warming areas in eastern and parts of central Europe, as well as the European Arctic.
