World.title: B.C. wildfire conditions 'explosive and extremely dangerous' as crews brace for more heat, dry lightning
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The latest on the wildfires:

The Pear Lake wildfire is the largest burning in B.C. right now, at roughly 1,247 square kilometres. The Thompson-Nicola Regional District says about 120 properties , not including the Village of Clinton, have suffered structural loss.

, not including the Village of Clinton, have suffered structural loss. The chief of the Okanagan Indian Band estimates at least 200 homes have been destroyed by the Bradley Creek wildfire, west of Vernon. It's grown to roughly 28.5 square kilometers.

by the Bradley Creek wildfire, west of Vernon. It's grown to The Regional District of Northern Okanagan expanded an evacuation order on Tuesday, due to the Bradley Creek and Quilpituk Creek wildfires, to include several dozen more properties.

on Tuesday, due to the Bradley Creek and Quilpituk Creek wildfires, to include several dozen more properties. Across B.C., about 8,000 people are under evacuation order and 7,100 are under evacuation alert.

Wildfire officials say conditions are "explosive and extremely dangerous," with a forecast of hot temperatures and potential lightning ahead.

Hotter weather returns

The period of cooler, more humid weather that provided some relief for crews battling the Pear Lake wildfire has come to an end, according to the B.C. Wildfire Service (BCWS).

It says hotter, drier conditions have returned and are expected to increase fire activity in the coming days.

In the southern Interior, temperatures are expected to hit the mid-30s this week, with the possibility of dry lightning.

Last weekend, wildfire crews battled the Bradley Creek fire burning near Vernon amid 80 km/h winds, with gusts reaching 115 km/h at higher elevations.

"We are seeing fuel conditions that we have never seen before. We are seeing fire behaviour and fire growth that we have never experienced in B.C. up until this point," said BCWS director of wildfire operations Cliff Chapman.

"It is an explosive and extremely dangerous situation."

Damage count

Officials say hundreds of properties have been damaged or destroyed in multiple parts of the province.

The Thompson-Nicola Regional District says about 120 properties have experienced structure loss from the Pear Lake wildfire, excluding the Village of Clinton.

The hardest-hit places include Big Bar Lake, south of Clinton near Highway 97, an area west of Clinton around Kelly Lake Road and the Chasm area north of the village.

The Wait Creek wildfire is seen from above on Monday, Aug. 3. (B.C. Wildfire Service)

District spokesperson Clinton Davies said the number will likely increase as crews safely reach more affected areas.

West of Vernon, Okanagan Indian Band Chief Dan Wilson estimates the Bradley Creek wildfire has destroyed at least 200 homes, though the figure is preliminary.

He said the fire has been “one of the most devastating events in our history," and many people in the community have lost everything they own.

Evacuation orders

About 8,000 people across B.C. are under evacuation order, while another 7,100 are under evacuation alert and have been told to be ready to leave at a moment’s notice.

Many of those impacted are being threatened by the Quilpituk Creek and Bradley Creek wildfires, both burning along Okanagan Lake.

The Central Okanagan Emergency Operations Centre says 2,223 properties remain under evacuation order due to the Quilpituk Creek fire, while another 425 properties are under evacuation alert.

The Regional District of Northern Okanagan expanded an evacuation order on Tuesday, as a result of both fires, to include several dozen more properties.

Evacuation orders also cover the Okanagan Indian Band.

The Spallumcheen evacuation order and alert areas related to the Bradley Creek fire were shrunken on Tuesday.

A map showing the expanded evacuation order for the Bradley Creek and Quilpituk Creek wildfires as of Aug. 4. (Regional District of North Okanagan)

Those in need of emergency support services are being directed to the Westbank Lions Community Centre in West Kelowna and Kal Tire Place in Vernon.

Evacuation orders remain in effect for the French Bar Creek fire in the Thompson-Nicola Regional District, the Pear Lake fire near Clinton and the Brunswick fire complex near Boston Bar.

In the East Kootenay, an evacuation order was partially downgraded to an alert on Sunday after crews made progress on the Wait Creek wildfire.

Road closures

According to DriveSafeBC, several major routes remain closed because of wildfire activity.

Highway 1 is closed between Toll Road and Jackass Summit, north of Hells Gate, because of the Brunswick wildfire complex. Drivers are being directed to use highways 3 or 5.

Further north, just past Cache Creek, Highway 97 is closed between Loon Lake Road and 76 Mile Frontage Road. Traffic is being detoured using highways 5 and 8, through Merritt.

Westside Road along Okanagan Lake is closed between Shelter Cove and Highway 97 north, cutting off a key route. The road is open as far as Shelter Cove, with Highway 97 serving as the alternate route.

Toward the U.S. border, Silver Skagit Road is closed south of Flood Hope Road to the Canada-U.S. border because of the Hozomeen Mountain wildfire. Silver Lake remains open, but Ross Lake Campground and Skagit Valley Provincial Park are closed.

World.title: 'Everyone's in a super great mood': Dozens line up to cross Gordie Howe bridge for 1st time on bike, by foot
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Some cyclists and pedestrians said they were “excited” and “overwhelmed” as they crossed the Gordie Howe International Bridge for the first time, using the new multi-use path Wednesday morning.

The path opened at 8 a.m. ET, allowing people to walk or cycle across the bridge linking Windsor, Ont., and Detroit.

“This is a historic moment,” said cyclist Collin Vassell, who crossed from the Canadian side with his wife, Kim.

“Who's going to be able to say that they … rode their bike across the bridge on the ... first day that it was open? Like, seriously.… I was actually overwhelmed with some emotions doing this experience with my wife.”

Cyclists and pedestrians had been unable to cross a bridge between Windsor and Detroit since they were barred from doing so on the Ambassador Bridge decades ago.

On Wednesday morning, people snapped photographs in front of the Canadian and American flags on the path, and vehicles honked their horns as they passed.

'Everyone's in a super great mood'

Canada Border Services Agency (CBSA) mascot Buddy the Bear also made an appearance.

Kevin Hinman, who crossed from Detroit with his wife Sophie, said the bridge was less crowded than he expected, so the journey was pleasant.

“Everyone's in a super great mood — got a lot of 'Good mornings' and 'Hellos.'”

Mondrell Pickens, who crossed with 13 other family members, some pushing strollers, said they wanted to make a memory together that they could pass down to their children.

Collin Vassall said he was overcome with emotion as he crossed the Gordie Howe International Bridge by bicycle on Aug. 5, 2026. (Peter Duck/CBC)

“We all wanted to do it together,” he said.

“Something to remember for the rest of our lives, that we all … walked on this bridge when it first was built in Canada.”

Around 100 people were lined up at the Canadian entrance to the path as the gate opened; they were separated from the roadway by yellow tape stretched between orange stanchions.

Among them was Kevin Keeper, dressed in a T-shirt with Canadian and American flags on it. He was hoping to become the first American to cross from the Canadian side.

“I’m just overcome with emotion,” Keeper told CBC.

“It's just so exciting to be here as part of the very first morning and on a sunny day here in beautiful Windsor.”

400 cyclists preparing to cycle from Detroit

The Windsor-Detroit Bridge Authority (WDBA) set up porta-potties outside the entrance to the Canadian side of the path for the day.

It also had a covered booth with balloons on hand and bridge merchandise for sale.

On the Detroit side of the river, 400 members of the Gordie Howe International Bike Club were preparing to cross the bridge at 10:15 a.m., organizer Amanda Ray told CBC’s Windsor Morning.

The group hopes to make additional crossings at 1:30 and 6 p.m.

The CBC's Emma Loop crosses the Gordie Howe International Bridge on foot | Duration 2:54 The CBC's Emma Loop walks across the Gordie Howe International Bridge on foot as the bridge's multi-use path opens on Aug. 5, 2026.

Ray said the goal of the group is to create friendships and connections across the bridge.

“I feel like we have more in common with the Canadians and people that live in Windsor than we do necessarily with people that live in Nebraska."

The WDBA is asking people to be patient as they wait their turn to cross the bridge.

“With the anticipated high number of path users, expect line-ups entering the path and line-ups at border processing,” it wrote on its website.

“WDBA is limiting the number of people that can be on the path at any one time over the initial opening days to support smooth operations.”

The bridge authority estimates it will take people approximately 45 minutes to make the three-kilometre trek on foot from one border inspection booth to the other.

WATCH | Dozens line up to cross Gordie Howe International Bridge on foot or by bike: Dozens line up to cross the Gordie Howe International Bridge on foot or by bike | Duration 4:01 Dozens lined up to cross the Gordie Howe International Bridge on foot or by bike Wednesday morning as the bridge's multi-use path opened to the public.

It estimates the same trip will take around 20 minutes by bike.

There is a posted speed limit on the path of 20 km/h.

Both the bridge authority and the CBSA are reminding people to bring their travel documents onto the bridge even if they aren’t planning to cross into the United States.

Path users who return to the Canadian side of the bridge will have to report to the CBSA before exiting, the agency said, and people without proper documentation could be held up while officials try to verify their identity and status.

The bridge authority is also reminding people there is no on-site parking at either port of entry. It's advising people to park at the Malden Park trailhead in Windsor or the Clark Park trailhead in Detroit.

World.title: Lloyd Robertson dead at 92: Peers and friends pay tribute to iconic broadcaster's career
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Lloyd Robertson, who delivered the news to Canadians in an authoritative and unflappable manner for more than 40 years as anchor for the flagship news programs of CTV and CBC, has died. He was 92.

His death was first reported by CTV and was confirmed by a family member to CBC News.

Robertson stepped away as CTV National News anchor in 2011 after 35 years, having joined the network in a move from CBC that reshaped Canadian broadcast news. He had been anchor of CBC's The National for six years.

"Someone came along with this … on my terms, in my life at precisely the right moment, and it was irresistible. I couldn't turn it down," he told CBC's Take 30 in 1976, days after accepting the offer.

At CTV, Robertson helped lead coverage of 11 federal elections, three Canadian-hosted Olympic Games and two Quebec referendums, as well as tragedies like the 1985 Air India bombing, 1989 Montreal massacre and the Sept. 11 attacks. He also helped share inspiring stories such as Terry Fox's Marathon of Hope.

WATCH | Robertson announces retirement: Lloyd Robertson retires | Duration 3:50 CTV anchor stepping down after decades-long career, including 22 years at CBC

Robertson frequently spoke of enjoying being at the centre of attention for events shaping Canada and the world, but his on-air style was once accurately described as "self-effacing and lacking in the watch-me swagger of most news anchors," by Globe and Mail television critic John Doyle.

Robertson was "the guy with the smallest ego I've ever seen in the television business, when he has a right to the largest one," Henry Kowalski, former CTV news chief, told the same newspaper in 2001.

"He was not just a fine journalist but a fine person," said Peter Mansbridge, former chief correspondent for CBC News, describing Robertson as a "friend and colleague of mine for more than 50 years.

"His audience believed him, and they trusted him. He set the bar for those who anchored newscasts across the country, and he will always be remembered for that.”

In addition to a number of industry awards during his career, he was inducted as an officer into the Order of Canada in 1997 and into the Canadian News Hall of Fame for the Canadian Journalism Foundation in 2016.

"If you find something that you love to do, and you're able to do it, that's about as good as it gets in life," Robertson said in a 2012 CTV documentary And That's the Life I Led.

WATCH | Robertson reports on new skateboarding fad in 1965: The scoop on 'skurfing' | Duration 2:19 The teenage president of the Ontario branch of the National Sidewalk Surfers of Canada explains her organization's reason for being.

Robertson was born in Stratford, Ont., on Jan. 19, 1934, to parents George and Lilly, the youngest of their two children by nine years. He also had eight older half-siblings from the first marriage of his father, whose ancestors emigrated from Scotland in the mid-19th century.

He hung on the advice and political musings of his father, a Canadian National Railway machinist, and the pair enjoyed radio comedies together.

But it was often a "dreary home life," he wrote in his 2012 memoir The Kind of Life It's Been, owing to his British mother's struggles with mental illness. Prone to bouts of paranoia and obsessive-compulsive behaviour, she would be lobotomized when he was 14, quelling her mind to a degree but dulling her emotional connection with her son.

"I couldn't have kids to the house, I couldn't tell them about her," he told CBC's George Stroumboulopoulos Tonight in 2012.

High school classmates, in the 2012 CTV documentary that accompanied his memoir, remembered a friend who gave little sign of turmoil. Robertson was popular, participating in debate and a barbershop quartet at Stratford Central Secondary School.

WATCH | Lisa LaFlamme on Robertson's legacy: ‘My life changed because of Lloyd Robertson’: Lisa LaFlamme reflects on the passing of her mentor | Duration 9:50 Former CTV National News anchor Lisa LaFlamme reflects on the passing of her friend and mentor, Lloyd Robertson, who has died at age 92. LaFlamme remembers Robertson’s belief in her during her time at CTV News, his dedication to fairness and humanity in news, and how he shaped her life beyond the newsroom.

22-year run at CBC

Already gifted with a smooth voice, he'd been intrigued by radio after standing near reporters covering a post-war parade in his hometown in 1946.

"I just remember being fascinated by the voices of the two commentators as they painted vivid pictures of the marchers and the joyous crowds," he wrote in his memoir.

At just 17, he persuaded Stratford radio station CJCS to give him an opportunity, overcoming an early on-air bungled pronunciation of the city name as "Strat-herd."

He didn't consider going beyond high school, learning the craft of radio at private stations in Stratford and Guelph, before beginning a 22-year run with the public broadcaster in 1954 in Windsor.

WATCH | Robertson anchors CBC in 1970: Lloyd Robertson, rookie news anchor | Duration 1:43 Lloyd Robertson was an anchor at the CBC before he became the face of CTV News.

For Robertson, 1956 was a momentous year — his elderly father died just months after he landed at CBC Winnipeg for his first foray into television.

That year he also married Nancy Barrett, a high school sweetheart with whom he had remained in touch. The couple would welcome four daughters born in Winnipeg, Ottawa and Toronto, reflecting Robertson's peripatetic, upward climb.

In his memoir, he remembered his four-plus years in Winnipeg as "among my happiest and most productive," and he even donned Western garb to host the country-flavoured Saddle Songs. He then honed political chops with a two-year stint with CBC Ottawa — though it wasn't all Parliament Hill business, as he hosted a show about the CFL's Ottawa Rough Riders.

WATCH | Peter Mansbridge on being a Robertson colleague and competitor: Lloyd Robertson, veteran news anchor, dead at 92 | Duration 10:43 Celebrated Canadian news anchor Lloyd Robertson has died at age 92. The veteran journalist began his career in local radio in 1952 before joining the CBC as an announcer in 1956. Robertson moved to CTV National News in 1976, serving as co-anchor and later chief anchor until his retirement in 2011. Former CBC News chief correspondent Peter Mansbridge shares his memories of Lloyd.

In 1962 came an offer from the corporation the couple couldn't refuse, and another move. Robertson would remember being at the "bottom of the pile" of 30 announcers, all male, at CBC Toronto.

Robertson would separate himself over time, displaying adaptability by hosting a kid's show, the athletics program Kaleidosport, and a host of news and magazine programs. Many Canadian radio listeners first heard of John F. Kennedy's assassination in 1963 from Robertson, and he would score high-profile network assignments for the 1964 Tokyo Olympics and Expo '67 in Montreal.

Robertson was cool and collected on air, but admitted years later that co-anchoring the 1969 moon shot by U.S. astronauts gave him pause.

"I had to pinch myself to be sure I was really living through this momentous time," he wrote.

Robertson would be rewarded with the network's plum assignment of anchoring The National in late 1970. It was a baptism by fire, as within days the Front de libération du Québec would plunge the province and country into crisis, kidnapping British diplomat James Cross and ultimately killing provincial minister Pierre Laporte.

CBC's news and current affairs roster was deep in the first years of that decade — future Canadian news anchors Peter Kent, Peter Trueman, Peter Mansbridge and Jan Tennant, along with budding stars like Adrienne Clarkson, Barbara Frum and Alex Trebek.

But there were also increasingly outdated union strictures involving studio and field work. Robertson once shared his workplace frustrations with Walter Cronkite on a trip to U.S. He recounted that the CBS news titan was incredulous that CBC anchors couldn't write their own copy, and were limited in reporting outside of the studio.

Move to CTV

In a time where NBC and ABC were employing multi-anchor formats in the U.S., Robertson was promised more freedom upon joining CTV National News in 1976, even as Harvey Kirck remained on the desk.

"Life with Harvey was sometimes tumultuous, occasionally precarious, but never dull," he wrote in his memoir of a co-anchor he described as loyal, but who caused the news division headaches with impaired driving citations.

Robertson adjusted to private-sector reality — more commercials, and local affiliates with clout — but he was welcomed by colleagues.

WATCH | Robertson on why he moved to CTV: Career change for Lloyd Robertson | Duration 1:39 The CBC's Larry Stout learns why money wasn't the only thing that motivated Lloyd Robertson to leave CBC for CTV. Aired on CBC's The National on June 21, 1976.

"What Lloyd did is [he] gave us instant credibility, and our numbers began to climb, and we've never retreated, really," said Craig Oliver, a top CTV political reporter and off-air friend, in 2012.

Kirck's departure in 1984 established Robertson's pre-eminence. Around the same time, coincidentally, he was approached by the Conservative Party to run as an MP. He wrote years the prospect held "some appeal," but he rebuffed that entreaty, and one by the Liberal Party in the early 2000s to serve as a senator.

By the 1990s, Roberton was ending the newscast with what would become a trademark: "And that's the kind of day it's been." He was firmly established as an éminence grise in the industry, winning three Geminis that decade for best host, anchor or interviewer.

Robertson stands with his star at Canada's Walk of Fame in Toronto in June 2007. (Mark Blinch/Reuters)

Robertson initiated a plan to step back from anchoring in 1996 and give way to CTV reporter Keith Morrison, but, he wrote years later, it imploded due to a combination of corporate resistance and misunderstandings. He expressed regret that the personal relationship with Morrison was ruptured beyond repair.

Robertson would still be in the anchor chair in the next decade and beyond, pulling a 14-hour shift on Sept. 11, 2001, the day of the terrorist attacks on U.S. soil by Islamist militants.

"The magnitude of this crisis is truly breathtaking," he told viewers. He admitted to The Canadian Press that days later his voice "may have been trembling a little bit," describing the scene as tens of thousands who had gathered on Parliament Hill for several minutes of silence in honour of what would be nearly 3,000 innocent victims, including 24 Canadians.

PHOTOS | Robertson through the years:

Robertson tributes flowed in 2010, and the year after, as he gave a year's notice of his intention to leave the anchor post.

"I've never seen Lloyd angry," Kent, then a federal politician, marvelled at the time. "Lloyd is a gentleman and a paragon of integrity."

Robertson remained with the network for several more years, contributing to investigative program W5, and he continued charitable work that included raising awareness of mental illness.

He was able to spend more time with his children and grandchildren, who were used to that sometimes-booming baritone.

"There's a line that we use: 'Dad, I'm in the room,'" daughter Susan Robertson told CTV in 2012. "But that's his trademark, that's his voice."

While straight-laced on air, Robertson wasn't overly fussy with his image, appearing in comedic skits with the Royal Canadian Air Farce, and with Drake in a taped segment for the Juno Awards. As to SCTV's newscaster "Floyd Robertson," he told CBC he thought the portrayal by Joe Flaherty was "marvelous."

World.title: The next Toronto? Reports of urban raccoons on the rise in Calgary
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Sean Halvorsen never thought he would be sharing his house with a raccoon.

That changed about a month ago, when his son caught a glimpse of a black-and-white bandit atop their McKenzie Lake home.

"All of a sudden the cat freaked out and my son looked out and saw what he thought was a cat, but it was actually a raccoon on the roof," he said.

"That's where I first realized I might have a raccoon problem."

Raccoons are seldom seen in most of Alberta, where harsh winters and abundant predators are among the challenges they've faced. Unlike in other urban centres like Toronto and Vancouver, where they've garnered reputations as mischievous "trash pandas," Calgary's raccoons prefer to lay low in the city's many forested areas and green spaces.

WATCH | Raccoons in Calgary? You bet there are: Raccoons in Calgary? You bet there are | Duration 1:08 Turns out trash pandas are actually in Calgary, and one wildlife biologist says their numbers could be rising.

A couple weeks after the roof incident, when a neighbour told him they had seen a raccoon enter his garage, Halvorsen decided enough was enough.

"I heard a whole bunch of rustling going on up in the roof, so [I realized] I for sure have a raccoon problem," he said.

Sean Halvorsen found out his McKenzie Lake home had a raccoon problem when his son saw one on the roof. (Mantai Chow/CBC)

Halvorsen decided that, as cute as raccoons are, the mammal wasn't welcome in his home.

"I was like, 'I have an old can of bear spray, maybe I can poke that up there,' but then the more rational side of me eventually thought maybe I should call some professional help."

LISTEN | Calgary homeowner, pest control pro and wildlife enthusiast talk raccoons: This is Calgary 19:10 Into the Raccooniverse of Calgary Raccoons are still something of a novelty for most Calgarians. But they're becoming more common [https://www.cbc.ca/news/canada/calgary/raccoon-observations-parks-calgary-9.6937091]... and can get into mischief. First, we talk to a local guy who's been trying in vain for FIVE years to spot a raccoon here. Then we head to southeast Calgary, to find out whether a homeowner managed to get the raccoon out of his garage attic.

He hired Calgary-based Peregrine General Pest Control, and the company successfully evicted the raccoon without harming it.

"The raccoon has vacated, so it's obviously worth the money," Halvorsen said.

On top of getting rid of the raccoon, Halvorsen said the pest control company performed a full inspection of his house to proactively seal other potential entry points to prevent future issues with wildlife.

26 raccoon calls so far this year, pest control company says

Stephen Hoare, Peregrine General Pest Control's service manager, says calls about raccoon problems have been on the rise, with calls this year among the highest the company's ever experienced.

Hoare says when he entered the pest control industry in 2017, the company received only one or two raccoon calls a year, which were typically incidents involving animals accidentally transported from British Columbia in shipping containers or vehicles.

"But as our winters have been getting warmer and warmer, it seems every year we've getting more and more calls," Hoare said.

Stephen Hoare, service manager with Peregrine General Pest Control, says it took time for the company to refine its raccoon removal strategy. (Mantai Chow/CBC)

He said ra ccoon calls have increased by at least 10 per cent year-over-year. While calls averaged about 10 per season between 2020 and 2022, they rose to 20 last year, and have already reached 26 this year.

"It's been of a bit of an experience learning how to handle raccoons," he said. "It's taken years for us to to figure out the best way to evict them out of someone's attic."

One of their tried-and-true methods involves using a "raccoon eviction lure" — male raccoon urine purchased from a distributor — to get female raccoons with young to leave of their own accord.

"That makes the female raccoon think that a male is in the area, and that's why it wants to grab its kits and leave to go find another place to live that they feel is much safer," Hoare said, pointing to the fact that male raccoons will kill a female's offspring in an effort to mate.

WATCH | Steer clear and don't feed them: Raccoon bites are up in Windsor-Essex: Steer clear and don't feed them: Raccoon bites are up in Windsor-Essex | Duration 1:44 The Windsor-Essex County Health Unit says raccoon bites are on the rise in Windsor-Essex, with 14 reported in the first six months of this year — eight of those at Ojibway Park. Here's what you need to know.

Other options include using specialized one-way doors to get the raccoons out, as well as live trapping — though that can be problematic.

"When you trap something something and relocate it more than five kilometres from its home zone, it can be a bit of a death sentence at times," Hoare said. "It's giving it a 50 per cent chance of actually surviving."

The company tries to avoid lethal control as much as possible.

"We want to get them out of the home and they're all good, they can go back to the river system and be living in tree hollows where they typically like to be," he said.

Where do Calgary's raccoons typically live?

Halvorsen and his neighbours are no stranger to raccoons in the southeast community of McKenzie Lake, which borders Fish Creek Provincial Park.

" We've had some Christmas cookies out [on the deck] and they got into them," Halvorsen said of the raccoons. "They actually opened the Tupperware up with their paws."

Raccoon populations are found in every Canadian province except Newfoundland and Labrador, though sightings have been known to happen there.

WATCH | Toronto has become synonymous with 'trash pandas': Is Toronto the raccoon capital of Canada? | Duration 7:52 CBC Toronto's Adrian Cheung digs into why "trash pandas" are the city's unofficial mascot — and why they thrive here.

According to the Alberta government, raccoons have traditionally lived primarily in the province's southeast region but have expanded their range to include urban and rural areas throughout Alberta.

Data from professional wildlife biologists and citizen scientists points to rising raccoon numbers in Calgary.

Wildlife biologist Sara Jordan-McLachlan, who works extensively with urban wildlife in Calgary, says reports of raccoons in the city date back about three decades.

"There was always that thought that one of the reasons we weren't seeing raccoons here was because they couldn't survive our winters, but as we're seeing milder winters and we're seeing different weather patterns, I think they're definitely able to adapt to that and it's definitely not a barrier for them anymore," she said.

Calgary's raccoon populations appear to be concentrated primarily in natural areas like Fish Creek Provincial Park, Weaselhead Flats and Carburn Park.

Jordan-McLachlan compared their range expansion to that of other Calgary wildlife.

"It definitely could be that, now that they've established themselves in the city, that they are starting to expand out of the natural areas, kind of similar to how bobcats seemed to be only in areas like Fish Creek, and now we're seeing them everywhere," she said.

"So raccoons may just be becoming more established and venturing out of those natural habitats."

A raccoon in southwest Calgary's Weaselhead Flats Natural Environment Park, which is among the natural areas where raccoons inhabit tree hollows. (Amir Said/CBC)

But while Calgary residents and pest control companies are dealing with more raccoon encounters than ever before, Jordan-McLachlan says the population growth of these animals faces significant hurdles in the city.

" They definitely face more challenges here," she said. "They have more competition because we do have coyotes, a very healthy coyote population which is definitely competition for them, and we also have bobcats. So they they have a steeper competition curve here comparatively to other places."

And whether raccoons are able to successfully establish themselves in more urban areas is dependent on human behaviour as well.

"If we are presenting them with opportunities to take advantage of things that we're doing, like leaving pet food out or not covering garbages, then we're going to habituate them and train them that this is something that they can take advantage of, and I think we'll see issues if we're not careful," Jordan-McLachlan said.

World.title: Abdul El-Sayed wins Michigan's Democratic Senate primary in major victory for party's progressive wing
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Abdul El-Sayed has won Michigan's Democratic nomination for the U.S. Senate, defeating Rep. Haley Stevens in a massive victory for the party's progressive wing in a battleground state.

The next and tougher test of El-Sayed's and progressives' strength will come in a November matchup against Republican Mike Rogers, a former congressman who ran unopposed for his party's nomination. The seat is pivotal to Democrats' chances of flipping the Senate and El-Sayed will face the challenge of uniting a divided Democratic base after a bruising primary.

In his final remarks at a primary night party before the race was called, El-Sayed said "tomorrow we begin to mend fences."

Stevens called El-Sayed to concede Wednesday, and she issued a statement saying she would back El-Sayed's candidacy.

"I am proud to offer my support as he takes on Mike Rogers in the general election," she said.

Stevens added, "This was a thorough and rigorous campaign that brought out the full span of views within the Democratic Party — and that is why we have primaries."

El-Sayed, left, and Rep. Haley Stevens appear on television during a debate at WoodTV studios on July 7 in Grand Rapids, Mich. (Kristen Norman/The Associated Press)

El-Sayed's win represents a significant shift for the Democratic Party. In 2018 he lost the gubernatorial primary to Gretchen Whitmer, now the governor, by 21 percentage points.

El-Sayed, a former health official, campaigned on "Medicare for All," halting military aid to Israel and campaign finance reform. He had support from progressive leaders including Sen. Bernie Sanders of Vermont and New York Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, who framed the race as a grassroots-focused movement and a broader fight against the establishment and big-money spending.

Stevens — a four-term congresswoman and more moderate candidate — was backed by Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer and tens of millions in outside spending, including the American Israel Public Affairs Committee's (AIPAC) largest outlay ever in a single race.

Her campaign focused on manufacturing and the economy. She stressed her past victories in tough races, saying she would be best positioned to beat Rogers.

The race for the Senate, during November's midterm elections, will help decide which party controls the chamber in the last two years of President Donald Trump's term. Those stakes added heat to the primary, with moderates arguing that El-Sayed would have a harder time than Stevens against a Republican in the general election.

Stevens won election to Congress in 2018 after serving as chief of staff to President Barack Obama's auto task force, which helped oversee the federal rescue of General Motors and Chrysler. Her campaign and allied groups have repeatedly highlighted that experience.

Clear differences

El-Sayed cast himself as the anti-establishment candidate and argued that Democrats need to reject corporate influence and embrace a more progressive agenda.

While El-Sayed has said he is not a democratic socialist, he found support from some who do. That included Melat Kiros, who recently beat a longtime incumbent in a Democratic primary for a Denver-based House seat, and Hasan Piker, a progressive and controversial influencer online.

The candidates' differences were clear to some voters.

Kenneth Woodside, 87, of West Bloomfield, said he voted for El-Sayed over Stevens because "the nation is ready for someone who wants to take some more action rather than on the road we are now, which is on the road to an oligarchy and authoritarianism."

LISTEN | What is AIPAC?: Front Burner 35:13 The backlash against AIPAC

Nessa Fuller, 51, of Birmingham, said she voted for Stevens because she will "fight to get the right things done, and she'll work with other people, which is really important to me."

National groups poured unprecedented sums into the race, making it one of the country's biggest tests of outside spending.

Groups backing Stevens spent more than $50 million US, led by more than $30 million US from AIPAC and its affiliates.

The spending thrust U.S. policy on Israel into the centre of the race even though the ads never mentioned it. While El-Sayed called for ending military aid to Israel, Stevens maintained strong support for the relationship.

Israel became a contentious issue within the Democratic Party amid a war in Gaza that killed more than 73,000 Palestinians in its retaliatory offensive after about 1,200 people were killed and 251 hostages were taken in attacks by the militant group Hamas in October 2023.

World.title: Filipino tennis star Alex Eala riding a wave of popularity into Toronto tournament
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

When rising Filipino tennis star Alex Eala plays on Canadian soil at the National Bank Open in Toronto, she'll be on centre court in front of a sold out crowd of 10,000.

The moment Eala's appearance was announced — a second round Wednesday night match — seats sold out within 30 minutes, according to Karl Hale, tournament director for the NBO, Canada's biggest tennis tournament and one of the most prestigious on the WTA tour.

"We've never seen a player ranked outside the top five have this type of effect," Hale said. "I think her fans were specifically waiting to see when she played."

And it's not just happening in Toronto.

The WTA tour is a gruelling season of more than 50 tournaments across dozens of countries, spanning multiple continents. And with every appearance, Eala's fans seem to find her.

"All the tournament directors are talking about it, everybody in the industry is talking about it," said Hale.

Eala's popularity has been driven by a massive Filipino diaspora, but also the vitality of her dramatic wins and charismatic interviews. She's a fresh face on the tour that has looked for star power following the retirement of big names like Serena Williams.

Eala kisses the championship trophy after winning the women's singles championship match at the Mubadala D.C. Open 2026, making her the first tennis player from the Philippines to bag a WTA title. (Scott Taetsch/Getty Images)

But with that growing popularity has come some backlash, with some online critics calling her overhyped.

However, Eala will play in Toronto fresh off a historic win at the Mubadala D.C. Open in Washington, D.C., making her the first tennis player from the Philippines to bag a WTA title.

"She's now 20 in the world. So she is really backing it up and she's growing her fan base," said Hale.

Big crowds at all tournaments

The early seeds of that fandom came when Eala reached the semifinals of another prestigious WTA tournament in 2025, the Miami Open. She beat out big names, including two top five players.

From there, the crowds only got bigger, extending even to the Grand Slams — the four biggest tournaments of the tennis season.

At last year's U.S. Open in New York, an energized crowd gave her first-round match the feel of a more consequential clash. Eala came from behind to win, marking the first time a player from the Philippines won a Grand Slam match.

From there, the so-called Eala effect seemed to catch.

Fans lined up for hours to catch her in the first round of this year's Australian Open in Melbourne. At the time, Eala was ranked 49th and lost that first match.

Her fans carried flags, signs and cheered so loud, it was noted by the opponent who beat her, American Alycia Parks.

After the match, Parks said, "It was difficult," mentioning that Eala definitely had a good crowd.

Then at Wimbledon in London, the crowd roared when she upset the defending champ Iga Swiatek in the third round.

"It is incredible to have my countrymen cheering me on, knowing that we are all in this together," Eala said in the post-match interview .

American tennis star turned-podcaster Andy Roddick has called it "Eala-mania."

On his podcast, he said: "Eala-mania is fun! When you have watch parties in arenas around your country for a fourth-round match, I'm in."

A new kind of tennis star

Eala's popularity signals a shift in tennis that many have long called for — more diversity.

The top-ranked players in the sport are concentrated in North America and Europe, with the dominant clusters in the U.S., Russia, Spain and France.

Asia has had few players break through the top ranks, while the Philippines, a country of 100 million people, has never produced a tennis star before.

Eala has noted this, embracing her Filipino fans and speaking in her native tongue often during her tournament interviews.

Alex Eala serves in a match at the U.S. Open in New York City in August 2025. (Kris Reyes/CBC)

As a Filipino Canadian tennis fan, I can speak to that pride. My whole family has been following Eala since she won the junior's girls title at the U.S. Open in 2022, excited at the prospect of cheering for another Filipino in a sport we already loved.

And there is a kind of thrill, hearing words like laban, the Tagalog word for fight, shouted from the stands at international tournaments.

It is a joy to watch an entire country, the Filipino diaspora and the rest of the tennis world get excited to walk alongside Eala in pursuit of bigger titles, even a Grand Slam trophy.

Eala's rise has put her on the cover of every major publication in her country, from Vogue to Tatler, while garnering congratulations from Filipinos everywhere in the world, including the Philippine president.

"Everywhere around the world, we have been watching you. We've been willing you on, and we have been so proud of you," President Bongbong Marcos said at a reception hosted for the athlete at the nation's presidential palace.

She's credited the love and support of her country for motivating her to continue battling on the court.

In an interview in 2022 with the WTA , she explained why she considers it a privilege to be a banner holder for the Philippines.

"It's important to me because I don't see a lot of Filipinos on the worldwide tennis stage."

World.title: Zelenskyy appeals for more air defences after Russia unleashes deadly wave of attacks on Kyiv
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy says Russian missile and drone strikes on Kyiv and the surrounding area left 17 people dead and dozens more injured. The latest Russian strikes come as Ukraine struggles with a limited number of key interceptors.

Russian missile and drone strikes on Kyiv and the surrounding region killed 17 people and wounded 44 others overnight into Wednesday, Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said.

The attack was the latest in a series of large-scale Russian ballistic missile strikes that have become near-routine this summer. The intensified barrages are exploiting Ukraine's critical shortage of interceptor missiles for the U.S.-made Patriot systems, the sole air defence system in its arsenal able to shoot down ballistic missiles.

Zelenskyy has pleaded with other countries to send more of the ammunition made scarcer by the Iran war.

"Ballistic interceptors are what could have saved the lives of those killed today," Zelenskyy said on social media. "It is very important for our partners to understand that delays in supplying them, or a reluctance to hand over anti-ballistic systems, lead directly to such horrific casualties and destruction."

Large warehouse fires burned in the city of Brovary and the villages of Velyka Dymerka, Kvitneve and Peremoha. (Anatolii Stepanov/Reuters)

Russia fired 24 ballistic missiles, four other missiles identified as either hypersonic Zircons or supersonic Oniks, and 115 drones, many of them jet-powered, in the attack.

Zelenskyy said the strikes mainly targeted warehouses belonging to civilian businesses, as well as infrastructure and a railway station, hitting sites that he described as "with no connection to the war"— including a brewing company, building materials warehouses and civilian logistics facilities.

Serhii Beskrestnov, an adviser to Ukraine's president on defence technology development, said the war of attrition has entered a new phase.

"The enemy is attacking everything indiscriminately — retail warehouses, food storage facilities, logistics hubs, enterprises, building materials warehouses," he said on Facebook.

See the aftermath of Russian strikes on warehouses around Kyiv | Duration 0:34 One woman described the stress of repeated attacks on Ukraine's capital as living in a state of 'constant fear,' saying there's no sleep for people in the area around Kyiv. Russia's latest wave of strikes killed at least 17 people and damaged warehouses and logistics centres, Ukrainian officials say.

Russia says it hit war-supporting companies

The Russian Defence Ministry said it struck transport, logistics and distribution centres involved in military activity. It listed four targets in Kyiv, claiming they ran war-related operations.

It was not immediately possible to reconcile the different accounts.

Ukraine's largest private postal operator, Nova Poshta, said a Russian cluster munition destroyed one of its sorting centres in Kyiv.

The Russian Defence Ministry said the centre was "storing and distributing dual-use goods, including those used in the production of long- and medium-range uncrewed aerial vehicles, as well as robotic systems and electronic warfare systems." It claimed that two other logistics centres in the Kyiv region stored drones or components for drones.

Separately, the ministry said its forces hit three bulk carriers on the Black Sea south of Odesa that it claimed were transporting weapons and military equipment for the Ukrainian armed forces. Ukrainian officials didn't comment on that claim.

One of the companies that came under heavy fire was the Epicentr, one of Ukraine's largest retail and construction chains. It said in a statement on Facebook that "in minutes, Russian missiles destroyed what the company had built over decades."

Ukraine President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said the strikes mainly targeted warehouses belonging to civilian businesses, as well as infrastructure and a railway station. (Kostiantyn Liberov/Libkos/Getty Images)

One employee was killed and three others were wounded. Russia hit two of the company's key logistics hubs.

According to the Russian Defence Ministry, the Epicentr site handled order processing, sorting, storing and delivery of dual-use goods and components for drone production.

Ukraine fires hundreds of drones

In its latest attack on logistics facilities of Wildberries, Russia's biggest online retailer, Ukrainian drones hit a warehouse in the Tula region south of Moscow, the company and the region's governor said Wednesday.

It was the 14th Wildberries warehouse to catch fire in less than three weeks, according to a Ukrainian tally. Ukraine says the company provides goods that can be used by the military. Kyiv is also keen to unsettle the Russian public with high-profile attacks.

Why attack 'Russia's Amazon'? | About That | Duration 1:45 Andrew Chang explains why Ukraine is carrying out drone attacks on warehouses owned by Wildberries — Russia's most profitable online retailer. (Photo credits: Wildberries, Reuters, Adobe Stock and Getty Images)

The Russian Defence Ministry said its forces downed 475 Ukrainian drones overnight over 16 Russian regions, as well as illegally annexed Crimea and the waters of the Sea of Azov and the Black Sea.

U.S.-led peace efforts to end the war that began with Russia's invasion in February 2022 have apparently stalled. Trump, at a NATO summit in Turkey last month, teased a plan for Ukraine to produce missile systems with U.S. defence contractors, but no details have followed and such a plan wouldn't be of immediate help.

World.title: Perez Hilton hospitalized following concerning livestream
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

WARNING: This story contains details of self-harm.

Blogger Perez Hilton is in hospital following reports that he had appeared to self-harm during a TikTok livestream.

In an email to CBC News, the Miami-Dade Sheriff's Office said "the individual has been safely recovered and transported by Miami-Dade Fire Rescue to a local hospital, where he is receiving medical attention."

Authorities were dispatched to his Miami home Tuesday night after receiving multiple calls from concerned fans regarding an individual who "was livestreaming acts of self-harm on social media."

Once on scene, deputies say they spoke to family members and confirmed he was alone during the time of the stream.

Following the incident, authorities say they have "tactically disengaged" and are continuing to monitor the situation while providing support to the family.

"In many incidents involving a person experiencing a mental health crisis or actively harming themselves, deputies prioritize de-escalation by creating time, distance and opportunities for communication," the spokesperson wrote in an email CBC News.

"Unless there is an immediate threat to others, slowing the situation and utilizing crisis intervention techniques can reduce the likelihood of a suicide-by-cop encounter and minimize the risk of injury to the individual, deputies and the public."

Representatives ask for privacy

Golden Artists Entertainment Co-CEO's Dante Rusciolelli and Rebekah Kochan, who represent Hilton, shared a statement on Instagram.

"We are aware of the concerning content circulating online involving our client, Perez Hilton," it reads, regarding the video and screen grabs that later spread on social media.

"At this time, we have not been able to make direct contact with him, despite our ongoing efforts to reach him. Our primary concern is Perez's health and well being, as well as the well being of his family. Until we have confirmed information, we will not speculate or comment further."

They conclude by saying they appreciate everyone's concern and ask that his privacy be respected during this time.

Hilton began his popular celebrity gossip blog in the early 2000s, where he provided readers with an unfiltered take on Hollywood's biggest moments.

World.title: Colombia’s left presents evidence suggesting De la Espriella won through fraud
World.content:
Colombia’s President Gustavo Petro and data analysts presented evidence suggesting that President-elect Abelardo de la Espriella won the election through the mass manipulation of tally sheets.

During a two-hour presentation, Petro claimed that almost all tally sheets that had been shared with his political party, the Historic Pact “lacked the Hash security lock,” which is inserted into official PDF documents to guarantee they can’t be changed.

The absence of a hash file implies that the so-called E14 tally sheets may have been altered, which appears to have happened, according to data analysts who accompanied the president.

Legal expert William Villanueva said that original tally sheets were scanned and subsequently reprocessed, removing the metadata that would allow them to determine whether the E14’s were uploaded or introduced digitally.

“We found documents marked ‘confidential’… and others that said ‘not digitized’ on a blank page, which—and this is important—were later republished with different information,” said one of the computer scientists.

The investigation, which was carried out by 75,000 “digital witnesses,” found that 95 municipalities had more voters than inhabitants. In all of these municipalities, the E-14’s gave De la Espriella landslide victories with more than 70% of the votes.

The president-elect’s opponent, leftist Senator Ivan Cepeda, achieved not a single victory in hundreds of towns where the electoral census was larger than 85% of the population.

In 1,350 polling centers in capital cities, the researchers found that block patterns in which De la Espriella won the first half of the voting booths and Cepeda won the second half.

According to a consulted statistician, this result would only be probably in some 80 polling stations, said Carlos Oñoro, one of the digital witnesses.

“This order is mathematically impossible for human voters,” Petro stated, arguing that automated software replaced actual citizen ballots.

The findings of the digital witnesses will be added to a lawsuit that seeks to nullify the election of De la Espriella and force the Council of State to order a recount of the votes.

Following the presentation, Cepeda said in a post on social media network X that “the competent authority must impartially examine our demands of nullity.”

World.title: De la Espriella says he won’t allow Colombia’s left to “destabilize democracy”
World.content:
Colombia’s far-right President-elect Abelardo de la Espriella said that he won’t allow his country’s left to “destabilize democracy” through civil disobedience against his US citizenship.

In his weekly address to the nation, De la Espriella stressed that after Friday he will be president and “with the force of the constitution and the law” ensure that his power will be upheld.

The civil disobedience announced by leftist opposition leader Ivan Cepeda “is nothing more than a euphemism for an attempt to destabilize democracy,” said De la Espriella.

“I will not allow it,” said the president-elect.

I am the president of all Colombians, and I will ensure, through the power of the Constitution and the law, that what the Colombian people decided—which was to elect me—is upheld. My call to the entire nation is that we stop normalizing what is wrong, illegal, and corrupt. Let’s call things by their proper names and confront them for what they are. This so-called “civil disobedience” is nothing more than a euphemism for an attempt to destabilize democracy, and I will not allow it. Abelardo de la Espriella

According to De la Espriella, the left “combined all forms of struggle,” a term used by the now-defunct guerrilla group FARC to justify the violence used by the insurgents, “and lost.”

Cepeda called on his followers to peaceful civil disobedience in response to the president-elect’s refusal to renounce his US citizenship.

The incoming opposition leader and his political party, the Historic Pact, support legal efforts to challenge De la Espriella’s election on claims that fraud concerns have not been tackled.

More radical elements within the Historic Pact, including outgoing President Gustavo Petro, have sustained that the far-right won the elections through deceit and fraud, but have failed to present evidence that would confirm a criminal conspiracy.

World.title: As De la Espriella takes office, his US-backed security policy for Colombia is raising questions
World.content:
Colombia’s far-right President-elect Abelardo de la Espriella assumes office on Friday, after elections with a razor-thin margin. He brings with him promises to wield “iron fist” policies against non-state armed groups (NSAGs) and organized criminal organizations in the country.

He has also promised to dismantle ongoing peace talks initiated by outgoing leftist President Gustavo Petro, including groups that are currently disarming. De la Espriella made scores of hardline promises on the campaign trail, many of which he will likely not be able to achieve with a minority coalition in the legislature, such as withdrawing Colombia from the United Nations.

On security issues, however, Colombia’s constitution grants the president broad unilateral powers. De la Espriella has promised to “end” armed groups within a month, an extremely unlikely goal. Despite the broad powers of the presidential office, De la Espriella faces historical and logistical limitations.

Despite claims from right-wing parties that Petro has gone easy on armed groups, Colombia’s military has been fully deployed against NSAGs in the country for the last two years.

As conflict expert Thomas Garrison reported for news website Pirate Wire Services in June, Colombia has ongoing and large military operations against FARC dissident group Estado Mayor Central (EMC), the National Liberation Army (ELN), and EMC splinter-group EMBF.

Colombia’s security forces are “already operating on all cylinders,” and “stretched to their limit,” according to the International Crisis Group. It isn’t clear how deployments can be increased without increasing the numbers of security forces themselves — hardly a goal that can be achieved in his first month in office.

Nonetheless, there are strategic changes that de La Espriella can impose to chart a more aggressive course. As part of those plans, the president-elect has promised to implement a “Plan Patriota remixed”, an allusion to highly aggressive US-backed military operations against armed groups under then-President Alvaro Uribe in 2003.

Uribe’s allies to this day hail Plan Patriota as a great success that forced the FARC to the negotiating table in 2016.

Critics, however, point to rampant human and civil rights violations, including working with paramilitary forces to kill thousands of civilians and frame them as guerrilla fighters to increase casualty counts.

The US, however, is pushing Latin America towards increased military spending and Bukele-style crackdowns on organized crime, and de la Espriella plans to comply.

What was Plan Patriota and how will Abelardo’s version be ‘remixed’?

Plan Patriota involved aerial bombardments, large-scale military deployments in FARC-controlled areas, and aggressive intelligence gathering against FARC guerrillas at the height of Colombia’s civil war.

Although paramilitary groups were not officially part of Plan Patriota, they cooperated closely with regular military forces during the operation, functioning as spies, informants, and death squads — ostensibly killing alleged guerrillas, but just as often murdering leftists in general, as well as non-politically involved civilians.

The operation, which continued until 2010, weakened the FARC considerably, but at a great price: gross human rights violations including massacres, torture, and using sexual violence against civilians as a weapon of war.

Paramilitary structures were also greatly empowered across the country, sowing the seeds of groups that still exist today, such as the Ejercito Gaitanista Colombiano (EGC) — often referred to in Western media as ‘the Clan del Golfo.’

The full extent of the atrocities committed by both sides of the war would not become clear until Colombia launched its Truth Commission in 2017. (De la Espriella wants to disband the Truth Commission as well as the Colombian Peace Court, which prosecutes the worst offenders of the civil war.)

Any new version of Plan Patriota would look very different. Colombia is not the same country it was in the early 2000’s. Modern armed groups are not interested in clashing with state forces on the battlefield. Most are not interested in overthrowing the state at all, and certainly not via military victory.

Technology has also advanced considerably. Drone warfare is a dangerous new weapon in the arsenal of NSAGs who wage asymmetrical attacks on state forces as well as one another. Digital surveillance and satellite optics also mean that unlike the FARC, which often relied upon jungle canopies to hide large training and logistics camps, modern NSAGs instead blend into civil society in the communities where they operate.

They do not wear uniforms to distinguish themselves and avoid direct confrontations with the military, which means there are no large targets to bomb, nor columns of marching fighters for the state to confront.

Modern NSAGs are far more flexible, transnational, and relatively decentralized in their operations compared to FARC at the height of the civil war.

De la Espriella’s security program is more likely to look like Daniel Noboa’s policies in Ecuador than the 2002 Plan Patriota. It will likely include US cooperation on target-finding, naval cooperation on drug trafficking, and joint US-Colombia operations within the country.

Most of those dynamics already exist. Despite a rocky relationship with Washington, D.C, Petro continued to cooperate with the US on intelligence-sharing and anti-narcotics operations.

Critics of de la Espriella, however, fear that logistics won’t be the only similarity to Ecuadorian-US operations, which have resulted in the murder of civilians by security forces, torture, arbitrary detentions, and bombings of civilian infrastructure.

One factor that may keep de la Espriella somewhat in check is a lack of a clear mandate. He won elections by less than 1%, and has already clashed with more established right-wing political parties, who will not be forming part of his coalition in the legislature.

De la Espriella signals he will follow Washington’s lead

On a recent trip to the U.S, de la Espriella’s vice-president, José Manuel Restrepo, met with US Deputy Assistant Secretary of War for the Americas, Joseph M. Humire, who spoke of investment by US companies in hydrocarbon and energy sectors as well as cooperation on security and migration issues.

“Colombia is historically one of the U.S. strongest security and defense partners,” he wrote on X on July 21. “Under the leadership of incoming President Abelardo De La Espriella, we plan to take this partnership to new levels with Plan Patriot 2.0.”

Before Humire joined the War Department, he worked as an anti-migration lobbyist propagating conspiracy theories that cartels have “weaponized” migrants as part of “asymmetrical warfare” against the U.S.

He falsely testified before the House Foreign Affairs Committee in February that Venezuelan gang Tren de Aragua had “opened” the Darien Gap to migrants during the Biden administration as part of a Venezuelan plan to destabilize the US.

De la Espriella has already signalled that he looks forward to closer cooperation with the administration of US President Donald Trump and largely follow the US lead on regional issues. Trump has made migration a key facet of his domestic and foreign policy.

The ultra-right Colombian president-elect has also promised to “secure” the country’s borders. Migrants “who are here illegally, or committing crimes will be deported to their countries of origin without delay,” he said in a press conference on July 13.

He has agreed, however, to keep commercial and migratory pathways open on the Venezuelan border. Petro re-initiated diplomatic and commercial ties with Venezuela in 2022.

De la Espriella has not criticized Chavista governments as heavily as many other right-wing politicians in the country, and provided legal representation for Maduro loyalist Alex Saab, who has been extradited for a second time to the US to face money laundering and corruption charges.

Aggressive military strategies have failed in the past

The nature of conflict has changed drastically in Colombia since the civil war, and presidents have tried aggressive military tactics against criminal organizations and NSAGs before.

Former President Ivan Duque failed to slow the rapid growth of either during his time in office from 2018 to 2022.

The Colombian state failed to fulfill its promises to invest in legitimate economies and develop regions long ignored by Bogotá. Regions that had previously been governed by the FARC became power vacuums that were quickly filled by other criminal organizations and NSAGs.

Duque left office the least popular president in the country’s history since records have been kept, in part because of his security policy. Bombings on rebel camps that killed minors created significant public controversy. When Petro turned to similar strategies, the military inadvertently killed children in bombings in children as well.

Armed groups have continued to grow under Petro despite his employment of increasingly aggressive military strategies. De la Espriella has not offered details about his plans, and it is unclear what he could do that Duque and Petro did not, or why the results would be any different for his administration when similar tactics have failed before.

Trump, however, has gained a new ally in the region. The US president has often shown that projection of US power is an end in and of itself, and de la Espriella is likely to allow Trump to do exactly that.

World.title: Colombia Reports and 21st-century fascism
World.content:
The coming four years will probably be the toughest yet and I will need your support to keep Colombia’s longest-living news source alive.

The Espriella administration will be the third far-right government I have reported on since I started Colombia Reports in 2008.

I expect the incoming government to be the worst because it seeks to undo socio-economic policies that pulled 4 million people out of poverty and end peace processes that kept us safe.

Independent journalists (and the New York Times) have criticized Abelardo de la Espriella for his ties to the now-defunct paramilitary organization AUC and drug traffickers, and his alleged corruption of the judicial system, specifically in Colombia.

Many of these journalists have been harassed by De la Espriella’s law firm through at least 109 frivolous lawsuits, and the publication of their private information.

I can only guess what’s ahead for us after De la Espriella appointed reported frauds as his spokespersons and put a conspiracy theorist in charge of my visa.

I will need your support as what’s coming is probably going to be expensive. The last time I reported on a far-right government, I was forced to spend months in my native country, the Netherlands.

If you are not yet a paid subscriber, please become one. If you don’t want to commit to a monthly contribution, please make a one-time donation.

I promise I will continue reporting on Colombia and will update you on the political situation in Colombia through my podcasts with Richard McColl of Colombia Calling.

World.title: De la Espriella desists from holding swearing-in ceremony at military base
World.content:
President-elect Abelardo de la Espriella has apparently given up trying to be sworn in before the military and asked Congress to allow the ceremony to take place in Cali, Colombia’s third largest city.

In an address to the nation, De la Espriella said Sunday that volcanic activity made travel to Popayan, the capital of Cauca, made a “secure, well-organized” inauguration ceremony all but impossible.

“For this reason, I respectfully ask the honorable House of Representatives, which has not yet debated my inauguration in a plenary session, to convene the August 7th session in the city of Cali,” said the president-elect.

“As soon as I am sworn in as president of the republic, my government’s first security council will be held in the Marco Fidel Suarez airbase in the city of Cali,” added De la Espriella, suggesting he has given up his aspiration to be sworn in inside a military base.

In an interview, Santiago de Cali University president Carlos Andres Perez, told Blu Radio on Tuesday that Valle del Cauca Governor Dilian Francisca Toro told him the university theater would be used for the inauguration.

Following the main ceremony, De la Espriella will travel to the Pichincha Military Canton, the base of the 3rd Division, to assume his role as supreme commander of the armed forces.

The apparent decision to desist from a military inauguration comes after major tensions with the outgoing government of President Gustavo Petro, who ordered the military not to cooperate with his elected successor.

An inauguration at a military base was also opposed by the Democratic Center, the largest political party in De la Espriella’s far-right congressional coalition.

The opponents claimed that Colombia’s constitution submits the armed forces to civilian authority. A swearing-in ceremony before them would have been confusing and inappropriate.

According to De la Espriella, his intention meant to stress his support for the Colombia’s “heroes.”

World.title: Colombia’s “Shield of the Americas” to operate from Medellin: De la Espriella
World.content:
Medellin will be the home of the US-led “Shield of the Americas” security program, according to Colombia’s President-elect Abelardo de la Espriella and Mayor Federico Gutierrez.

At a meeting with authorities from the Antioquia province, De la Espriella and Gutierrez agreed that Colombia’s second largest city is the “head of the snake of drug trafficking and organized crime.”

From Medellin, the metropolitan area, most orders are sent out to the rest of the country. So we’re going to focus our efforts on Medellin to fight crime. Abelardo de la Espriella

The announcement followed alleged calls between De la Espriella, US President Donald Trump and US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, and meetings between incoming Defense Minister Jorge Mora and the US’ Deputy Assistant Secretary of War for the Americas, Joseph Humire.

Following the meeting, Mora and Humire announced “Plan Patriota 2.0” and the creation of a “Regional Training Center against Drug Trafficking and Transnational Threats,” which would be “aimed at improving interoperability, operational readiness, and cooperation with allied countries” from the Americas.

During these meetings, the parties explored the joint development of a new bilateral program for cooperation and strategic assistance with a regional scope, known as Plan Patriota 2.0. This initiative is conceived as part of Colombia’s accession to the American Coalition Against the Cartels and is based on the design of the new Policy on Defense, Security, and Civic Coexistence, as well as on the strategy for military and police campaigns in priority areas for the restoration and stabilization of security. Jorge Mora

Plan Patriota was a US-backed military strategy that was implemented by former President Alvaro Uribe between 2003 and 2006.

The plan sought to dismantle the military organization of the now-defunct FARC guerrilla group, which it largely did while also killing thousands and forcibly displacing hundreds of thousands civilians.

De la Espriella has said that he seeks to restart Plan Colombia and seek to militarily destroy groups that were formed during and after peace processes with the FARC and the now-defunct paramilitary organization AUC.

World.title: “Water will run out:” Colombia declares emergency over upcoming El Niño
World.content:
Colombia’s government agreed to declare a national emergency over the consequences of El Niño, a climate phenomenon that is expected to bring extreme drought in December.

According to the government’s environmental institute, IDEAM, this year’s Niño could become the worst since the 1950’s and will peak between November 2026 an March 2027.

During a minister’s council, President Gustavo Petro said that excessive heat and water shortages could lead to energy shortages in regions that rely on hydroelectric dams for their electricity.

Petro asked Finance Minister German Avila to transfer COP4 trillion ($1.2 billion) to disaster management agency UNGRD to double the purchase of solar panels to lessen the demand on these hydroelectric dams.

In December last year, the UNGRD already signed a COP4.2 trillion deal with electricity firm Gecelca to buy solar panels.

In order to maintain food production, the president ordered the purchase of desalination plants for the Caribbean region.

Water is what’s going to run out—we don’t know to what extent, but hopefully Bogotá won’t have to suffer through this again. So, any drinking water supply project that’s already been designed but lacks funding must be funded. Drinking water—all the desalination plants we can bring in, because we don’t build them in Colombia — in all the towns in the northern Caribbean. President Gustavo Petro

Last but not least, Petro urged the Justice Ministry to secure “the accelerated surrender of lands, 500 thousand hectares, that have not been awarded” to landless farmers.

“Provide more land and more water to grow food, grow more food in Colombia, because the sun is going to scorch a lot of food and burn crops. And so it’s likely that we’ll be able to make up for the loss in food supply over these six months with new food supplies,” said the president.

Petro urged his ministers to be careful of corruption, which sank the UNGRD in a crisis in early 2024 and resulted in the detentions of multiple government officials.

World.title: De la Espriella denied aspired control over Colombia’s Congress
World.content:
Colombia’s Congress denied control over the legislative agenda to President-elect Abelardo de la Espriella and voted for a president loyal to former President Alvaro Uribe.

De la Espriella proposed his friend, Senator Alfredo Deluque of the U Party, to assume the leadership of the Senate, which would have given the government control over the congressional agenda.

Ahead of the vote, eight parties expressed their support for Deluque’s candidacy, which would have given him a 55-vote majority in the anonymous vote.

Former President Alvaro Uribe, whose Democratic Center party would be granted the presidency, accused “Abelardo’s circle” of trying to “get rid of this party” and vowed to “defend ourselves.”

Uribe had put up Democratic Center Senator Honorio Henriquez for the job and ordered his 17 senators to stick to their original vote.

If the Tiger roars to destroy the Democratic Center, we’ll have to become hardworking bees and defend ourselves, just like bees do when they’re attacked… I’m frightened by the idea circulating among De La Espriella’s inner circle of destroying that party. Former President Alvaro Uribe

The former president got the support of President Gustavo Petro, arguably Abelardo’s biggest political enemy.

At a rally that was held ahead of the vote, Petro warned senators of his leftist Historic Pact party “not to vote for fascism.”

Under the leadership of Senate bench leader Ivan Cepeda, who lost the presidential election to De la Espriella last month, all 26 of the pact’s senators voted for Henriquez.

Enjoying the secrecy of their vote, dissidents from the parties who were ordered to vote Deluque also turned on the president-elect and delivered Henrique 56 votes. Deluque ended up with only 45.

Less than three weeks before taking office, De la Espriella lost the loyalty of its largest coalition partner in Congress and will have to negotiate his agenda with them.

World.title: Chile’s Municipalities, Senapred Meet Ahead of Storm Forecast
World.content:
SANTIAGO, Chile â As Chile prepares for an approaching winter storm system, the Association of Municipalities of Chile (Amuch) held a high-level coordination meeting with the National Disaster Prevention and Response Service (Senapred) to strengthen municipal emergency response measures.

The discussions focused on improving collaboration among municipalities, national agencies, and private service providers to better protect residents during severe weather events.

Power Companies Face Pressure Over Response Times

A central topic in the meeting was the performance of electric utilities during past emergencies. JosÃ© Manuel Palacios, mayor of La Reina, expressed concern over delayed responses from power companies in recent years.

âWe are exploring ways, together with Senapred and other institutions, to develop more efficient actions and hold the companies accountable to meet the response times our residents need,â Palacios said.

Rural Water Supply Risks Tied to Electricity

For rural municipalities, electrical outages pose a dual threat, as potable water systems often rely on electric power. Paula GÃ¡rate, mayor of Melipilla, emphasized the heightened vulnerability of rural areas during storms.

âLosing electricity also means losing access to potable water. Many rural water systems depend on electricity, and that remains our greatest concern,â GÃ¡rate noted.

Coordinated Municipal Efforts to Mitigate Risks

Senapred Director Alicia CebriÃ¡n highlighted the essential role of municipal governments in both preparation and response phases.

âMunicipalities play a crucial role in coordination, information gathering, and implementing mitigation works to reduce the impact of winter threats on residents,â CebriÃ¡n stated.

She underscored that emergency prevention and mitigation is a shared responsibility across public agencies and institutions. âPublic authorities who are directly involved in disaster management bear this responsibility, and we are committed to fulfilling it,â she added.

Winter System Expected to Test Emergency Readiness

The coordination meeting comes as Chileâs central regions brace for a frontal system expected to bring heavy rain and strong winds. Authorities emphasized that ongoing preparation and inter-agency cooperation will be key to minimizing disruption and protecting vulnerable communities.

World.title: Brian Wilson, Legendary Beach Boys Co-Founder, Dies at 82
World.content:
LOS ANGELES â Brian Wilson, the legendary musician, songwriter and co-founder of The Beach Boys, has died at the age of 82, his family announced.

“We are heartbroken to announce that our beloved father Brian Wilson has passed away,” the family said in a statement. “We are at a loss for words right now. Please respect our privacy at this time as our family is grieving. We realize that we are sharing our grief with the world.”

Born in 1942 in Hawthorne, California, Wilson formed The Beach Boys in 1961 with his younger brothers Carl and Dennis, cousin Mike Love, and friend Al Jardine. The band became one of the most influential and commercially successful acts in music history, selling over 100 million records worldwide.

Wilson was the creative force behind the groupâs distinctive harmonies and groundbreaking studio sound. His 1966 album Pet Sounds is regarded as a masterpiece that reshaped the boundaries of pop music production.

Among The Beach Boys’ many hits, Wilson co-wrote and produced I Get Around, Help Me, Rhonda, and Good Vibrations. Rolling Stone ranked The Beach Boys 12th on its list of the “100 Greatest Artists of All Time.”

Tributes poured in following news of his death. Nancy Sinatra shared a photo with Wilson on Instagram, writing, âHis cherished music will live forever as he travels through the Universe and beyond. God bless you, sweet Brian.â
