A First Time in Limache

On Sunday 9 August 2026, Mauricio Redolés performs in Limache for the first time in his long career. The show starts at 3:00 p.m. at the Centro Cultural La Vaguada, on Angamos 396, and is billed as a family afternoon of poetry, music and humour.

Limache, a town in Chile’s Valparaíso region, rarely lands artists of Redolés’s stature, which is part of what makes the date notable. It is the second half of a short regional run rather than a one-off appearance.

The concert reworks his best-known songs in a rock format, backed by a full band, giving longtime fans and curious newcomers a fresh take on a familiar catalogue.

Who Is Mauricio Redolés?

Redolés is one of the most singular voices in Chilean music and literature, with a career spanning more than four decades. His work blends rock, spoken-word poetry and a sharp, often absurd sense of humour.

His story is bound up with Chile’s recent history: he began performing in the public jail of Valparaíso while held as a political prisoner, and he has since toured stages across Chile, Latin America and Europe.

That biography gives his songs an unusual weight. Beneath the jokes and wordplay sits a body of work about memory, resistance and everyday life that has earned him a devoted following.

The Band and a Special Guest

For these shows Redolés is joined by Los Alegres de Tocornal, a band of Valparaíso-based musicians: Takurí Tricot on guitar, Sebastián Redolés on drums and Pablo López on bass. Together they translate his catalogue into a rock setting.

Both concerts also feature a notable guest: Kiuge Hayashida, who was Charly García’s guitarist for more than twenty years and recorded six albums with the Argentine rock icon. He toured much of Latin America at García’s side.

His presence connects Redolés’s regional dates to the wider history of Latin American rock, adding star power to an intimate small-town bill.

The Songs

On stage, Redolés draws on old and new material, including “¿Quién mató a Gaete?”, “Química”, “Llegando a Yungay” and “Marcando Ocupado.” The set balances crowd favourites with more recent work.

He is also performing his latest single, “La cumbia china,” an unusual collaboration with Dr. Isabel Yuxiu Wu that mixes music, poetry and humour while playing with language and popular imagery across two cultures.

Reworking these songs in a rock format is part of the appeal: the arrangements give poems that many fans know by heart a louder, more physical charge.

Two Anniversaries

The 2026 dates fall on meaningful anniversaries. Redolés says the year marks 51 years since he first began performing, and three decades since his landmark 1996 album “¿Quién mató a Gaete?”.

That record has been ranked by Rolling Stone among the 50 best Chilean albums of all time and appears in surveys of the country’s greatest rock releases, cementing his place in the national canon.

His honours include three Altazor awards, a National Humour Prize in 2015, a culture-ministry literary prize, and, in 2022, the President of the Republic’s National Music Award, handed to him by President Gabriel Boric.

Why It Matters for the Region and Expats

Bringing an artist of Redolés’s standing to Limache is part of a broader push to spread cultural life beyond Chile’s big cities. For residents of the Valparaíso region, it means access to a major act without travelling to Santiago.

The Sunday matinee format, in a community cultural centre, makes it especially accessible for families and for newcomers still finding their footing in the local scene. Tickets are sold online through the portaldisc platform.

For expats, it is also a crash course in Chilean culture: Redolés’s blend of poetry, politics and humour is a direct line into the country’s artistic sensibility, delivered in a relaxed, small-town setting.

Frequently Asked Questions

When and where does Mauricio Redolés play in Limache?

Mauricio Redolés performs in Limache for the first time on Sunday 9 August 2026 at 3:00 p.m., at the Centro Cultural La Vaguada (Angamos 396). It is billed as a family show of rock, poetry and humour.

Who plays with him?

He is backed by Los Alegres de Tocornal — Takurí Tricot, Sebastián Redolés and Pablo López — with special guest Kiuge Hayashida, who was Charly García’s guitarist for more than twenty years.

Is there another concert in the region?

Yes. Before Limache, Redolés plays Viña del Mar on Friday 7 August 2026 at 8:30 p.m. at the bar Journal. Tickets for both shows are available online through the portaldisc platform.

World.title: Cuba’s First Elpidio Valdés Cultural Hub Opens in Havana
World.content:
Culture: Havana

Key Facts —Centre. La Manigua is the first cultural centre in Cuba devoted to the work of animator Juan Padrón, opened in March 2026 near Havana’s Plaza de la Revolución. —Character. It celebrates Elpidio Valdés, the machete-wielding mambí hero and Cuba’s best-loved cartoon character. —Anniversary. Elpidio first appeared on 4 August 1970 in the magazine Pionero; the opening show honoured his 55th anniversary, and he marked 56 years in August 2026. —Leadership. The project is led by Silvia Padrón Durán, Juan Padrón’s daughter and the guardian of his legacy. —Exhibition. Its inaugural interactive show, “¿Quién llamaba a Elpidio Valdés?”, gathered more than 60 artists across several generations.

In a rehabilitated space near Havana’s Plaza de la Revolución, a new cultural centre called La Manigua is keeping Cuba’s best-loved cartoon hero, Elpidio Valdés, alive as the mambí character marks another August anniversary.

Havana, home to La Manigua, the first Cuban cultural centre devoted to animator Juan Padrón. (Photo: Wikimedia Commons). (Photo: Wikimedia Commons)

A New Home for Elpidio Valdés

On 14 March 2026, the Espacio Cultural y Creativo La Manigua opened its doors just steps from the Plaza de la Revolución in Havana. It is the first cultural centre in Cuba dedicated entirely to the work of the animator Juan Padrón, creator of Elpidio Valdés.

Walking in feels like stepping into Elpidio’s universe. Early storyboards, magazine covers and memorabilia trace the life of the character who has become a fixture of Cuban popular culture over more than half a century.

The centre is run by Silvia Padrón Durán, Padrón’s daughter, who has taken on the task of keeping her father’s creations relevant for new generations of Cuban children.

Who Is Elpidio Valdés?

Elpidio Valdés is a mambí — a fighter in Cuba’s 19th-century wars of independence against Spain. Created by Juan Padrón, he first appeared on 4 August 1970 in the weekly magazine Pionero and went on to star in comics and animated films.

Produced through the ICAIC animation studios, his adventures became a touchstone for Cuban audiences. His catchphrases are woven into everyday speech, and his gentle humour made the story of the island’s fight for sovereignty approachable and fun.

For a foreign reader, the closest comparison is a national cartoon hero who doubles as a history lesson — a character children love and adults quote, whose appeal cuts across generations and politics.

What ‘La Manigua’ Means

The name is deliberate. In Cuban usage, la manigua is the dense bush or wilderness where the mambí independence fighters took cover — the natural habitat of a character like Elpidio Valdés.

The idea for the centre was first floated in December 2018, nurtured by Juan Padrón and his daughter Silvia before his death in 2020. Bringing it to life took years of effort in difficult economic conditions.

Silvia Padrón has said the project was built “al machete” — by sheer determination — and that opening in one of the country’s hardest moments was itself a statement about the enduring spirit of her father’s work.

Inside ‘¿Quién llamaba a Elpidio Valdés?’

The centre’s inaugural exhibition, “¿Quién llamaba a Elpidio Valdés?”, was conceived as a tribute to the character’s 55th anniversary and remained on view into the northern summer of 2026. It was designed to be played with rather than simply observed.

Children run through an immersive space with video mapping, a timeline of the character’s history, a solemn bust of the animated hero, and a collection of reinterpreted mambí hats. Visitors can build their own animation scenes or get temporary tattoos of favourite characters.

More than 60 visual artists, illustrators and designers took part, from Padrón’s brother Ernesto and niece Gabriela to figures such as Roberto Fabelo, Eduardo Roca “Choco” and Silvio Rodríguez, alongside young graduates of Havana’s art schools.

An Anniversary and a Living Legacy

Elpidio’s birthday is fixed to 4 August 1970, the date of his first public appearance. Having turned 55 in 2025, the character marked another year in August 2026, giving La Manigua a natural moment to celebrate his enduring place in Cuban life.

Juan Padrón, born in 1947, died in March 2020, but his influence on Cuban animation is hard to overstate. The centre frames its mission as updating the “affective memory” of his entire body of work, from comics to film.

As Silvia Padrón puts it, one of the strengths of her father’s work is that Elpidio is common ground — a figure who unites Cubans of all ages and backgrounds around shared humour and history.

Why It Matters for Visitors

For expats and travellers in Havana, La Manigua offers a different kind of cultural stop — less monument, more workshop — where the emphasis is on play, animation and creativity for children and families.

Practical details reflect the realities of today’s Cuba: the centre concentrates its public programme on weekends, partly because of fuel constraints, while running community projects during the week. Visitors should check current opening hours before going.

Even for those who did not grow up with Elpidio Valdés, the centre is a window into how a single cartoon character can carry a nation’s memory — and how a family is working to pass that legacy on.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is La Manigua?

La Manigua is the first cultural centre in Cuba dedicated to the work of animator Juan Padrón. It opened in March 2026 near Havana’s Plaza de la Revolución and is led by his daughter, Silvia Padrón Durán.

Who is Elpidio Valdés?

Elpidio Valdés is Cuba’s best-loved cartoon character, a mambí independence fighter created by Juan Padrón. He first appeared on 4 August 1970 in the magazine Pionero and later starred in comics and ICAIC animated films.

What was the centre’s first exhibition?

Its opening show, “¿Quién llamaba a Elpidio Valdés?”, was an interactive tribute to the character’s 55th anniversary featuring more than 60 artists. It let children play, create animation scenes and explore Elpidio’s world.

World.title: Bongo Charlie, Suriname’s Recycled-Sound Pioneer, Dies at 70
World.content:
Obituary: Paramaribo

Key Facts —Who. Leon “Charlie” Lemmer, known across Suriname as Bongo Charlie, was a percussionist, instrument maker and sound artist. —Death. He died on the evening of Sunday 2 August 2026 at the age of 70; he had reportedly suffered a stroke around May. —Signature. He built instruments from natural materials and recycled junk, guided by his lifelong motto, “Everything is sound.” —Inventions. His creations included the jungle tambourine, the tobobas, the quicka, a home-made xylophone and the EBS-drum, made from discarded utility-pole insulation wood. —Legacy. Based in rural Commewijne, he shaped Suriname’s music and art scene for decades and taught children through hands-on sound workshops.

Suriname has lost one of its most original artists: Leon Lemmer, the percussionist and instrument maker known as Bongo Charlie, has died at 70, leaving behind a world of sound built from recycled scrap and the raw materials of nature.

Paramaribo, the cultural heart of Suriname, where Bongo Charlie left his mark for decades. (Photo: Wikimedia Commons). (Photo: Wikimedia Commons)

A Singular Voice in Surinamese Music

Bongo Charlie, whose real name was Leon Lemmer, died on the evening of Sunday 2 August 2026 at the age of 70, the Paramaribo newspaper de Ware Tijd reported. He had suffered a stroke around May and, after a hospital stay, had been discharged only days before his death; the exact cause was not disclosed.

For decades he was one of the most distinctive figures in Surinamese music — a percussionist and instrument maker whose work sat somewhere between concert, craft and quiet philosophy. Fellow musicians responded with an outpouring of tributes.

His passing, colleagues said, leaves the country without an artist whose legacy will nonetheless keep resonating through the instruments and sound worlds he created.

‘Everything Is Sound’

Bongo Charlie’s guiding idea was disarmingly simple: “Everything is sound — even the wind.” That conviction turned the world around him into a workshop, where discarded metal strips, rubber blocks and hollow stems were all potential instruments.

He became known as a kind of recycling guru, coaxing music out of materials most people throw away. The approach was both artistic and practical, a way of making beauty from scarcity that felt deeply rooted in his rural surroundings.

That philosophy also shaped how he taught. He spoke warmly of workshops in which dozens of children swept bundles of coconut leaves through the air to make sound, discovering music in the most ordinary objects.

The Instruments He Invented

Over the years Bongo Charlie designed a personal orchestra of invented instruments. Among them were the jungle tambourine, the tobobas, the quicka, a home-made xylophone and the EBS-drum, built from insulation wood discarded from electricity poles.

Others were pure ingenuity: a “rainmaker” carved from bush papaya and filled with rice that whispered like a tropical downpour, a flute fashioned from a bicycle pump, and a harp-like string instrument he rebuilt from memory after seeing one in a shop.

He first presented this world of self-made instruments, masks and sculpture at Suriname’s National Art Fair in 1990, and later sold some pieces through the Readytex gallery in Paramaribo.

From Nickerie to Amsterdam and Back

Leon Lemmer grew up in Nickerie, in western Suriname, raised in the foster family of a respected local figure, Alwin Orna. Music surrounded him from the start; as a boy he played in a band with drums made from biscuit tins and oil barrels.

At 13 he moved to Paramaribo, and by the 1970s he was living in Amsterdam, immersed in the era’s rock scene and the clubs around the Leidseplein. He often cited bands like Deep Purple and Grand Funk Railroad as part of that formative period.

City life, though, had its limits for a man who said he needed nature to create. At the end of 1978 he returned to Suriname — and it was then, he said, that his real work began, as he started building drums and listening more closely to the land.

A Life Lived Close to Nature

Bongo Charlie settled across the Suriname River in Commewijne, on the grounds of a former plantation, where the sounds of the countryside fed his imagination. He built instruments, ran workshops and lived simply, close to the materials he loved.

His recorded output included the 1991 cassette “Authentic Feelings,” with tracks such as “Mother Africa” and “Universal Rhythms,” praised in the Surinamese press for its clarity and beauty. He also played in groups such as Mix Water and the peace-themed band Noyaso.

In 2024 he mounted a solo exhibition, “Sound of Nature,” showing his hand-made instruments — a late reminder of how completely his art and his environment had merged.

Remembering Bongo Charlie

Tributes came quickly from across the Surinamese music world. Singer Rosita Leeflang recalled their collaborations and jam sessions, while bassist Glenn Teixeira and keyboardist Sonny Khoeblal praised his creativity and craftsmanship.

Saxophonist Robin Austen called him “a unique sound artist who never got the appreciation he deserved” — a line that captured a widely shared sense that his originality had been under-recognised at home.

For expats and visitors curious about Suriname’s cultural life, Bongo Charlie is a reminder that the country’s music runs far beyond the mainstream, into workshops where a discarded pipe or a hollow stem could become an instrument.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who was Bongo Charlie?

Bongo Charlie was the stage name of Leon Lemmer, a Surinamese percussionist, instrument maker and sound artist known for building instruments from natural and recycled materials. He died on 2 August 2026 at the age of 70.

What instruments did he create?

He invented instruments such as the jungle tambourine, the tobobas, the quicka, a home-made xylophone and the EBS-drum, built from discarded utility-pole insulation wood, along with a bush-papaya ‘rainmaker’ and other pieces made from recycled objects.

Why was he important to Surinamese culture?

For decades he shaped Suriname’s music and art scene with a philosophy that ‘everything is sound,’ teaching children through workshops and exhibiting his self-made instruments. Fellow musicians remembered him as a uniquely creative, under-appreciated artist.

World.title: Free Mulled Wine Festival in Córdoba Honors Italian Roots
World.content:
Food: Córdoba

Key Facts —Event. The fifth Festival del Vin Brulé takes place on Sunday, 9 August 2026 at the Centro Cultural “Dr. Juan Carlos Cimadamore” in Despeñaderos, Córdoba province, Argentina. —Theme. The free event honours the town’s Italian-immigrant roots and is billed by local media as a trip to Italy without leaving Córdoba. —Star drink. Vin brulé — vino caliente, or mulled wine — is a spiced hot-wine recipe traced to ancient Rome and revived here each winter. —Program. Typical Italian food, tastings, live cooking demonstrations, stage shows, an artisans’ fair, a children’s area and a musical bingo fill the day. —Access. Admission is free; the festival is organised by the Despeñaderos municipality with support from Córdoba’s provincial tourism and culture agencies.

The Córdoba town of Despeñaderos hosts the fifth edition of its Festival del Vin Brulé on Sunday 9 August 2026, a free winter celebration of Italian food, music and mulled wine.

The city of Córdoba anchors the Argentine province whose town of Despeñaderos hosts the Vin Brulé festival. (Photo: Wikimedia Commons). (Photo: Wikimedia Commons)

A Winter Festival Built Around Mulled Wine

On Sunday 9 August 2026, the small town of Despeñaderos, south of the city of Córdoba, stages the fifth edition of its Festival del Vin Brulé. The gathering unfolds at the Centro Cultural “Dr. Juan Carlos Cimadamore” and, as in previous years, admission is free and open to everyone.

The festival has grown into a fixture of the regional winter calendar. It celebrates the Italian heritage of the community through food, music and the hot spiced wine that gives the event its name. Organisers say the aim is to strengthen local tourism and give the area’s small producers a showcase.

For a foreign visitor, the appeal is simple: a single, walkable afternoon that turns a quiet Córdoba town into an open-air Italian street party in the middle of the Southern Hemisphere winter.

What Vin Brulé Actually Is

Vin brulé — known in Spanish as vino caliente, and in English as mulled wine — is a hot drink made from wine simmered with sugar and spices. Local cooks trace the recipe to ancient Rome, where a warm, fortifying cup helped people get through the coldest days.

The preparation is part of the show. Wine is heated with ingredients such as citrus peel, cloves, cinnamon, star anise and sugar, then briefly set alight so the alcohol burns off before it is served steaming. Piedmontese descendants in the area prepare it live for the crowd.

In northern Italy, the drink is a symbol of hospitality, traditionally shared after Christmas Eve mass. That warmth and sense of welcome is exactly what the Despeñaderos festival tries to recreate each August.

A ‘Journey to Italy’ Without Leaving Córdoba

Córdoba province — in central Argentina, not the Spanish city of the same name — received waves of Italian immigrants who settled its towns and valleys. Despeñaderos is one of many communities where that ancestry still shapes surnames, cooking and festivals.

Local outlets have described the event as “a trip to Italy without leaving Córdoba,” a phrase that captures its ambition. Rather than a straightforward wine fair, it is a cultural homage designed to keep immigrant traditions alive for younger generations.

The programme is backed by Italian-community bodies alongside provincial agencies, and past editions have drawn thousands of visitors. That mix of grassroots pride and official support has helped the festival scale up edition after edition.

What’s on the Program

The day leans heavily on food. Recent editions featured masterclasses in Neapolitan pizza, chicken ravioli, focaccia and ancestral crostata, plus stands selling pasta, cured meats, sweets and regional specialities. Live demonstrations let visitors taste and learn at the same time.

Around the gastronomy sit stage shows, ballet and live music, a parade of classic Vespa scooters, an entrepreneurs’ market and a play area for children. A musical bingo has become one of the more popular crowd-pleasers.

The full 2026 line-up is released by organisers in the days before the event, but the structure is well established: a rolling schedule of cooking classes, folk and lyric performances and tastings that runs through the afternoon.

Where Despeñaderos Fits on the Map

Despeñaderos lies in the Santa María department, in the Valle de Paravachasca, a short drive south of the city of Córdoba. That makes it an easy day trip for anyone already based in or visiting Argentina’s second-largest city.

August falls in the depths of the Argentine winter, when the sierras draw visitors looking for crisp air, hearty food and warm drinks. A free festival built around hot wine fits neatly into that seasonal rhythm.

For travellers building a Córdoba itinerary, the festival pairs well with the region’s better-known winter attractions, from colonial towns to the Jesuit estancias that dot the province.

Why It Matters for Visitors and Expats

Free, family-friendly cultural events are among the easiest ways for newcomers to get a feel for local life, and the Vin Brulé festival is a low-commitment entry point. There is no ticket to buy and no camping to plan — just an afternoon in a welcoming town.

It also offers a window into the deep Italian roots of Argentine culture, which shape everything from everyday language to the national love of pasta and wine. Seeing that heritage celebrated in a small town says more than any museum plaque.

Anyone planning to attend should check the municipality’s channels for the final schedule and travel advice, dress for the cold, and arrive hungry. The combination of mulled wine, live cooking and music is best enjoyed slowly.

Frequently Asked Questions

When and where is the 2026 Vin Brulé festival?

The fifth Festival del Vin Brulé takes place on Sunday 9 August 2026 at the Centro Cultural “Dr. Juan Carlos Cimadamore” in Despeñaderos, in the province of Córdoba, Argentina. Admission is free.

What is vin brulé?

Vin brulé, or vino caliente, is a mulled wine made by simmering wine with sugar and spices such as cloves, cinnamon and citrus, then burning off the alcohol. The recipe is traced to ancient Rome and kept alive by the town’s Italian community.

How much does it cost to attend?

Entry to the festival is free and open to the public. Food, drinks and some activities are sold on site by local vendors and entrepreneurs, but there is no admission charge.

World.title: Free Uruguay Youth Festival Draws Thousands to Punta Del Este
World.content:
Community: Maldonado

Key Facts —Event. The Intendencia de Maldonado has launched Mes de la Juventud (Youth Month) 2026, a department-wide program for teenagers and young adults. —Dates. Activities run from 5 August to 12 September 2026, across the Uruguayan department that includes Punta del Este and San Carlos. —Cost. Every listed activity is free of charge. —Program. The calendar mixes sport, music, urban art, gaming and job-skills workshops, from social football to freestyle-rap battles and a closing rock festival. —Organizer. It is run by the Intendencia’s Directorate of Childhood, Adolescence and Youth, with events centered on Parque La Loma and the Casa de la Cultura.

Maldonado has opened its 2026 Youth Month: a five-week run of free sport, music, gaming and training aimed at young people across the Uruguayan department that includes Punta del Este.

Punta del Este anchors the department of Maldonado, host of the 2026 Youth Month. (Photo: Wikimedia Commons). (Photo: Wikimedia Commons)

A Five-Week Program for Young Residents

The government of Maldonado, the Uruguayan department that takes in Punta del Este, San Carlos and Piriápolis, has rolled out its 2026 Mes de la Juventud, or Youth Month. It runs from 5 August to 12 September, stretching the “month” across roughly five weeks.

The program targets teenagers and young adults and is organized by the Intendencia’s Directorate of Childhood, Adolescence and Youth. Its stated goal is to offer sport, culture, art, recreation and training in one coordinated calendar.

Crucially for families, every activity is free. The lineup ranges from social football and esports to freestyle shows, comics conventions and job-skills workshops, most clustered around Parque La Loma and the Casa de la Cultura in the city of Maldonado.

Sport, From Social Football to ‘Phygital’ Matches

Sport opens the program. A social football meetup launches the month on 5 August at the Miniestadio La Loma, framed as a low-pressure gathering for children and teenagers who play recreationally.

On 8 August, the Oficina Joven at Parque La Loma hosts a “Día Gamer,” an interactive video-game showcase with individual and team esports tournaments, a nod to how central gaming has become to youth culture.

A week later, on 15 August, “Phygital Football” blends a traditional match on the grass with digital competition, mixing physical and screen-based play in the same session.

Music and Urban Art on the Calendar

The arts strand runs the length of the program. On 6 August, young artists paint the skate park in San Carlos in an urban-art intervention, turning a sports space into a public canvas.

On 29 August, the Teatro Cantegril hosts “Parate de Rima Deluxe,” an evening of freestyle-rap battles that closes with a live show by artists from the genre, one of the marquee cultural nights of the month.

The program ends on a high on 12 September with “Rock del Este,” a festival of local rock bands on an open-air esplanade at Parque La Loma, paired with a food-and-crafts fair.

Geek Culture, Role-Play and Comics

A run of “geek” events fills out the calendar. On 15 and 16 August, “Punta Anime” takes over the hall of the Casa de la Cultura theater with stands and activities around film, series, comics, video games and board games, according to the Intendencia de Maldonado.

On 30 August, “Forjadores de Leyendas” gathers fans of tabletop role-playing and board games in the same venue, a dedicated space for a hobby that thrives on in-person play.

The comics thread returns on 5 September with “Maldonado Comics,” a convention of comic art and illustration featuring stands, exhibitions and workshops, a recurring fixture of the department’s youth programming.

Workshops Aimed at Jobs and Wellbeing

Beyond entertainment, the month carries a practical layer. On 12 and 13 August, a “McTrabajo” session at the Maldonado campus offers talks on getting hired, aimed at young people interested in work at McDonald’s.

Running through August and September, an online course in artificial intelligence, delivered with the national training agency INEFOP, teaches basic AI concepts and skills, reflecting a wider push to prepare youth for a changing job market.

A parallel initiative, “Ni Silencio Ni Tabú,” developed with the national youth institute INJU, holds sessions on the emotional wellbeing of adolescents and young adults, folding mental health into the program.

What It Signals for Families and Newcomers

For expat families settling around Punta del Este, Youth Month is a useful map of what the department offers young people outside the summer tourist season. The winter timing shows local life carrying on well after the beach crowds leave.

Because the activities are free and spread across several towns, they are easy to sample. Newcomers can use the calendar published by the Intendencia to find events near them, from La Loma in Maldonado to the skate park in San Carlos.

The breadth of the program, spanning sport, tech, mental health and the arts, also hints at how a Uruguayan department invests in its youth, a quality-of-life detail that often matters to families choosing where to live.

Frequently Asked Questions

When is Maldonado’s Youth Month 2026?

The Mes de la Juventud 2026 runs from 5 August to 12 September 2026, with activities across the department of Maldonado, Uruguay.

How much do the activities cost?

All listed activities are free of charge. They are organized by the Intendencia de Maldonado’s Directorate of Childhood, Adolescence and Youth.

What kind of events are included?

The program spans sport (social football, esports, “phygital” football), music and urban art (a rap-battle night and a closing rock festival), geek conventions (anime, role-play, comics) and workshops on jobs, artificial intelligence and wellbeing.

World.title: Miró Da Muribeca Honored at Recife’s Free Joyism Day Fest
World.content:
Culture: Recife

Key Facts —Event. Joyism Day (Dia do Alegrismo) is a date on Recife’s official cultural calendar honoring the late poet Miró da Muribeca. —Date. It falls on 6 August, the poet’s birthday; in 2026 he would have turned 66. —Organizer. The Museu de Artes Afro-Brasileiras Rolando Toro (Muafro) leads the programming, backed by federal Lei Paulo Gustavo funds via the Recife City Hall. —Program. Activities typically include poetry recitals, saraus, workshops, storytelling, film screenings and live music, all staged free of charge. —Where. Events center on the Muafro and the wider Recife Antigo district, including the poet’s statue on Avenida Rio Branco.

Each 6 August, Recife pauses to celebrate Joyism Day in memory of Miró da Muribeca, the Black, peripheral poet whose streetwise verse turned the city itself into a stage.

Recife's historic center is the backdrop for Joyism Day each 6 August. (Photo: Wikimedia Commons). (Photo: Wikimedia Commons)

A City Holiday Built Around a Poet

In most cities, a public honor day marks a battle, a saint or a founder. In Recife, one such date belongs to a poet. Joyism Day, known in Portuguese as Dia do Alegrismo, is written into the city’s official calendar of events and falls each year on 6 August.

The date is not random: it is the birthday of Miró da Muribeca, who would have turned 66 in 2026. Rather than a somber memorial, the day is conceived as a celebration, matching the humor and warmth that ran through his work.

The programming spreads across the city with free access, gathering poets, musicians, actors and neighbors around the memory of a writer who made everyday Recife his subject.

Who Miró da Muribeca Was

Born João Flávio Cordeiro da Silva in 1960, Miró took his stage name from the Muribeca neighborhood in Jaboatão dos Guararapes, part of greater Recife. He died in 2022, remembered as one of the most original voices in contemporary Brazilian poetry.

He published 17 books, some translated into other languages, and was known above all as a performer, reciting verse that mixed social criticism, street life, love and faith with sharp, disarming humor. Audiences who saw him rarely forgot the experience.

His standing is now cemented in public space. A statue of Miró stands on Avenida Rio Branco in the Bairro do Recife as part of the city’s Circuito da Poesia, and his work features in the Museu da Língua Portuguesa in São Paulo.

What ‘Alegrismo’ Means

The word “Alegrismo” is coined from “alegria,” the Portuguese for joy, and it is often rendered in English as “Joyism.” It nods to Miró’s own outlook; one of his best-known lines insists that, side effects aside, love is still the best medicine.

Organizers describe the day less as a tribute than as a manifesto, a way to keep alive the spirit of a Black poet from the periphery who made people laugh and think at the same time.

That framing matters in a city where poetry, street culture and Afro-Brazilian heritage overlap. Joyism Day places a peripheral, working-class artist at the very center of Recife’s cultural identity.

How the Celebration Usually Unfolds

Across its editions, the day has followed a full program of free activities: poetry recitals, saraus, writing and storytelling workshops, film screenings, theater and live music, running not only on 6 August but often across the following days. Coverage in Folha de Pernambuco has documented this pattern year after year.

Daytime tends to belong to younger audiences, with workshops and storytelling aimed at students, while evenings shift to screenings, saraus and concerts in cultural venues around the old center.

A recurring highlight is a gathering at the poet’s statue on Avenida Rio Branco, where recitals and performances close the celebration in the open air, in the neighborhood most tied to his image.

The Muafro and the Support Behind It

The programming is led by the Museu de Artes Afro-Brasileiras Rolando Toro, the Muafro, a museum in the Bairro do Recife that has become a hub of the district’s Afro-Brazilian cultural circuit, working with local producers to stage the events.

Funding has come through the federal Lei Paulo Gustavo, a national culture-support law, channeled via the Recife City Hall. That public backing is what allows the day to stay free and open to all.

The partnership signals how Recife values the arts: a municipal holiday, a public museum and federal cultural funds combine to keep a single poet’s legacy in active circulation.

Why It Resonates for Expats in Recife

For newcomers, Joyism Day is a low-cost, high-context window into Recife’s culture. The events are free, centered in the walkable Recife Antigo, and rooted in local life rather than a tourist script.

Even for those still learning Portuguese, the performative, musical side of the day carries much of the meaning, and the setting, the historic port district, is worth the visit on its own.

More than that, the celebration introduces a figure every long-term resident eventually hears about. Understanding Miró da Muribeca is a shortcut to understanding how Recife sees itself.

Frequently Asked Questions

When is Joyism Day in Recife?

Joyism Day (Dia do Alegrismo) is held every 6 August, the birthday of poet Miró da Muribeca. It is part of Recife’s official calendar of cultural events.

Who organizes it and how much does it cost?

The Museu de Artes Afro-Brasileiras Rolando Toro (Muafro) leads the programming, supported by federal Lei Paulo Gustavo funds via the Recife City Hall. The activities are free and open to the public.

Who was Miró da Muribeca?

He was a Recife poet (1960–2022), author of 17 books and a celebrated performer of his own verse, honored with a statue on Avenida Rio Branco and a place in the Museu da Língua Portuguesa in São Paulo.

What the Second Cycle Puts on View

The Bienal de Artes Plásticas y Visuales is a recurring showcase of contemporary art run by the city of Bogotá. Its eighth edition is being staged in two cycles, and the second has now opened, gathering five exhibitions under a shared focus on how cities are built, remembered and reshaped over time.

Organizers frame the cycle around territory, collective memory, architecture and urban transformation. Rather than a single subject, the works pose a common question: what holds a city together, and what is lost as it changes.

With this cycle, the biennial completes the ten projects chosen for the current edition, splitting them across two rounds so each group of works has room to breathe in the halls.

Five Exhibitions, One Question About the City

The cycle brings together five shows. “Lo que soporta la montaña” (What the Mountain Holds Up), by Lucas Gallego and Carolina Borrero, and “Fábrica” (Factory), by César Faustino, anchor the group, alongside “SPOLIA,” developed by the collective Studio GL.

Two further projects, “Metrópolis 2027” and “Armas de negación de área” (Area-Denial Weapons), round out the selection. Each proposes its own reading of the contemporary city, using installation, intervention and visual research to connect art, architecture and society.

For a visitor, the payoff is variety within a clear thread. The works move from the physical weight of landscape to the machinery of industry and the layered reuse of old materials, a concept the Latin term “spolia” describes directly.

The curators lean on the idea that urban space is never neutral. Occupation, memory and the ways communities live with their surroundings surface across the five shows, turning the halls into what the foundation calls spaces of dialogue.

Where to Find the Biennial in La Candelaria

All five exhibitions are concentrated in one place: the exhibition halls and auditorium of the Teatro FUGA, at Calle 10 #3-16, in the historic La Candelaria district at the heart of Bogotá.

La Candelaria is the city’s colonial core, a walkable grid of museums, universities and government buildings. Placing the biennial here lets visitors pair it with nearby cultural stops without crossing the city.

The single-venue format is convenient for newcomers. There is no need to map out scattered galleries; the full cycle can be seen in one visit, which suits travelers and residents short on time.

Who Runs It and Why the FUGA Matters

The biennial is produced by the Fundación Gilberto Alzate Avendaño, known as the FUGA, a public cultural institution attached to Bogotá’s district government. It programs exhibitions, concerts and public events from its base in La Candelaria.

As a city entity, the FUGA leans toward free, accessible programming and toward Colombian artists and collectives. The biennial is one of its flagship platforms, giving selected projects a professional exhibition space and a public audience.

That civic backing shapes the tone. The foundation presents the cycle as a tool for understanding social and urban change, positioning art as a way to think through the transformations residents live with every day.

How to Visit, and What It Costs

Admission is free for everyone, with no ticket required. The cycle is open Tuesday through Saturday, from 10:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m., according to the Bogotá city government.

The second cycle runs from 31 July to 5 September 2026, so visitors have several weeks to catch all five shows. A weekday morning usually means quieter halls and more time with each work.

Because everything sits inside the Teatro FUGA, planning is simple: arrive during opening hours, and the full route through the exhibitions is available on site.

Why the Biennial Speaks to Expats in Bogotá

For foreign residents, the biennial is an approachable entry into Colombia’s contemporary-art scene. The works are visual and spatial, so language is rarely a barrier, and the themes of memory and city-making translate across cultures.

It also doubles as a guided reason to explore La Candelaria, the district many newcomers visit first. A morning at the FUGA can anchor a wider walk through Bogotá’s historic center.

More broadly, a free, city-run biennial signals how Bogotá treats culture as public infrastructure. For expats weighing the city’s quality of life, that steady stream of accessible art is part of the appeal.

Frequently Asked Questions

When and where is the second cycle of the Bogotá biennial?

The second cycle (Ciclo II) of the VIII Bienal de Artes Plásticas y Visuales runs from 31 July to 5 September 2026 at the Teatro FUGA, Calle 10 #3-16, in La Candelaria, Bogotá.

How many exhibitions are there and what are they?

There are five: “Lo que soporta la montaña,” “Fábrica,” “SPOLIA,” “Metrópolis 2027” and “Armas de negación de área,” together completing the ten projects of this edition.

How much do tickets cost?

Entry is free for all visitors, with no ticket required. The halls are open Tuesday to Saturday, 10:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m.

World.title: Brazilian Singer Sérgio Santos Plays Free Fortaleza Show at 70
World.content:
Music: Fortaleza

Key Facts —Event. Singer, composer and guitarist Sérgio Santos, from Minas Gerais, marks his 70th birthday with a concert in Fortaleza, capital of Ceará. —When and where. The show is on Thursday 13 August 2026 at 8 pm, at the Banco do Nordeste Cultural (Centro Cultural Banco do Nordeste), Rua Conde D’Eu 560, in the city centre. —Admission. Entry is free (entrada franca), with an open age rating. —Format. Santos performs solo in a voice-and-guitar format, drawing on his new album “Todo Samba” and songs from across a 45-year career. —Guests. Special guests from Ceará’s music scene join him, in what is his first performance at this Fortaleza venue.

Brazilian music master Sérgio Santos celebrates his 70th birthday with a free voice-and-guitar concert in Fortaleza on Thursday 13 August 2026, sharing songs from a new album and a 45-year career with a Ceará audience.

Fortaleza, capital of Ceará, hosts Sérgio Santos's 70th-birthday concert. (Photo: Wikimedia Commons). (Photo: Wikimedia Commons)

A 70th-birthday concert in Fortaleza

Sérgio Santos, one of Brazilian popular music’s most respected composers and interpreters, turns 70 in 2026, and he is marking the milestone with a concert in Fortaleza. The show doubles as a career celebration, folding in 45 years of work.

It is, notably, his first time performing at the Banco do Nordeste Cultural in the Ceará capital. The choice of an intimate cultural centre, rather than a large arena, fits the reflective, career-spanning nature of the evening.

For a foreign reader, Santos may be an unfamiliar name, but within Brazil he is a heavyweight — a singer, composer, guitarist, arranger and researcher whose songs have been recorded and celebrated across generations.

Who is Sérgio Santos

Born in Minas Gerais, Santos built his reputation as much on his pen as his voice. He is one of the most prolific partners of lyricist Paulo César Pinheiro, and together the pair have written more than 300 songs, including the acclaimed album “Áfrico,” which left a lasting mark on Brazilian music.

His path crystallised early. In 1981 he joined the choir of the “Missa dos Quilombos,” a landmark work performed with Milton Nascimento, and from there committed fully to a life in music.

Across the decades he has moved between samba, Minas Gerais song traditions and sophisticated arrangement, earning a reputation as a musician’s musician — admired by peers as much as by audiences.

The new album “Todo Samba”

The Fortaleza concert arrives as Santos releases “Todo Samba,” an album of previously unreleased songs. It is built around an instrumental partnership with Nailor Azevedo, the celebrated clarinettist and arranger known as Proveta.

The record also gathers longtime collaborators. It features contributions from Francis and Olivia Hime and from Paulo César Pinheiro, underscoring how much of Santos’s work is rooted in decades-long creative friendships.

In 2026 Santos also lent his voice to a tribute album for the late Ceará master Tarcísio Sardinha, singing the samba “No Revés dessa Voz” — a connection that gives his Fortaleza visit added local resonance.

What to expect at the show

The concert is staged in a voice-and-guitar format, stripping the music back to Santos’s singing and his own accompaniment. That intimate setup puts the songwriting front and centre, spanning both the new album and different phases of his career.

He will also welcome guest performers from Ceará’s own music scene, turning the evening into a meeting between a Minas Gerais master and local artists. The result is pitched as a one-off, celebratory encounter rather than a standard tour stop.

Entry is free, with an open age rating, making it an accessible night out for curious newcomers as well as devoted fans.

The venue and Fortaleza’s cultural calendar

The Banco do Nordeste Cultural, also known as the Centro Cultural Banco do Nordeste, sits at Rua Conde D’Eu 560 in Fortaleza’s Centro district. It is one of a network of bank-run cultural centres that host free concerts, theatre and exhibitions across the Northeast.

For expats in Fortaleza, these centres are among the easiest entry points into Brazilian cultural life: central, free and consistently programmed. A concert like this one offers a chance to hear a nationally significant artist without leaving the city centre.

The visit also feeds a busy local calendar. The day after the concert, on 14 August, Santos takes part in an event tied to the new Instituto Tarcísio Sardinha, deepening his ties to Ceará’s music community.

Practical details

The concert takes place on Thursday 13 August 2026 at 8 pm at the Banco do Nordeste Cultural, Rua Conde D’Eu 560, Centro, Fortaleza. Admission is free, and the age rating is open to all.

Because free cultural-centre shows can fill quickly, arriving early is wise. Anyone keen to hear Santos’s new material live will find the intimate room well suited to a voice-and-guitar performance.

Frequently Asked Questions

When and where is Sérgio Santos’s Fortaleza concert?

The concert is on Thursday 13 August 2026 at 8 pm at the Banco do Nordeste Cultural (Centro Cultural Banco do Nordeste), Rua Conde D’Eu 560, in the Centro district of Fortaleza. Admission is free.

Why is the concert significant?

It celebrates Sérgio Santos’s 70th birthday and 45-year career, and marks his first performance at the venue. He presents his new album “Todo Samba” alongside songs from across his career.

What is the format of the show?

Santos performs solo in a voice-and-guitar format, joined by special guests from Ceará’s music scene, in an intimate cultural-centre setting rather than a large concert hall.

World.title: Costa Rica Airport Laser Incidents Reach Record High
World.content:
Reports of people pointing laser beams at aircraft near Juan Santamaría International Airport in San Jose have reached their highest level since officials began tracking the incidents in 2016. The airport registered 74 laser interference reports during the latest annual reporting period, a 72% increase from the previous period’s 43 cases.

The increase cannot be explained only by the growth in air traffic. The rate rose from 0.93 to 1.37 reports for every 1,000 aircraft operations during 2025, indicating that the practice itself has become more frequent. Airport officials warned that laser beams can temporarily impair a pilot’s vision during takeoff and landing, when crews depend heavily on visual references and must make decisions within seconds.



In one reported incident, a captain transferred control of the aircraft to the first officer after the laser affected the captain’s vision. Other crews reported temporary visual problems while approaching the airport from distances of approximately 5.5 to 11 kilometers (3 to 6 nautical miles).

None of the incidents caused an accident or prevented an aircraft from landing safely. However, officials said the reports show that laser interference is having a real effect inside aircraft cockpits. Exposure to a laser beam can cause glare, temporary blindness, lingering images and distraction. Even when the effects last only briefly, they can increase the crew’s workload during the most demanding stages of a flight.

Most of the incidents occurred between 6 p.m. and 11 p.m., with the highest concentration between 7 p.m. and 9 p.m. Laser beams are more visible at night and can reach aircraft several kilometers from the runway. December, January and February recorded the most reports. Those months coincide with Costa Rica’s peak tourism season, holiday travel and some of the busiest periods of operation at the country’s main international airport.



Juan Santamaría handles the majority of Costa Rica’s international passenger traffic. Aircraft approaching the airport pass over several heavily populated areas, making it difficult for authorities to immediately find the person responsible for a laser incident.

Airport officials have urged residents to understand that pointing a laser at an aircraft is not a harmless joke. A beam that appears small from the ground can spread across a cockpit window, filling a pilot’s field of vision with bright light. Costa Rica’s Penal Code establishes prison sentences of two to six years for knowingly carrying out an act that endangers an aircraft or the safety of air transportation.

The incidents are reviewed by the airport’s operational safety committees, while prevention campaigns have been coordinated with Costa Rica’s civil aviation authorities. Anyone who sees a laser being pointed toward an aircraft or airport area should contact the 9-1-1 emergency system and provide the location from which the beam appears to be coming. Authorities said precise location details can help police respond before another aircraft is targeted.

Airport officials are particularly concerned because most cases occur while aircraft are making their final approach to the runway. At that stage, pilots are flying at lower altitudes, monitoring instruments and maintaining visual contact with the runway and surrounding traffic. The record number of reports has renewed calls for greater public awareness and stronger prevention efforts in communities along the airport’s main flight paths.

World.title: Carlos Alcaraz Withdraws From Cincinnati Open With Wrist Injury
World.content:
Carlos Alcaraz has withdrawn from the 2026 Cincinnati Open as he continues to recover from the wrist injury that has kept him away from competition since April. The ATP Tour confirmed the decision Tuesday, ending hopes that the defending champion would make his long-awaited return at the Masters 1000 tournament in Ohio.

Alcaraz had entered Cincinnati as part of a planned comeback ahead of the US Open. Tournament organizers initially included him among a field led by Jannik Sinner, Alexander Zverev, Novak Djokovic, Taylor Fritz and Ben Shelton. However, the 23-year-old Spaniard has not recovered sufficiently to compete in the Cincinnati main draw, which begins August 13.

“We know Carlos is doing everything he can to get back to playing tournaments as soon as possible,” tournament director Bob Moran said in a statement. The withdrawal extends an absence that began at the Barcelona Open in April. Alcaraz has since missed several of the biggest tournaments on the calendar, including the French Open and Wimbledon.

Cincinnati would have provided his only scheduled competitive preparation before the US Open men’s singles tournament begins August 30 in New York. Alcaraz has not announced that he will miss the US Open, but his Cincinnati withdrawal raises further questions about whether he will be ready for the final Grand Slam of the season.

Returning directly at a best-of-five-set tournament would leave him without a competitive match in more than four months. The wrist injury interrupted what had been an outstanding start to the year. Alcaraz opened the season by winning the Australian Open, completing the career Grand Slam and becoming the youngest man to win all four major singles titles.

He has compiled a 22-3 record and won two ATP titles in 2026 despite playing his most recent match in April. The ATP Tour listed him as the world No. 2 when announcing his Cincinnati withdrawal. Alcaraz was due to defend 1,000 ranking points in Ohio after winning the 2025 Cincinnati title. He claimed the championship when Sinner was forced to retire from their final.

His absence removes one of the tournament’s leading attractions and eliminates the possibility of another Cincinnati meeting between the two biggest stars in men’s tennis. Sinner will now enter as the clear headline player in the men’s field. The Italian won Wimbledon earlier this summer and has been the dominant player at Masters 1000 level during the 2026 season.

The Cincinnati Open has not yet announced how Alcaraz’s place in the field will be filled. His withdrawal could allow the next eligible player into the main draw or create an additional opening for a qualifier or lucky loser, depending on when the draw is finalized. For Alcaraz, the immediate priority remains completing his recovery rather than rushing back before the US Open. His status for New York will now become one of the biggest questions in tennis over the coming weeks.

World.title: Costa Rica Police Report Links 116 Officers to Criminal Groups
World.content:
A confidential police intelligence report has flagged 116 Fuerza Pública officers stationed along Costa Rica’s southern border, describing alleged collaboration with drug trafficking, liquor smuggling and migrant smuggling networks in a region that has drawn increasing law enforcement attention.

The report dated April 12, was produced by the Directorate of Intelligence and Criminal Analysis of the Ministry of Public Security and addressed to Marlon Cubillo, then director general of the Fuerza Pública. The review was ordered by its own senior command amid suspicions that organized crime had penetrated policing in the area.

Investigators examined the backgrounds of 122 officers assigned to the Brunca Sur regional directorate, covering the Golfito, Coto Brus, Corredores and Puerto Jiménez delegations, and recorded observations on 116 of them. The report states explicitly that its findings do not constitute judicial evidence. No officer named in it has been charged in connection with the review.

According to the analysis, several of the officers appear in the registry maintained by the Costa Rican Drug Institute as suspected collaborators of trafficking organizations. The roles attributed to them include escort work, logistical support, coordinating the landing of aircraft on clandestine airstrips, and moving drug shipments through the southern zone. The report also alleges that officers received payments in connection with those aircraft arrivals and, in some instances, provided cover from police vehicles for cars carrying narcotics.

The single largest concentration of alleged infiltration involves not drugs but alcohol. Intelligence analysts concluded that at least 44 officers maintained suspected links to a liquor smuggling organization known as Los Whiskeros, allegedly warning the group about checkpoints, passing along restricted information about planned operations, coordinating vehicle movements and, in some cases, escorting illegal shipments in exchange for payment.

Drawing on human sources, the document identifies an officer surnamed Moya as the alleged organizer of the structure inside the Fuerza Pública, describing him as recruiting other officers and directing institutional personnel and equipment according to the needs of the criminal groups.

Beyond the trafficking allegations, the review flagged individual officers in connection with other suspected offenses, including one case of femicide, three of rape, one of domestic violence and five of aiding an offender. The findings arrive alongside a series of separate cases involving police personnel. Prosecutors have charged a group of officers in the Caribbean lowlands over alleged assistance to the organization led by Alejandro Arias Monge, known as Diablo, in a file built largely on intercepted phone calls.

A former Fuerza Pública officer from Corredores, within the same southern region covered by this review, is being held for extradition to the United States on drug trafficking allegations. And evidence presented to a federal court in Texas in an unrelated prosecution described payments to National Coast Guard personnel in exchange for allowing cocaine shipments to pass.

The intelligence unit attributed the vulnerability primarily to two factors. The first is financial pressure on officers, which the report’s confidential sources described as making collaboration attractive as supplementary income.

The second is weak oversight by mid-level commanders over the use of patrol vehicles and communications equipment. The analysis further warned that officers with personnel under their command are especially likely to be involved, and that their supervisory position makes them particularly valuable to criminal organizations.

The report recommended relocating officers with no established ties to the southern zone and referring its findings for administrative and criminal investigation. The areas covered by the review sit along the Panama border and the Osa Peninsula, taking in the Paso Canoas crossing, the Golfo Dulce and the airstrips and coastline that have featured repeatedly in trafficking prosecutions.

The document was written nearly four months before it became public, and it remains unclear what action the Fuerza Pública took on its recommendations in the interval, or whether the disciplinary and criminal referrals it proposed were opened.

World.title: Where Fixed Internet Still Does Not Reach in Costa Rica
World.content:
If your income depends on a stable connection, the area you pick in Costa Rica matters more than the country you picked. Nearly three in ten households here have no fixed internet at all. That gap is not spread evenly, and it sits heaviest in exactly the rural and coastal places that show up on relocation shortlists.

A new analysis from the Telecommunications Administration Chair at the Universidad Estatal a Distancia (UNED), built on figures from the telecom regulator SUTEL, maps that gap across the country. The regulator counts fixed subscriptions against population rather than households, which puts the national figure at 22 per 100 residents. Forty-two areas fall below that line, and five sit far below it.

Area Subscriptions per 100 residents Guatuso 3.4% Los Chiles 3.5% Upala 4.6% Talamanca 6.3% La Cruz 8.8% The five lowest-ranked areas for fixed internet, measured as subscriptions per 100 residents. The national figure is 22 per 100. Source: Reporte Cantonal de Servicios Fijos, prepared by SUTEL’s Markets Directorate, using December 2023 data.

Nandayure, Matina, Buenos Aires, Alvarado, Abangares and Sarapiquí sit just above them. Read those names against a map and the pattern is obvious. Talamanca is Puerto Viejo and Cahuita. Guatuso sits in the northern lowlands near Tenorio Volcano National Park. Nandayure covers a stretch of the Nicoya Peninsula. La Cruz runs to the Nicaraguan border above Guanacaste’s beach towns. These are not remote outposts. They are places people move to on purpose.

One caveat matters before you plan around these numbers. They date from December 2023, and they count subscriptions against population, so one household line covers everyone under that roof. Measured the other way, against homes rather than people, national coverage has climbed steadily, from 64.6% of households at the end of 2023 to 66% at the end of 2024 and 71% during 2025.

The regulator’s 2024 report switched to districts and to that household measure, so its figures do not line up against the table above. What that leaves you with is a direction rather than a number. The areas listed have almost certainly improved since the count, but nothing published since tells you by how much.

What the 2024 report does show is where the shortfall sits now. The Central, Chorotega and Pacific Central regions all met or beat the national household penetration rate of 66%. Brunca, Huetar Caribe and Huetar Norte fell below it. Average download speeds split along the same line, running 122.1 Mbps in the Central region against 82.8 Mbps in Pacific Central, 74.3 in Chorotega, 61.5 in Huetar Caribe, 46.6 in Huetar Norte and 44.7 in Brunca.

Parts of that will surprise you. Santa Cruz in Guanacaste carries 21,915 fixed internet subscriptions, third highest of any district. Nosara runs 99% of its connections on fiber or coaxial cable. Tamarindo posts the fastest average download speed on the Chorotega side, and La Fortuna leads the Huetar Norte.

But read that fiber figure carefully, because it describes the share of existing connections that are high speed, not the share of homes that have one. A place can run almost entirely on fiber and still leave most of its houses unconnected. Nosara at 99% tells you the connections there are good. It does not tell you how many houses have one.

The reason your street may not have fiber has little to do with demand. It has to do with poles. Fiber optic lines and mobile base stations ride on electrical posts, and Costa Rica has more than 500,000 of them spread across eight electricity companies. A diagnostic by the Infrastructure Commission found that 95% of operators run into obstacles getting access.

Sometimes the pole is already full. Sometimes it is too short to carry another line safely. Sometimes it is in poor physical shape, or the permit to attach anything to it takes months to clear. Any one of those stops a build, which is why a neighborhood can sit a few kilometers from fiber and never get it.

Poles are only half the story. When the regulator asked people in the Huetar Norte why they had no fixed line, the answers pointed at the household rather than the network. Fifty-seven percent said the service cost too much. Another 14% said they did not know how to use it. Walter Herrera, who directs the regulator’s markets division, singled out that second number as the one worth pausing over, since no amount of fiber addresses it. For you the practical read is different. Low penetration in an area does not always mean no service reaches it. Sometimes the cable already runs past the door and the neighbors have decided they cannot justify the bill.

Mobile is what fills the hole. Fixed internet reached 71% of households during 2025, but mobile internet runs at 106% per inhabitant, roughly 5.5 million subscriptions in a place of about five million people. In the low-coverage areas, that is not a statistic. It is how people actually get online, through an LTE router or a satellite dish rather than a cable.

So test before you commit. Ask your landlord or seller what is physically installed at the address, not what is available in the district. Run a speed test standing in the room you would work from, at the hour you would work. Ask neighbors what happens in heavy rain, because saturated mobile cells and aging poles both fail in weather. If the answer is a mobile router, budget for a backup line on a second carrier. That advice applies whether you are arriving on a remote worker visa or buying a house outright.

José Roberto Santamaría Sandoval, who heads the UNED chair, said the divide is no longer a technology question. He said a family without access faces greater difficulty studying, working, starting a business, reaching public services or taking part in the digital economy, and that this turns into a social gap. He added that infrastructure alone is not enough, and that digital skills have to be built alongside it, particularly for people on lower incomes, with less schooling, older adults and those living outside the Greater Metropolitan Area.

The cost of the lag has been put in numbers. The Ministry of Science, Innovation, Technology and Telecommunications estimated in 2024 that Costa Rica forgoes up to $1.587 billion in economic development opportunity because of the accumulated delay in deploying next-generation telecom infrastructure. Santamaría framed what that means at community level, saying a place without good connectivity loses more than internet access. It loses the ability to attract investment, build businesses, support remote work arrangements, raise productivity and create jobs.

Some of the response is arriving piecemeal. UNED has installed ten satellite internet antennas through its RED UNED project, reaching rural, coastal and Indigenous communities with little or no connectivity and serving more than 250 students. The telecom sector itself is not struggling, having generated revenue of ₡804.95 billion during 2025, grown 4.9% and sustained 11,777 direct jobs.

The next pressure is already visible. Artificial intelligence tools demand more processing capacity and more electricity, and the analysis warns Costa Rica will need to strengthen both its energy supply and its technology infrastructure to meet that. Santamaría said the challenge is not simply adopting the technology but building the infrastructure, energy, regulation and skilled workforce to use it safely and sustainably. For the areas still waiting on a fiber line, that debate arrives well ahead of the connection.

World.title: National Commission for Families and Children launches child protection training
World.content:
National Commission for Families and Children launches child protection training

By Zoila Palma: The National Commission for Families and Children (NCFC), with the support of the Ministry of Education, Culture, Science and Technology, launched the first child protection training session for teachers from Wesley College, Excelsior High School, and Gwen Lizarraga High School.

The NCFC explained that as mandatory reporters and a critical line of defense for vulnerable children, teachers play a vital role in recognizing signs of abuse, reporting concerns, and safeguarding children’s rights and well-being.

This initiative will strengthen educators’ knowledge of child protection, safeguarding, and their responsibilities under Belize’s child protection framework, with a total of 80 teachers expected to be trained to help ensure every child is protected, heard, and supported.

World.title: Ministry of Agriculture hosts soil sampling methodologies training in San Antonio, Cayo
World.content:
Ministry of Agriculture hosts soil sampling methodologies training in San Antonio, Cayo

By Zoila Palma: On August 4th 2026, a Soil Sampling Methodologies training was conducted in San Antonio, Cayo with the SAYAB Farmer’s Cooperative.

A total of 16 cooperative members comprising the SAYAB cooperative were present this morning in the execution of Soil Sampling Methodologies.

The cooperative was founded in 2017 as non-traditional producer of vegetables and spices such as arugula, thyme, basil and other nice spices that are very much used in both Belizean and American cuisine.

Today, Enrique Rivas and Israel Pech delivered a Soils Sampling Methodologies training; and their experiences so that the cooperative members would be able to make more educated decisions when it comes to their soils and fertilizer amendments.

Soils are very rich in nutrients nevertheless as years pass; the producers need to make better amendments to compensate for those that are being depleted by the different crops cultivated.

The Ministry says that the cooperative is now fully capable of doing their samples and ship them to the different laboratories to get the results of their soil samples.

Once this information is received, they will also get the recommendations from the Ministry of Agriculture, Food Security and New Growth Industries in the amends that they will need to conduct so they are safer and more productive in their production parcels.

The collaboration between MAFSNGI and IICA focuses on assisting farmers with the knowledge for them to make better decisions in their farms.

The event was coordinated with Dale Pech, extension officer of the COSAL Project for the Inter American Institute for Cooperation on Agriculture (IICA).

World.title: Galen University, Transparent BPO partner with Corazon Creek Technical High School to expand higher education and employment opportunities
World.content:
Galen University, Transparent BPO partner with Corazon Creek Technical High School to expand higher education and employment opportunities

By Zoila Palma: Representatives from Galen University and Transparent BPO visited Corazon Creek Technical High School (CCTHS) on Monday, August 3, to advance a new initiative aimed at expanding access to higher education and employment opportunities for students in Corazon Creek and neighboring communities.

The partnership will allow the first cohort of Galen University students to begin classes during the upcoming fall semester while working at Transparent BPO, which will operate from the CCTHS campus.

The program is designed to enable students to earn an income, gain valuable professional experience, and pursue their university education at the same time.

Representing Galen University during the visit were Dr. Cynthia Eve Aird, Provost, and Hiram Ochaeta, Director of Digital Strategy and Strategic Management. Transparent BPO was represented by Angie Westby, Human Resources Business Partner, and Abraham Middleton, Vice President of Network Infrastructure.

The initiative reflects a collaborative effort to create new educational and career pathways for young people in southern Belize, helping to reduce barriers to higher education while preparing students for the workforce through practical experience.

Galen University said it looks forward to strengthening its partnership with Corazon Creek Technical High School under the leadership of Board of Management Chairman Justo Veliz Jr., as the institutions work together to provide students with greater opportunities for academic and professional success.

World.title: We bid, we lost: Recinos Group answers procurement questions
World.content:
We bid, we lost: Recinos Group answers procurement questions

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): The Recinos Group of Companies has issued a public statement addressing what it describes as recent questions concerning its participation in government procurement processes, declaring that its construction arm submitted a proposal in the process at issue, did not win the bid, and was not awarded the contract.

The statement, dated August 3, 2026, responds to public commentary which, according to the group, has referred to a well-known entrepreneur from the Cayo District whose career began in the beauty industry. The group says it considers it important to provide a more complete understanding of the businesses involved and their history.

According to the statement, Maria Estella Recinos has built and expanded a diverse group of businesses over more than three decades, operating across retail trade, construction, importation, exportation, distribution, beauty services, logistics, and entrepreneurship initiatives. The group includes K&M Construction Company Ltd., Salon Essentials Ltd., Maria Estella’s Beauty Salon, and other affiliated enterprises and initiatives, including Women in Business. K&M Construction is described as a Belizean construction company engaged in construction-related works and services, including the execution and support of building and infrastructure projects.

The group states that its businesses have maintained commercial relationships with customers, suppliers, contractors, and institutions in Belize and abroad, including partners in Guatemala, El Salvador, the United States, and Guyana, and that, like many established Belizean companies, members of the group have participated in public procurement processes, supplying goods and services to both public and private sector clients in the ordinary course of business.

On the matter driving the commentary, the statement is direct: “The receipt of an invitation to participate in a procurement process is not, in itself, evidence of wrongdoing, nor does the submission of a proposal guarantee that a contract will ultimately be awarded.” It continues, “In this instance, K&M Construction Company Ltd. submitted a proposal but did not win the bid and was not awarded the contract.”

The statement closes on the principle at the heart of the season’s procurement debates: “The public has every right to expect transparency and accountability, and we support that principle fully. Equally, however, we believe that the public is entitled to receive complete, accurate, and properly contextualized information concerning the work that our businesses have undertaken over many years.”

It should be noted that the statement does not identify the specific procurement process in question or the source of the public commentary it addresses, and no allegation of wrongdoing against the group has been established in any official forum. The statement represents the group’s account of its position.

The exchange lands amid a period of heightened public attention on government procurement across several ministries, a climate in which established businesses and public institutions alike are finding their processes under the microscope, and in which, as this statement illustrates, the right of reply is being exercised as vigorously as the scrutiny itself.

World.title: One month of summer left: Cahal Pech Village Resort is the family’s last hurrah
World.content:
One month of summer left: Cahal Pech Village Resort is the family’s last hurrah

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP):The school year is coming, uniforms are being fitted, and the summer holidays have entered their final stretch. Cahal Pech Village Resort in San Ignacio is making the case that August deserves one proper family escape before the routine returns.

The hilltop resort above San Ignacio is built for exactly that kind of trip. The pools handle the day shift, keeping children happily occupied for hours, while the views across the Cayo countryside handle the parents’ end of the bargain, best enjoyed from the bar with a cold drink as the sun drops. On-site dining means nobody has to cook on holiday, and the thatched cabana setting delivers the away-from-it-all feeling minutes from town.

For families who want one more adventure in the memory bank, the location does the heavy lifting: the ancient Maya site of Cahal Pech sits right beside the resort, with Xunantunich, cave adventures and the San Ignacio market all within easy reach.

Bookings are one call away at 824-3740, on WhatsApp at 671-5737, or online at www.cahalpech.com.

Summer is not over yet. Close it out on the hilltop.

World.title: Galen University opens MBA applications with online delivery built for working Belizeans
World.content:
Galen University opens MBA applications with online delivery built for working Belizeans

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): Belizean professionals eyeing the next rung on the career ladder have a homegrown option on the table. Galen University is accepting applications for its Master in Social Work, a two year programme delivered fully online and, in the university’s own words, designed for Belize and Belizeans.

The structure targets the working professional squarely. Online delivery means managers, public officers and business owners can pursue the degree without leaving their jobs or relocating to campus, and the two year duration gives a clear finish line. Galen has also put its pricing in plain view: $600 BZD per credit hour, allowing applicants to plan the investment semester by semester.

The localization is the quiet selling point. A masters designed for the Belizean context means coursework and case discussion grounded in the economy graduates will actually lead in, and classmates drawn from the country’s own professional ranks, the network that pays dividends long after graduation.

The timing carries urgency. Galen’s admissions window for the September intake closes August 19, with classes beginning September 7, leaving roughly two weeks to apply.

Applications and information are available at www.galen.edu.bz, by email at [email protected], or by phone at +501 614-6415. This could be you.

World.title: Recinos Group says procurement participation was routine, says K&M Construction did not win Government bid
World.content:
By Zoila Palma: The Recinos Group of Companies has issued a statement addressing public concerns over the participation of businesses within the group in government procurement processes, saying it is important to provide additional context about its operations and business history.

In the statement released on August 3, the company said the recent public discussion had centered on “a well-known entrepreneur from the Cayo District whose career began in the beauty industry,” adding that it believed “it is important to provide a more complete understanding of the businesses involved and the history of their operations.”

The group noted that Maria Estella Recinos has spent more than three decades building and expanding businesses across multiple sectors, including retail trade, construction, importation, exportation, distribution, beauty services, logistics, and entrepreneurship initiatives.

The company said its operations include K&M Construction Company Ltd., Salon Essentials Ltd., Maria Estella’s Beauty Salon and other affiliated enterprises. It described K&M Construction as “a Belizean construction company engaged in construction-related works and services, including the execution and support of building and infrastructure projects.”

The statement also noted that the group’s businesses have maintained commercial relationships with customers, suppliers, contractors, and institutions in Belize and abroad, including partners in Guatemala, El Salvador, the United States, and Guyana.

Addressing questions surrounding public procurement, the company said participation in government bidding is a normal part of doing business for many established firms.

“The receipt of an invitation to participate in a procurement process is not, in itself, evidence of wrongdoing, nor does the submission of a proposal guarantee that a contract will ultimately be awarded,” the statement said.

It added that, in the case under discussion, “K&M Construction Company Ltd. submitted a proposal but did not win the bid and was not awarded the contract.”

The Recinos Group concluded by reaffirming its support for transparency and accountability while urging the public to consider the full context of its business operations. “The public has every right to expect transparency and accountability, and we support that principle fully,” the statement said, adding that the public is also “entitled to receive complete, accurate, and properly contextualized information concerning the work that our businesses have undertaken over many years.”
