World.title: Râșnov Film and Histories Festival opens with concerts, outdoor screenings
World.content:
The Film and Histories Festival in Râșnov (FFIR) opens this weekend its 18th edition, showcasing an extensive program of film screenings, concerts, debates, theatre performances, and other events.

The festival kicks off at Feldioara Fortress, where children are invited to take part in interactive workshops, followed by concerts, performances, and open-air film screenings throughout the opening weekend. On August 7, the public will be able to attend a concert by Grupul Om Bun, before watching Andrzej Wajda's classic Katyn, according to a release quoted by News.ro.

In Brașov, the festival begins on August 7 with FFIR Pop-Up: Coresi Edition, a family-oriented program covering sports games, workshops and cheerleading demonstrations by Râșnov Stars. The evening program includes a concert by Watzzy.

On the same day, Codlea hosts a concert by the Romanian Youth Jazz Orchestra at the Evangelical Church, followed by a screening of the Romanian documentary The -escu Family Diary, directed by Șerban Georgescu.

On August 8, the Weavers' Bastion in Brașov (pictured) hosts a solo concert by Radu Almășan (Bosquito), followed by a screening of The Last Viking, the latest feature by Danish director Anders Thomas Jensen.

The opening weekend marks the start of the program running through August 23, bringing together more than 100 events and around 100 guests from the fields of culture, history, journalism and public life across the festival's four host towns.

This year's edition features more than 50 film screenings, 18 debates and lectures, 20 concerts, three theatre performances, four special events, and the FFIR Summer School, which will bring together more than 70 high school and university students. Events will take place in Râșnov, Brașov, Feldioara and Codlea.

The festival will take place August 7-9 in Feldioara, August 7-13 in Brașov, August 8 in Codlea, and August 14-23 in Râșnov.

World.title: Wolt launches split payments for group orders in Romania
World.content:
Wolt announced that it launched its Split Payments feature in Romania, allowing customers placing group orders to pay individually for their own items directly through the app. The feature went live at the end of July and is set to be rolled out to other markets in the coming period.

Previously, group orders required one person to cover the full cost and collect money from the other participants afterwards. Under the new system, each member of the group can add their items and pay their share separately.

Shared costs, including delivery and service fees, are automatically divided among participants. If the person who creates the group order has an active Wolt subscription, eligible benefits such as free delivery or discounts can apply to the entire order.

To use the feature, one customer starts a group order, selects Split Payments, and shares an invitation link or QR code. Other participants can then join, select their items, and pay directly through the app, the company said.

Once everyone has completed their part of the order, the person who created it confirms the purchase, with all items delivered to a single address. Each participant receives a separate payment confirmation and can see their purchase in their personal order history.

Wolt said the feature can also be used for workplace orders, with participants able to use eligible meal benefits for their individual share.

Split Payments joins other features available through the platform, including Gifting, which allows customers to send orders with a personal message, and Scheduled Orders for arranging deliveries in advance.

Wolt has operated in Romania since May 2025 and is currently present in 34 cities and surrounding areas.

World.title: Romania's industrial, logistics demand rises 11% in H1 as developers resume speculative projects
World.content:
Demand for industrial and logistics space in Romania increased by 11% year-on-year in the first half of 2026, reaching 569,000 sqm, according to a report by real estate consultancy Cushman & Wakefield Echinox. Leasing activity accelerated particularly in the second quarter, when around 329,000 sqm was transacted.

New demand accounted for 58% of the total volume in the first half, while developers have also begun resuming speculative projects after several years in which new developments were generally launched only after securing significant pre-leasing.

Romania's stock of modern industrial and logistics space reached 8.14 million sqm at the end of the second quarter, of which approximately 4 million sqm was in Bucharest and the surrounding area. Another 532,000 sqm was under construction nationwide.

The return of speculative development contributed to an increase in the nationwide vacancy rate to 6.7%, from 5.4% at the end of 2025. Bucharest's vacancy rate stood at 6.3%.

"The H1 results confirm that Romania's industrial and logistics market remains one of the most dynamic segments of the commercial real estate sector," said Ștefan Surcel, Head of Industrial Agency at Cushman & Wakefield Echinox.

"Another positive sign is the return of speculative developments, following several years during which most new projects were launched only after securing a high level of pre-leasing," he added.

Bucharest continued to account for the largest share of leasing activity, with 386,000 sqm transacted in the first half, including 255,000 sqm in the second quarter alone.

Timișoara recorded 73,600 sqm of leasing activity during H1 and had a total modern stock of 807,700 sqm. Meanwhile, Ploiești had 574,500 sqm of industrial and logistics space and a vacancy rate of just 0.8%.

Among the larger transactions signed during the second quarter were FM Logistic's pre-lease of 10,300 sqm at CTPark Bucharest, Novaintermed's 6,300 sqm lease at VGP Park Bucharest A3, and Lift Banat's 5,900 sqm lease at VGP Park Timișoara A1.

Prime headline rents in Bucharest edged up to EUR 4.80 per sqm per month in the second quarter, while rents in regional logistics hubs remained broadly stable at EUR 4.30-4.65 per sqm per month.

World.title: A new major seismic retrofitting project in Bucharest: the "Bulandra" Theatre building at 1 Schitu Măgureanu Street to be reinforced and modernized
World.content:
News from Companies

Concelex, a leading Romanian construction company, will design and carry out the reinforcement, rehabilitation and modernization works for the building at 1 Schitu Măgureanu Street, which houses the "Lucia Sturdza Bulandra" Municipal Theatre and premises belonging to the University of Bucharest. Listed under seismic risk class I (RsI), the building is managed by the Municipal Administration for the Consolidation of Buildings at Seismic Risk (AMCCRS) and is located in a protected area.

"By signing this contract, we are taking another concrete step forward in the Municipality of Bucharest's seismic reinforcement program. No. 1 Schitu Măgureanu is a complex project, in which we must strike a balance between three essential objectives: seismic safety, protection of built heritage, and bringing the building up to current standards of operation and energy efficiency. We are not just reinforcing a structure, we are protecting a place that is part of Bucharest's cultural and academic memory. For AMCCRS, the signing of the contract marks the beginning of a stage in which our responsibility is to ensure the investment is implemented rigorously, respecting quality, deadlines and the building's architectural value." said Răzvan Munteanu, Executive Director of the Municipal Administration for the Consolidation of Buildings at Seismic Risk.

"This is a special project, not only because of its technical complexity, but also because of the building's architectural and cultural significance, for students, professors, actors, theatre lovers and the Bucharest community, as a whole. Our mission is to bring it up to modern standards of safety and energy efficiency while preserving its identity. Concelex's experience with integrated solutions, as well as with similar projects, gives us the tools we need to manage a project of this scale." said Cătălin Vișan, Deputy CEO, Concelex.

The project aims to achieve seismic reinforcement as well as improved energy efficiency, with a contract value of 98.6 million lei. Up to 90% of the funding comes from the National Program for the Consolidation of Buildings at High Seismic Risk, financed by the Ministry of Development, Public Works and Administration, and implementation is carried out by the Municipality of Bucharest through the Municipal Administration for the Consolidation of Buildings at Seismic Risk. The intervention seeks not only to secure a building at seismic risk class RsI, but also to preserve its architectural and cultural value and adapt it to current requirements for operation, safety and energy efficiency.

The project adds to a broad portfolio of reinforcement works; among the historic buildings Concelex has rehabilitated or has under way are the Mihai Eminescu building of the Bucharest University of Economic Studies, the Bacău Administrative Palace, the National Bank of Romania (BNR) branch in Galați, and Buildings A and B of the interwar building at 2 Boteanu Street. The company has also recently won the reinforcement project for the Dacia-România Palace (Pinacoteca).



The building on Schitu Măgureanu has a total floor area of over 11,800 sqm and involves a complex intervention: structural reinforcement, repair and restoration of architectural elements and artistic components, modernization of building systems, and the introduction of fire safety solutions. In addition, the works will cover thermal insulation, waterproofing, window and door replacement, and the installation of energy-efficient equipment, with an impact on energy consumption and greenhouse gas emissions. The project also involves partial demolitions, ground improvement works for the foundation, as well as utility connections and disconnections.



Through an integrated approach to the intervention, structural reinforcement, restoration, modernization of building systems and improved energy performance, the Municipality of Bucharest and AMCCRS aim for the investment to generate long-term benefits, both in terms of user safety and in terms of heritage preservation and reduced building operating costs.



Located at the intersection of Schitu Măgureanu Boulevard and Calea Plevnei, the building is one of the most important architectural landmarks of the Cișmigiu area, with a 100-year history. The complex was built in stages, with construction of the main building beginning in 1926 as the Palace of the League for the Cultural Unity of Romanians. Between 1950 and 1977, it housed the Institute of Theatrical and Cinematographic Art, and today it serves the "Lucia Sturdza Bulandra" Municipal Theatre and the University of Bucharest, with lecture halls, amphitheatre, library, archive and offices.

World.title: Romanian cinema: Florin Șerban’s latest feature selected in Locarno Film Festival’s international competition
World.content:
The film You Don’t Belong Here, directed by Florin Șerban, will premiere at this year’s Locarno Film Festival, where it has been selected in the International Competition.

The film explores the complex relationship between a father and his son. It follows a physician as he learns the police suspect his teenage son of murdering an old Romani man, then discovers his son has a secret life.

The cast includes Adrian Văncică, Teodor Butănescu, Alex Conovaru, Cristina Richter, Janir Izdrăilă, and Cosmin Dominte.

The world premiere will take place on August 9 at Forum - Spazio Cinema. Following the screening, members of the film's crew will take part in a Q&A session. Additional screenings are scheduled for August 10 and August 11.

You Don’t Belong Here has also been selected in the main competition of the Sarajevo Film Festival.

Florin Şerban's debut feature, If I Want to Whistle, I Whistle, premiered in the competition section of the 2010 Berlinale, where it won the Silver Bear and the Alfred Bauer Prize.

Held from August 5-15, 2026, the Locarno Film Festival is one of the world's oldest film festivals. Founded in 1946 in the aftermath of the Second World War, it has built its reputation on championing freedom of expression, independent cinema, and auteur filmmaking.

World.title: Falling Water Levels on Danube Threaten Serbia’s Electricity Supply
World.content:
The low level of the Danube is especially affecting electricity generation.

However, Dusan Zivkovic, director of the Electric Power Industry of Serbia, EPS, told RTS on Wednesday that the electricity supply was stable – and would remain so.

“This is a period of major challenges, but I would again emphasise that citizens and businesses should not be concerned about the regular supply of electricity,” Zivkovic said.

He expects the period of low inflows to continue, partly because of limited snowfall in the Alps during the last winter as well as more recent weather.

World.title: Turkey Submits Long-waited PKK Disarmament Law to Parliament
World.content:
Turkey’s parliament received a long-awaited framework law on Wednesday aimed at providing the legal basis for disarming the outlawed Kurdistan Workers Party, PKK, and regulating the judicial procedures for people linked to it, marking the most comprehensive legislative step yet to end the four-decade-long conflict.

Ruling AKP Group Chairman Abdullah Guler said the proposal should not be seen as an amnesty but as a legal framework for managing the post-disarmament process.

“The legislation is intended to place the process on a clear legal footing, while preserving Turkey’s fight against terrorism and ensuring that all measures are implemented under the rule of law,” Guler said.

The “Law on Strengthening National Solidarity and Social Integration” was submitted to the Grand National Assembly with the signatures of 360 lawmakers.

Support came from the ruling Justice and Development Party, AKP, its nationalist ally, the Nationalist Movement Party, MHP, the pro-Kurdish DEM Party, the pro-Kurdish and Islamist HUDA PAR, some MPs from the opposition Republican People’s Party, CHP, members of the New Path parliamentary group and several independents.

The draft law lays out the legal framework for the post-disarmament process, including temporary judicial provisions for eligible people convicted of, or investigated over, PKK-related offences.

It includes mechanisms such as supervised release, sentence postponement and judicial supervision under specified conditions following the organisation’s dissolution and disarmament.

The draft stipulates that its provisions would take effect only after Turkey’s National Security Council, MGK, determines that the PKK and its affiliated structures have fully disbanded and surrendered all weapons

Under Turkey’s constitution, 400 votes in parliament are required for the law to be adopted directly, while support from 360 lawmakers would be sufficient to send the proposal to a nationwide referendum.

The government has made clear it wants the legislation enacted by parliament rather than through a public vote.

But not all the parties support the initiative. The Good Party and Victory Party have declared opposition to the legislation.

The New Welfare Party has called for the proposal to be put to a referendum, while the New Party, recently established as Turkey’s new main opposition party, has yet to announce its position. With parliament seeking broader support, its stance is being closely watched.

The legislation follows political developments that began earlier. In February 2025, jailed PKK founder Abdullah Ocalan called on the group to lay down its arms. His appeal followed an unexpected peace initiative by Devlet Bahceli, leader of the MHP, a key ally of President Recep Tayyip Erdogan’s AKP.

The initiative led to the establishment of a parliamentary commission and regular visits to Ocalan by a delegation from the pro-Kurdish DEM Party. The new framework law is regarded as the closest Turkey has come to establishing a comprehensive legal basis for ending the decades-long conflict.

More than 40,000 people have been killed since fighting between the PKK and Turkish security forces began after Ocalan founded the group in 1984.

The vote on the bill is expected to take place after the summer recess, in autumn.

World.title: Kosovo’s Kurti Urged to Share Power, to Avoid New Polls
World.content:
LDK leader Lumir Abdixhiku (first left) and Vetevendosje leader Albin Kurti meet in Pristina, July 10, 2026. Photo: Albin Kurti/Facebook

Kosovo opposition parties urged incumbent Prime Minister Albin Kurti to give them a greater share in upcoming institutions – if he wants to avoid new snap elections.

Ramush Haradinaj, an MP for the Alliance, formerly the Alliance for the Future of Kosovo, AAK, told the media on Wednesday that in order to solve the current impasse over the next President, Kurti has to reach a political compromise.

“The [election] result demands joint decision making,” Haradinaj said one day before the new parliament, elected in June snap polls, holds its inaugural session.

“One of main posts, Prime Minister or President, belongs to the opposition parties. The election winner should read the election result this way,” he added.

In the June 7 elections, Kurti’s Vetevendosje Movement won 53 of the 120 seats, down four from the last December 2025 election, but well ahead of the Kosovo Democratic Party, PDK, which won 22 seats. The Democratic League of Kosovo, LDK, which is Kurti’s most likely coalition partner, won 18 seats.

A repeat of the parliamentary deadlock that paralysed the country for much of 2025, when no party had enough seats to elect parliamentary officials and form a government, has likely been avoided – but only when it comes to the election of a speaker and a government, for which the winning party needs only a bare minimum of 61 votes.

Kurti will likely obtain a simple majority to form the next government by again relying on the support of MPs from various ethnic minority communities – Roma, Ashkali, Egyptian, Turk, Bosniak – plus one of the Serbs.

However, the wider crisis that led to the June 7 snap elections has not been solved; the parties still need to come to an agreement to elect a new President. Failure to do this within two months of the inauguration of the new parliament would trigger another election.

“Kurti is seeking all the main posts and decision-making institutions for himself and is aiming to humiliate the opposition by offering them only participation in the government. This is not what voters have decided, this is the logic of a regime. Leaders of totalitarian regimes are afraid of shared decision making. I think the opposition can help in forming the institutions, but there should be joint decision making,” Haradinaj said.

His comments came a day after Kurti met LDK leader Lumir Abdixhiku in an attempt to find an agreement on forming new institutions. The meeting ended without a deal – but both sides sounded cautiously optimistic.

“We are ready to avoid the new elections at any price … Kosovo needs institutional stability, more work and not political drama,” Abdixhiku said, referring to the political deadlock that brought the country three elections in 16 months.

However, Abdixhiku sounded reluctant to take the post of parliamentary speaker for his party in return for supporting Vetevendosje’s candidate for President.

“The LDK has no appetite for [the post of] speaker, which is more of a ceremonial figure and should be proposed by the biggest party [Vetevendosje],” he said.

On the other hand, Kurti said there was still a will “to work together” with the LDK in future. “No one wants new elections but if we don’t have an agreement, if we don’t move ahead, they can unfortunately happen despite the lack of a wish [for them],” Kurti said

“We need a political agreement which respects the elections result – and is not a substitute for it,” Kurti added.

World.title: Croatia’s Operation Storm in Pictures, 31 years on: Homes Restored, Fewer People
World.content:
Storm was not only a legitimate liberation operation led by Croatia’s first president, Franjo Tudjman, Prime Minister Andrej Plenkovic said at the central ceremony marking the anniversary of Operation Storm.

It was also, he added, an action that saved Bihac in northwest Bosnia and Herzegovina from a looming humanitarian catastrophe, changed the balance of power in Bosnia and paved the way for peace and the Dayton Agreement, which ended the 1992-5 war in Bosnia.

Croatia is neither engaged in an arms race nor threatening anyone, Plenkovic continued. However, “We are not afraid of anyone” and “will know how to respond to any threat” he warned.

He stressed that Croatia would never again be unprepared or unprotected, guided by the principle: “If we want peace, we must be able to defend it.”

Plenkovic said Croatia was not alone in this effort as it is a member of NATO. He stressed that investing in defence is not preparation for war but an investment in the security of the country, its homes, schools and factories. Such investments, he said, also strengthen investor confidence and make Croatia a more attractive place to live and work.

To compare the wartime landscape with the present day, BIRN set out to recreate photographs taken on August 5 and 6, 1995, with the help of two photographers.

One of them, artistic and documentary photographer Zeljko Gasparovic, 72, from Novska, volunteered during Croatia’s War of Independence and never parted with his camera. As a result, he built one of the largest private photographic archives documenting the war.

All photos can be slid left and right to compare the past and present.

World.title: EU Caught Between Child Protection and Privacy With Encryption Rules
World.content:
Sasa Mrdovic, Professor of Computer Networks at the Faculty of Electrical Engineering of the University of Sarajevo, said from a technical perspective it is difficult to clearly determine which communications should be exempted from encryption protection – i.e. to enable their decryption for the purpose of detecting criminal offences, including the most serious forms, such as child sexual abuse.

He explained that the fundamental characteristic of end-to-end encryption is precisely that the content of a communication can only be read by the end users participating in the conversation.

He added that removing encryption, or enabling access to communications, would raise additional questions regarding jurisdiction and security.

He recalled that such an approach was simpler in traditional communication systems. In order to intercept communications, postal services or telecommunications providers could grant access, and law enforcement agencies, with court orders, could obtain access to telephone conversations.

Modern digital communications operate differently.

“Here, because the infrastructure through which communications are transmitted is not under the control of a state, institution, or a single organisation, it is much more complicated to find a way to enable lawful access to communications while at the same time not compromising the privacy and security of all users,” Mrdovic concluded.

Agovic Djozo said a more effective approach to detecting and combating online material depicting child sexual abuse requires action at multiple points in the system before such content reaches private encrypted communications.

In her view, technology companies must apply the principle of “safety by design”, meaning they should assess risks and build protective measures before products are launched on the market.

Instead of focusing solely on private messages, efforts should also target the services, platforms, and infrastructure that enable the production and distribution of illegal content.

As an example, she cites the Internet Watch Foundation, IWF, which identified AI-generated child sexual abuse material on a hidden version of a chatbot site where users could select sexualized personas and generate additional images.

She noted that financial investigations can play an important role in combating commercial networks that distribute child sexual abuse material.

According to her, data from the company Chainalysis shows that commercial CSAM networks use subscription models and cryptocurrencies, but the public and permanent nature of blockchain transactions can enable the tracking of payments, the linking of addresses, and the identification of infrastructure.

In one case, according to those findings, a network was identified involving more than 5,800 crypto addresses and over $530,000 in received payments.

Additional measures include simpler content reporting, more effective removal of known CSAM, digital forensics, international data sharing, specialized investigative teams, victim support, and preventive education for children and parents.

BIRN also requested a comment from Meta, but no response was received by the time of publication.

World.title: Montenegro’s EU Accession is Critical Test of Europe’s Resolve
World.content:
On June 3, an Air Serbia charter from Belgrade landed at Tivat, on Montenegro's Adriatic coast, carrying 87 men. Police searched the plane and found a banner reading "Serbia wins" – the campaign slogan of Serbian President Aleksandar Vučić's ruling party – a long-range communication device, and a marine radio.

By late afternoon, all 87 were deported. Two days later, European Commission president Ursula von der Leyen and French and German presidents Emmanuel Macron and Friedrich Merz landed in Tivat to declare Montenegro's EU membership within reach.

Montenegrins had seen this film before: a decade ago, a plot to storm parliament on election day nearly derailed the country's path into NATO. The plane, though, is the threat at its crudest – visible, physical, stoppable.

World.title: In Playing Kosovo Card, Serbian Students Risk Losing Liberals in Snap Polls
World.content:
Serbia’s students and their professors may have been prompted to protest by the lack of accountability for the fatal collapse of an outdoor canopy at a railway station in late 2024, but their talking points have since broadened considerably. Not without risk.

At a recent rally in the central Serbian town of Kraljevo, the main theme was not their demand for elections, for a proper fight against corruption, or for the rule of law to finally apply to all.

It was Kosovo.

“We live in difficult times because those who rule over us can imagine a Serbia without Kosovo and Metohija, without clean drinking water, without justice, without humanity, kindness and freedom,” said one the speakers, Nemanja Karovic, an assistant professor at the teacher training faculty of the University of Belgrade.

World.title: Kosovo Detains Third Suspect as Mass Grave Probe Expands in North
World.content:
The Kosovo prosecution announced on Tuesday that investigations into the remains of missing persons from the Kosovo 1998-99 war are being conducted in a third location in the Serb-majority north of the country, as three persons suspected of war crimes have been detained.

“The Special Prosecution … confirms that, in coordination with the Kosovo Police, investigations regarding the war crimes case in the municipality of Zubin Potok are proceeding intensively.

“To date, three individuals have been arrested on suspicion of committing the criminal offence of ‘War crimes against the civilian population.’ Several locations have been searched during the investigations. Remains found in the village of Jabuke will undergo forensic examination and DNA analysis for identification purposes, while excavation work continues in the village of Kalluder e Vogel/Mala Kaludra. Currently, investigations are also underway at a third location,” the prosecution wrote on Facebook.

The Pristina Basic Court on Monday ordered one month’s pre-trial detention for a suspect identified only as J.R., who is under investigation for alleged war crimes against civilians and was arrested on August 2 in connection with the investigation. The court said there was a risk that the suspect, a Serbian citizen, “could flee to avoid prosecution … and could influence witnesses or evidence if released”.

“The measure of detention is necessary to ensure the defendant’s presence and the uninterrupted conduct of criminal proceedings,” the court said.

J.R. is the third person arrested in the case. Two other suspects, M.J. and M.B., were detained as excavation work began in the village of Kalluder e Vogel/Mala Kaludra on July 28. Both remain in custody.

The Special Prosecution has not given details on the specific allegations against the suspects but has said that their arrests are “related to the investigation into alleged war crimes against the civilian population” during the Kosovo war. The Prosecution said there is evidence that one of the suspects had been “mobilised and served actively in the former Yugoslav Army during the Kosovo war”.

Excavations at Kalluder e Vogel/Mala Kaludra began on July 28 after the Special Prosecution sought a court order to investigate a suspected mass grave containing victims of the war.

Acting Prime Minister Albin Kurti said these remains might belong to the so-called “group of intellectuals” – a group of Albanian civilians, including doctors, professors and lawyers, who disappeared on April 19, 1999. “We cannot confirm that they are the victims in question but that was our immediate suspicion. We must wait for our institutions to determine exactly what has been found there,” Kurti said on July 29.

On August 2, the Special Prosecution and police announced that investigators had identified a second suspected burial site in the nearby village of Jabuke, also in Zubin Potok municipality.

Late on Monday, the government’s Commission on Missing Persons said excavations had continued at both sites. “Because of the terrain, work focused on Jabuke, where the remains of four individuals were exhumed,” it said. adding that preliminary assessments indicate that the victims were likely people who were forcibly disappeared during the Kosovo war. “The remains have been transferred to the Institute of Forensic Medicine for examination and DNA identification,” the Commission said.

Acting Interior Minister Xhelal Svecla, who visited the site, said the “victims were thrown into a lime pit after being executed”.

While the investigation is continuing, there were reports that Serbian authorities had arrested a Kosovo citizen from Istog on suspicion of espionage. Kosovo officials have linked the arrest to the ongoing search for wartime mass graves.

Svecla accused Serbia of “refusing to provide information about people who disappeared during the war while intimidating those who cooperate with investigations.

“This state, on the one hand, refuses to provide information about forcibly disappeared persons, while on the other hand threatens and imprisons its own citizens who cooperate in locating these graves,” he said.

Acting Minister for Labour, Family, Social Welfare and War Veterans Andin Hoti described the reported arrest as “an attempted murder of the truth”, alleging that it was intended to discourage witnesses from assisting investigations into missing persons.

A report published on July 29 by Kosovo’s Institute of Crimes Committed During the War said 1,578 people remain missing from the 1998-99 Kosovo war.

World.title: Veteran Recalls the Moment Operation Storm Began
World.content:
August the 5th, 2026 – On the 31st anniversary of Operation Storm, Croatian veteran Ivan Mikulić recalls the moments when he and his fellow soldiers realised that a major operation was about to begin – even before they knew its name.

Mikulić, a member of the 3rd Battalion of the 4th Guards Brigade, spoke about the days that changed the course of the war and the emotions surrounding Croatia’s advance toward Knin. At the time, soldiers on the ground had not been officially told that Operation Storm was beginning, but many sensed that something extremely significant was approaching.

“Our unit was in Donji Kazanci, on the Livno–Grahovo route. On August the 3rd, we were moved to Pržine, near Grahovo, to a peat factory. At that point, we concluded that an operation could begin in the morning, even though we knew nothing about Storm. But as soon as we were moved there, we knew we were going forward in the morning,” Mikulić recalled.

When artillery fire began around 05:00 on August the 4th, the uncertainty entirely disappeared. “There was a sense of anxiety and excitement among the soldiers. People had already heard that the operation was definitely starting. When the artillery barrage began, there was an explosion of sheer joy. Some even raised a toast,” he said.

The long Road to Knin

Mikulić also remembers the moment his unit entered Knin and moved toward the city’s famous fortress. The soldiers did not immediately enter the fortress area, as security positions had already been established ahead of them and some units encountered delays along the way. “We reached the fortress and stopped there. We sat down on the wall,” he recalled.

Soon, local residents began approaching the soldiers and offering them refreshments.

“The beer had already arrived, Karlovačko had already reached the fortress. However, it was no longer possible to actually enter the fortress,” Mikulić said. At that moment, the Croatian flag had not yet been raised on the fortress, but the approach had already been secured.

A Victory Marked by Sacrifice

Despite the intense heat and the expectation of heavy fighting, the battle in Knin did not unfold as many soldiers had anticipated.

“We expected a fight, but there wasn’t one because they had all fled. It was complete and utter chaos. There were civilians hanging around in the city itself as well, but overall everything went well,” Mikulić said. However, victory came with a heavy price. He noted that the 4th Guards Brigade lost four soldiers in Knin itself.

memories that will remain forever

Over three decades later, Mikulić says the memories of those days remain vivid and clear.

During the war, he served on many fronts, from Kruševo and Zadar to Dubrovnik and Mostar. “I lost many friends, and that cannot be forgotten. It really wasn’t that long ago,” he said. As Croatia remembers Operation Storm, stories from veterans like Mikulić serve as a reminder that behind the historic images of victory were the experiences, sacrifices, and personal memories of the people who lived through those defining moments.

World.title: Remembering Three Young Croatian Soldiers Who Fell in the Final Battle of Operation Storm
World.content:
August the 5th, 2026 – As we mark the 31st anniversary of one of the most important events in modern Croatian history, we remember the thousands of defenders who fought for freedom. That includes three young Croatian soldiers of the 4th Guards Brigade who tragically lost their lives in the very final hours of Operation Storm.

Ivan Svalina, Stipan Dundović, and Miroslav Vođera all lost their lives killed on the 5th of August, 1995, in a small hamlet not far from Golubić, as Croatian forces advanced toward Knin and the final victory of Operation Storm. Their deaths came on the very day when the operation was reaching its historic conclusion, a reminder that even in the final moments of victory, Croatian soldiers continued to face fierce fighting and sacrifice.

The Final Battle Near Knin

Ante Brekalo, commander of the 2nd Company of the 2nd Battalion of the 4th Guards Brigade, led the advance across Dinara toward Knin. When his unit reached Golubić, they encountered very strong resistance.

“I was honoured to have such men in my company, men I could lead,” Brekalo later recalled. He said the three young soldiers lost their lives during intense close combat. Miroslav Vođera, who had previously served in the Yugoslav Army before joining the Croatian Army, was killed near a house during the fighting. His fellow soldier Ivica Bošnjak remembered him as a true example of what a soldier should be.

“His life ended only a few hours before it was announced that everything was free,” Bošnjak said. He also recalled the intensity of the battle, describing how fighting continued with gunfire and grenades exchanged between the two sides. Vođera, he said, attempted to call for surrender but was killed while trying to enter the building.

Remembering Young Comrades

Miro Moro was among those who discovered the bodies of Stipan Dundović and Ivan Svalina. These three soldiers were only 20, 22, and 23 years old. Moro, who had witnessed many difficult moments during the war, said that this particular memory remained especially painful. He especially remembered Svalina, a young man from his own village.

“That was a child from my village. That morning I saw him with a smile on his face,” Moro recalled. Svalina had joined the unit as a teenager, and his commanders remembered him as a cheerful, friendly and very dependable soldier. Brekalo described him as someone who always helped others and inspired confidence among his fellow soldiers. “He was a true fighter who never, ever left anyone behind,” he said.

A Tradition of Remembrance

Every year on the anniversary of Operation Storm, veterans gather at the site where the three soldiers fell, where a memorial has been built in their honour. Veterans from across the region, including Zadar, Split, Sinj, Imotski, Šibenik, and parts of neighbouring Bosnia and Herzegovina, come together to remember them.

They also honour other fallen defenders from those final days, including Dražen Kuduz, who died in an accident on the approach to Knin on the same day. “They will never be forgotten for as long as we’re alive,” said Josip Bebek, president of the Association of Veterans of the 4th Guards Brigade in Šibenik-Knin County.

A Legacy That Lives On

In Crivac, the hometown of Ivan Svalina, the memory of their youngest fallen soldier remains especially strong.

Around 150 residents of the small village joined the Homeland War, almost half of the local population at the time. Svalina was the youngest from the village to lose his life. His sister Marija Vučić said losing him left a permanent emptiness. She and her other sister also served during the war, spending four years on front lines across Croatia, from Zadar to Dubrovnik. A monument dedicated to Ivan Svalina was unveiled in the centre of the village last year, created by sculptor Petar Melvan. His fellow soldiers plan to visit it every year in remembrance.

For those who knew them, Ivan Svalina, Stipan Dundović, and Miroslav Vođera represent more than names from history, they are remembered as young men whose courage and sacrifice became part of Croatia’s story of independence. The Municipality of Muć also plans to open a memorial room this autumn dedicated to all those from the area who lost their lives during the Homeland War and Croatia’s fierce struggle for independence.

World.title: 31 Years Since Operation Storm: Veterans Recall the Battle for Knin and the Moment History Changed
World.content:
August the 5th, 2026 – 31 years have passed since Operation Storm (Oluja) altered the course of the Croatian War of Independence, and veterans have recalled the fierce battle for Knin.

Today, Croatia marks Victory and Homeland Thanksgiving Day, the Day of Croatian Defenders, and the 31st anniversary of Operation Storm, the military and police operation that became a turning point in the country’s modern history. Launched on August the 4th, 1995, Operation Storm saw Croatian forces manage to regain control of areas that had been held by rebel Serb forces, opening the path toward the final stages of the Homeland War.

Over three decades later, those who took part in the operation continue to remember the days that changed the course of Croatia’s modern history. Among them is Perica Prpić, president of the Association of Special Police Units from the Homeland War “Sharks”, who recalled the moments before the operation began while stationed with fellow soldiers on Velebit Mountain.

He remembers hearing the announcement from Croatia’s first president, Franjo Tuđman, before the operation began, while artillery fire could already be heard in the distance. “The moment I remember the call from President Tuđman, I still get goosebumps. We heard the artillery preparation in the distance. It had begun. You cross yourself, hug your fellow soldier, and start moving down Velebit. It’s just a unique feeling when you know there’s no turning back now,” Prpić said in an earlier interview.

The Battle for the “Igla” Position

Josip Bebek, a member of the 4th Guards Brigade who participated in Operation Storm, also recalled the beginning of the operation.

His unit advanced toward Knin from the direction of Bosansko Grahovo in the early hours of August 4, but encountered heavy resistance along the way. The obstacle was a strategically important hill known as “Igla” (“Needle”), which was held by rebel Serb forces. “We got about halfway there and then we stopped. We faced strong resistance. They held a position called Igla. It was extremely difficult to capture. Once we took Igla, everything moved forward more smoothly,” Bebek recalled. Taking control of that position became a key moment in the advance toward Knin.

Entering Knin

The following morning, after artillery preparation, Croatian forces entered Knin. “We literally walked into Knin,” Bebek said, describing the city at the time. He recalled that the city was largely empty and that his unit encountered no significant resistance after entering. “The 7th and 4th Guards Brigades never killed anyone, there was no resistance, and thankfully there was no need for it,” he said.

Bebek also remembers a personal encounter that stayed with him. He helped an elderly man and brought him to the military barracks, where he was later able to choose whether to remain in Knin or leave for Serbia. “I don’t know what he eventually decided, but later I met his brother, who actually told me their life story,” he said.

From Adrenaline to unbelievable levels of Pride

Although 31 years have passed since Operation Storm, Bebek says the emotions connected to those days remain strong and the memories vivid. “The dream of every Croatian soldier was to reach Knin. After every liberation operation we were happy, but we knew entering Knin would mean the end. That was the finish line,” he said.

At the time, he remembers the feeling of adrenaline and youthful determination. Today, those memories are replaced by pride and gratitude. “When I think about it today, I feel happiness and tears still fill my eyes with pride. We have our own country; we achieved that dream. May God ensure this never, ever happens to anyone again,” Bebek said.

After the war, Bebek remained a professional soldier. In 2003, he moved from Split to Knin, where he still lives today. For him, life in Knin is now simply everyday life.

As Croatia marks 31 years since Operation Storm, veterans continue to remember not only the military victory, but also the experiences, sacrifices, and personal stories behind one of the most significant events in the country’s history.

World.title: Croatia to Experience Peak Heat on Thursday With Temperatures Up to 42 Degrees
World.content:
August the 5th, 2026 – Croatia is currently under a particularly strong heat dome, with the peak of that heat set to beat down on the country on Thursday. In some areas, the temperatures could reach a dizzying 42 degrees.

Index reports that a very powerful “heat dome” traps extremely hot air over southern and southeastern parts of the continent. According to meteorologists from Severe Weather Europe, the hottest conditions are expected over the Balkans, Italy, Greece, and parts of the western Mediterranean, with some locations forecast to reach or exceed 42 degrees.

For Croatia, the forecast indicates that temperatures will continue climbing through the week, with Thursday expected to be the peak of the heatwave. Inland parts of the country face the highest temperatures, potentially approaching 42 degrees, while the Adriatic coast will also experience very hot weather, although sea breezes should keep coastal temperatures somewhat lower than inland areas.

a high pressure system from north africa

The extreme heat is being driven by a strong high-pressure system stretching from North Africa into southern and central Europe. This atmospheric pattern allows very warm air from the Sahara to spread northward while preventing cooler Atlantic air from moving into the region. As a result, the hot weather is expected to persist for several days.

Meteorologists warn that the prolonged high temperatures significantly increase health risks, especially for older adults, young children, and people with chronic medical conditions. Authorities advise people to stay hydrated, avoid all kinds of more strenuous outdoor activities during the hottest part of the day, seek shade or air-conditioned spaces whenever and wherever possible, and check on vulnerable family members and neighbours.

The article also highlights an increased wildfire risk all across southern Europe. The combination of extreme heat, dry vegetation, and periods of gusty winds creates conditions where fires can ignite easily and spread rapidly. Fire services across several Mediterranean countries remain on heightened alert.

a colder front is coming!

Looking beyond the peak heat, the forecast suggests that a cold front will begin moving into central Europe later in the week, bringing thunderstorms to some regions and a noticeable drop in temperatures. Croatia is expected to see this change after Thursday, although forecasters caution that any storms accompanying the front could be locally severe, with heavy rain, strong wind gusts, hail, and frequent lightning possible.

Overall, the article’s main message is that Thursday is expected to be the most dangerous day of the current heatwave in Croatia, with temperatures possibly reaching 42 degrees in some inland areas before a cooler, more unstable weather pattern arrives later in the week.

World.title: Bizarre Medieval “Vampire” Found in Pakrac Cemetery
World.content:
August the 4th, 2026 – An extremely bizarre Medieval “vampire” has been found in a Pakrac cemetery, with archaeologists believing that the particular method of burial was to “prevent the vampire returning among the living”.

Index reports that a very mysterious medieval burial discovered at the Stari Grad Pakrac archaeological site has once again brought attention to ancient beliefs about vampires and the fear of the dead returning among the living. Archaeologists uncovered the remains of a person buried face down, an unusual burial position that experts believe may have been an intentional ritual. According to archaeologist Krešimir Vacek, the way the body was placed suggests that people of the time wanted to prevent the deceased from returning after death.

The “vampire” burial likely dates back to the late 13th century and was found at a medieval cemetery connected with the former settlement around Stari Grad Pakrac. Archaeologists have been researching the site for years, uncovering numerous graves and important historical remains.

This is not the first unusual discovery of its kind at the location. Earlier excavations revealed another so-called “vampire” burial, a skeleton inside a valuable sarcophagus that was missing its human head. Instead, researchers found animal remains believed to be part of a horse skull. Such practices were linked to medieval beliefs that certain people could return from the grave and harm the living.

In medieval Europe, fears of supernatural forces were widespread, and communities sometimes carried out unusual burial practices when they believed someone could become a threat after death. The latest discovery in Pakrac offers another rare insight into the beliefs, fears, and rituals of people who lived more than 800 years ago.

World.title: Animal Rights Group Sparks Debate After Tragic Zagreb Zoo Lioness Death
World.content:
August the 4th, 2026 – A prominent Croatian animal rights group Friends of Animals (Prijatelji životinja) has sparked fresh debate after the tragic death of a lioness at the jaws of a male line at Zagreb Zoo.

Index reports that an ongoing debate over the role and funding of zoological gardens has returned to the public scene in Croatia. It comes after the aforementioned animal rights organisation strongly criticised the way public money is used to support zoos, arguing that people contribute financially even if they never visit them.

The organisation claims that many people are unaware that municipal budgets are used to finance the operation of zoological gardens. According to Prijatelji životinja, taxpayers are effectively contributing to institutions they may never personally use, raising questions about whether public funds should support facilities that keep animals in captivity.

Their criticism focuses on the belief that the traditional zoo model is outdated and that keeping wild animals in enclosed spaces cannot fully meet their natural needs. The group argues that resources should instead be directed towards alternative approaches to animal protection and conservation.

A long-running debate over the purpose of modern zoos

The controversy reflects a much wider global discussion about the role of zoological gardens in the 21st century. Supporters of modern zoos argue that they are no longer simply places where visitors come to see exotic animals. Many contemporary institutions focus on education, scientific research, species protection and breeding programmes aimed at helping endangered animals.

Critics, however, question whether these goals justify keeping animals in captivity. Prijatelji životinja argues that no enclosure can truly replace an animal’s natural habitat and that conservation efforts should focus more heavily on protecting species in the wild.

Public funding remains at the very heart of the discussion

The financial side of the debate has become one of the main points of disagreement.

Prijatelji životinja has previously highlighted examples of cities allocating significant amounts of public money to maintain zoos, arguing that citizens who do not support the concept are still indirectly financing it through taxes. Supporters of zoological gardens, however, point out that these institutions provide educational programmes, contribute to biodiversity awareness and participate in international conservation projects. Modern zoos increasingly present themselves as centres for protecting endangered species rather than simply tourist attractions.

Zagreb Zoo highlights conservation and education

The debate comes at a time when the role of zoos continues to evolve. The Zoological Garden of the City of Zagreb promotes programmes focused on animal care, public education and conservation activities. The institution also offers initiatives such as animal adoption programmes, through which citizens can financially support the care of individual animals while they remain residents of the zoo. The zoo has also highlighted its involvement in international projects aimed at protecting wildlife and raising awareness about biodiversity.

A question with no easy answers…

The disagreement between animal protection organisations and zoo supporters is unlikely to disappear. For critics, the issue is about whether society should continue funding a model based on keeping wild animals in captivity. For supporters, zoos remain important centres for education, research and conservation.

As public discussions about animal welfare become increasingly prominent, the future of zoological gardens will likely depend on how successfully they can balance their traditional role with modern expectations about conservation, ethics and animal wellbeing.

World.title: Croatian High-Tech Trains: The Innovation Transforming Rail Transport
World.content:
August the 4th, 2026 – Croatian high-tech trains are the domestic innovation transforming rail transport as the country enters a new era of railway transport.

As Sinisa Malus reports for Poslovni, that era is being strongly driven by one of the country’s most advanced industrial achievements – modern trains developed and produced by Končar.

Often described as among the most complex technological products created by Croatian industry, these new-generation trains represent a combination of domestic engineering, advanced technology and a push towards greener transport solutions. Over 70 percent of their components are Croatian-made, while key systems and subsystems, including control systems, communication technology, traction transformers and other essential elements, are produced within the Končar Group.

To date, Končar has delivered 70 new-generation low-floor trains to Croatian railways, including 40 units delivered in less than five years. The company has also recently signed new agreements with HŽ Passenger Transport for six battery-electric trains and the construction of a hybrid charging station in Kotoriba, with a total value of 53.6 million euros.

Croatia’s first battery trains enter service

One of the biggest milestones has been the development of Končar’s battery-powered trains, which represent a major technological step for Croatia and one of the first examples of this type of commercial railway technology in Europe.

The battery-electric multiple unit (BEMV) uses fully electric propulsion, powered by onboard batteries as well as existing overhead electrical networks. This makes it particularly suitable for Croatia, where a significant part of the railway network is still not electrified. This type of technology allows the trains to operate on both electrified and non-electrified routes, creating a more sustainable solution for passenger transport across the country.

The train was designed for daily operation of up to 480 kilometres and up to 18 hours of service per day. On non-electrified lines, it can reach speeds of up to 120 km/h using battery power, while on electrified routes it can achieve speeds of up to 160 km/h. Another highly important innovation is the battery motor train (BMV), designed specifically for routes without overhead electrical infrastructure. It can reach speeds of up to 120 km/h and, depending on conditions, can travel more than 200 kilometres during testing on a single charge.

Designed for modern passengers

The new trains are not only focused on efficiency and sustainability but also on improving passenger comfort. They include wheelchair access ramps, dedicated bicycle spaces, accessible toilets, video surveillance, passenger information screens, audio announcements and free Wi-Fi. The trains can also be connected with other new-generation low-floor units already operating in Croatia, allowing increased capacity when needed.

A major investment in greener mobility

The development of these trains is part of the project “Application of Green Technologies in Railway Passenger Transport”, financed through Croatia’s National Recovery and Resilience Plan. Several charging stations have already been opened at railway stations in cities including Split, Osijek, Varaždin, Bjelovar, Virovitica and Pula. Further expansion is planned, with additional battery and hybrid trains expected to enter service in the coming years. A wider project financed through a European Investment Bank loan, worth almost €118 million, includes the delivery of additional trains and charging infrastructure.

New trains to connect Zagreb and Split

Končar is also preparing a new generation of long-distance trains that will connect Zagreb and Split.

The route between the two cities stretches for 429 kilometres, but only around a quarter of the line is electrified. Because of this, the new trains will combine electric and diesel propulsion, allowing them to operate efficiently across different sections of the route. The trains will reach speeds of up to 160 km/h and will be capable of connecting multiple units together to increase capacity. The first six trains are part of a larger agreement between Končar and HŽ Passenger Transport covering 19 new low-floor trains. Additional units are planned to connect cities including Osijek, Rijeka and Pula.

Croatian engineering on the international stage

The latest generation of Končar trains highlights the growing role of Croatian industry in advanced manufacturing and sustainable technology.

From battery-powered rail vehicles to modern mobility solutions, these projects show that Croatian companies are capable of developing complex products that compete in a highly demanding global market. As railway transport across Europe moves towards lower emissions and smarter infrastructure, Croatia’s domestically produced trains are becoming a symbol of innovation, engineering expertise and the country’s ambitions beyond traditional industries.

World.title: Croatian Pizza Prices Spark Debate as Bill Goes Viral
World.content:
August the 4th, 2026 – Croatian pizza prices have sparked fresh debate as a bill of 32 euros issued in Stari Grad on Hvar goes viral across social media.

Debates over prices on the Croatian coast have once again erupted on social media, with a restaurant bill from the island of Hvar becoming the latest trigger for a wider discussion about the cost of summer holidays in Croatia. Poslovni reports that this latest price-related controversy began after a guest shared a receipt from a pizzeria in Stari Grad, where a large pizza cost 22 euros. The post quickly spread online, dividing opinions between two opposing camps.

Some users described such prices as completely unreasonable and a sign of growing greed in the tourism sector. Others argued that restaurants clearly display their menus and prices, meaning guests can see the costs in advance and decide whether they want to order. The fact that another seaside bill became a viral topic highlights how strongly food and service prices continue to shape conversations during every tourist season. The debate has grown beyond the price of one pizza, becoming part of a larger discussion about Croatia’s tourism model.

22 euros is steep compared to a 7.50 euro pizza in italy

Soon, visitors began sharing their own experiences and comparing Croatian coastal prices with those in other popular European destinations. One social media user compared the situation with southern Italy, saying that in a restaurant in Ercolano, near Naples, a pizza cost just 7.50 euros, a beer 3 euros, and a bottle of white wine 10 euros.

Others shared less positive experiences from Croatian islands. One visitor said that while the island of Vis was beautiful, the prices were too high. She described paying €120 per person for a seven-hour speedboat excursion that included visits to three caves and two beaches, but without lunch included. She also pointed out that entering one of the caves cost an additional €15, even for those who chose to swim there themselves.

However, not everyone believes the criticism is justified. Some commenters argued that visitors simply choose where they travel and where they eat according to their own budgets. “Everyone goes where the food and prices suit them,” one comment said, summarising the opinion of those who believe customers have the final choice.

Many also pointed out that high prices will continue as long as there is demand and people willing to pay them.

“While there are people who will gladly pay 22 euros for a pizza, there will be prices like this. But tourism cannot rely on this forever,” one user wrote, warning that the current model may not be sustainable in the long term. Others noted that expensive pizzas are not only found on the coast, mentioning examples from Zagreb as well, expanding the discussion beyond seasonal tourism.

An even more expensive pizza becomes the symbol of the debate

The most attention, however, was attracted by a comment from a man who claimed that he had seen an even more expensive pizza on the island of Brač. “There are also pizzas for 32 euros. If it doesn’t suit you, the door is open for you to leave and go elsewhere,” he wrote.

The comment quickly became a symbol of the argument that prices are ultimately determined by supply and demand, with businesses charging what customers are prepared to pay. Another theory that appeared in the discussion was that some tourists deliberately visit the most expensive restaurants so they can later complain online and share their bills on social media, gaining attention. “They go there on purpose so they can complain about high prices afterwards,” one commenter suggested.

Guests complain, but the spending continues…

Although complaints about Croatian prices return every summer, financial data paints a more complex picture. Examples of expensive bills continue to circulate online, including a case of visitors from neighbouring Bosnia and Herzegovina who reportedly paid more than 50 euros for a jumbo pizza and two coffees near Dubrovnik, as well as a British tourist who paid a whole 42 euros for just two drinks in Split.

However, spending figures show that tourists are still opening their wallets. According to data from Croatia’s Tax Administration, consumer spending during the summer months has continued to grow. In July, the total value of fiscalised receipts increased by almost 24 percent compared with the same month last year, reaching 6.8 billion euros.

The hospitality sector also recorded growth, with more than seven percent more receipts issued and their total value increasing by over 11 percent. Tourism analysts say this shows that visitors continue to spend despite complaints, although they warn that such a trend may not be sustainable forever.

The picture is not the same everywhere

A closer look at the tourism sector shows that success is not evenly distributed. While luxury hotels and high-end campsites are recording strong occupancy and increased revenue, many small private accommodation providers and some restaurants are facing difficulties. June 2026’s figures showed a decline of seven percent in arrivals and six percent in overnight stays compared with the previous year, with the largest drops recorded in Istria, Kvarner and Zadar County.

The data suggests a growing divide within Croatian tourism. Luxury segments continue to perform well, while businesses offering average services at increasingly high prices are finding it harder to attract guests. Tourists appear to be paying closer attention to value for money and are becoming less willing to spend large amounts on experiences that do not match the expected quality.

Market rules apply, but guests are becoming more demanding

Tourism experts have repeatedly warned about price increases that are not matched by improvements in quality. While the government and the Ministry of Tourism have called for more reasonable pricing policies, Boris Žgomba, president of the Croatian Chamber of Commerce’s Association of Travel Agencies, has stressed that prices are ultimately determined by the market and the relationship between supply and demand. Croatia has positioned itself alongside other Mediterranean destinations such as Italy and Spain in terms of pricing, while Dubrovnik regularly ranks among the most expensive cities in the region.

At the same time, travellers are increasingly searching for authentic experiences, local culture and quieter destinations. This could create opportunities for parts of Croatia’s tourism industry that adapt to changing expectations.

If prices continue rising without a corresponding improvement in quality, some tourists may turn towards more affordable destinations such as Albania, which has experienced strong tourism growth by attracting visitors who find Croatia or Greece too expensive. As another busy summer season unfolds, prices on the Croatian coast and islands remain one of the most debated topics in Croatia, raising a continuing question: where is the line between market logic and genuine hospitality?

World.title: Estonia's Maarika Lepik crowned women's world champion in axe throwing
World.content:
Maarika Lepik is now women's world champion in double-bit axe throwing after reaching those heights in Bollnäs, Sweden.

Otto Peet claimed the junior crown for Estonia too.

Double-bit axe throwing is a precision target sport which has its roots in North American logging camp history. Competitors stand several meters away from a wooden target and throw a symmetric, dual-edged axe. To score, the axe must complete a single rotation in the air.

A total of 145 hopefuls from 12 countries took part in the three-day World Championships. In addition to Estonia and the host nation, competitors from Canada, the Czech Republic, Denmark, Finland, Germany, Ireland, Italy, the United Kingdom, the United States and Switzerland attended.

Lepik is a math teacher at a school in Viimsi by day, and she had posted her previous world championships best result four years ago, with fourth place. Two years ago, she narrowly missed the final, finishing first outside the cut.

This year was Lepik's year, however, as she scored 48 out of a possible 60 points in the semifinals, tying for second and third place and making it to the final.

That final involved eight women, down to three, one of them Lepik, after five rounds – the competitor with the poorest throw in each round was eliminated.

An Irish axe thrower had already made it to the final with 11 points, but Lepik tied on 9 points with a Canadian competitor, meaning a throw-off beckoned. The first two of these were a tie, but Lepik made the better third throw, to secure her place in the final.

Despite reaching that final second, the Estonian went on to win 12:11, claiming her first world title.

Of other Estonians taking part, Sirje Leini narrowly missed the final, finishing 10th with 40 points. A score of 41 would have been enough to reach the top eight and qualify for the final.

Karol Raidma, the women's silver medalist at the last event, scored 37 points in the semifinal and finished in a tie for 14th-16th place.

In the junior final, Peet was clearly dominant, defeating his opponent 8-0 in the throws for the gold medal. Also, Emma Liisa Toikka finished fourth for Estonia after posting the second-best result in the semifinal.

None of the Estonian representatives reached the men's semifinal, reserved for the top 27 competitors, from a field of 96 entrants, though two of these, Kristiar Papstel, tied for 28th-29th and Roland Peet, who came 30th, almost made it.

Marek Peet, one of the driving forces behind axe throwing in Estonia and who also took part in the Bollnäs event, said there is a chance that Estonia will be awarded the right to host the next World Championships in double-bit axe throwing, which take place in 2029.

World.title: OMD's Andy McCluskey: Even our best friends hated our first songs
World.content:
Speaking to the ETV show Ringvaade suvel, the band's singer and co-founder Andy McCluskey said he is looking forward to the Tallinn concert. The band last performed in Estonia in 2020, and has been in existence around half a century, becoming prominent in their home country at the beginning of the 1980s. OMD also had a huge following in Estonia almost from the outset, something which the weight of Soviet oppression could do little to squelch.

It's an honor to talk to you because I have to give you a quick personal story – I grew up as a teenager listening to OMD and it was behind the Iron Curtain, during the Soviet era so all the Western music was like a symbol freedom for me. So for me it's actually incredible to sit down and talk to you. You're going to be back in Estonia in August. What do you remember from your last gig, and what kind of memories do you have?

You're always a bit nervous when you play in a new country, because you think how many of these people have ever seen us before? Probably not many, so they don't know what to expect, and we don't know what to expect from them. Having played once, and remembering the concert was great, I'm looking forward to August 29th.

There is kind of a unique bond between OMD and the fans of Eastern Europe. Why do you think your music resonated so deeply with the people from our neck of the woods?

One of these things perhaps I've always thought about our music is that most of our songs, particularly in the early days, the chorus was not words, it was a melody, so you didn't have to speak English to sing along with OMD. Maybe that's it. Since the end of the Cold War, we'd been able to come and play in some of the countries that we couldn't play in in the 1980s.

Unfortunately with that we have made a bunch of bootleg copies of your albums and you never got royalties from that – sorry about that!

It's ok. You're forgiven, just tell everybody to buy a ticket and come and see the gig [Laughs].

What about the name Orchestral Manoeuvres in the Dark, it's quite a mouthful and it's a strange name for a pop band. What's the story behind that?

Well we weren't supposed to be a pop band: Paul [Humphreys] and I were writing music from when we were 16 years old, and frankly even our best friends hated it. So we finally dared, in 1978, almost 48 years ago, we finally dared to go on stage and play our songs.

What we didn't realize was we were actually writing very pop melodies, but wrapped in experimental ideas, and so the name of the band just came from – I used to write things on my bedroom wall, and we decided to do this one-off concert, we just thought well we need a weird name, as it was a weird idea, you know, two guys with a tape recorder playing songs that their friends don't even like [Laughs].

OMD's Paul Humphreys and Andy Andy McCluskey. Source: Press materials.

You guys kind of swam against the current, with a different style - even though you had some synth bands starting at the time as well.

I think the first two British synth bands that started were Orchestral Manoeuvres in the Dark and the Human League, and it was before the internet, so we didn't know the Human League were there, and they didn't know that we were there; I think both of us had found our alternative music just before punk, because I got into German music in 1975 with bands like Kraftwerk and La Düsseldorf and Neu, and so that was my alternative. The good thing about punk was that there were lots of new clubs opened up all around Britain, and they had a policy of letting anybody come and play, so we didn't have to be punk – we could play our synthesizers and take a tape recorder.

But yeah it was pretty different at the time, we were definitely not a punk band.

What was crazy was that we started in '78, the Human League started just a bit before us, and neither of us I think thought we were ever going to be pop groups – we were just making our music, it was our hobby really. But suddenly when Gary Numan had hits, then everybody was talking about electronic music, and there was more and more and more electronic music and suddenly something that seemed a crazy idea in 1978 was the new international pop music in 1980.

I read about how much guys you have been influencing different styles of music, it's pretty amazing how many different bands have named the influence by you guys. I can understand the electronic music – Moby's going to be in Estonia as well. But then the Red Hot Chili Peppers have mentioned you, U2, and the craziest for me would be ZZ Top – totally different style and everything.

ZZ Top is my favorite one, and it's true – one of the first TV shows we ever did in England was at the beginning of 1980, we did a program called the "Old Grey Whistle Test", and they have live bands; we were live in the studio, ZZ Top were live in the studio, and we were all like 19 and 20, and thought we were the new thing, and we thought they were old-fashioned, beardy Texas blues rockers and we didn't want anything to do with them, but they loved us. We didn't know this, but years later someone said 'I was reading a book about ZZ Top and they credit you with helping them go electronic, to make the Eliminator album which is the biggest album they ever made, and they used drum machines and synthesizers, and also the way I move with my bass guitar, swinging the bass guitar, they copied that in the videos, and years later in the 1990s I got into a lift in a hotel in Paris with Billy Gibbons, and I went '"hey Bill I'm Andy from Orchestral Manoeuvres," and he was "Hey Dustin, this is the guy that gave us the move we ripped off," so I heard it from Billy's mouth – they did copy OMD; can you believe that?!

You've built such a massive legacy from the 1980s. When you decided to get together, did you feel any pressure writing any new material to live up to this iconic OMD reputation of the eighties.

The first thing was really just to play live and have fun and see if people wanted to watch us play live again, and it's been great – you know, people have been really coming to see us, and they have enjoyed the gigs and in fact our live audience now is probably bigger than it was 40 years ago. But after two years, we were kinda like "OK is this it now, we're just going to play the old songs over and over again. Are we basically just a tribute band to ourselves?" And that's when we decided to do the crazy, stupid thing and write some new music; we're going to work hard on it and make it good, and actually I think the four albums that we've made in the last 17 years, people have been saying that they're actually as good as the albums from the early 80s. The last one got to number two in the U.K. – that woman Taylor Swift stopped us from being number one [laughs].

Your own personal influences – who have been the main idols for your music?

When I was a kid there was not much music I liked to be honest. It was the Düsseldorf bands, Kraftwerk and Neu, David Bowie, Roxy Music and Brian Eno, and the Velvet Underground, and that was it. I really didn't listen to anything else than that. Those were the people that influenced me, and I still listen to that music. The music you listen to on your journey from childhood to adulthood, the first part of your life where you grow into being an adult, that music becomes a soundtrack to your life forever.

OMD are appearing at the Birgitta Convent ruins (Pirita Klooster) on Saturday, August 29.

World.title: Concert organizer: world‑famous artists want to feel at home while on tour
World.content:
Liina Tammepõld, marketing manager for the large‑concert agency L Tips Agency in Estonia, says that world‑famous artists want to feel as comfortable as possible while on tour, and therefore their requests are not caprices or difficult demands.

"I studied advertising and imagology at Tallinn University and worked in a record store at the same time. My love for music started in childhood; I recorded songs from the radio onto cassette tapes and went to various summer tours in Estonia, I was a fan of many artists. Then I volunteered at the Positivus festival, and from there I was invited to do marketing and communication," said Liina Tammepõld, marketing and communications manager for the Estonian branch of L Tips Agency, which organizes large concerts in the Baltics.

L Tips Agency is organizing concerts by Moby, The Cure and OMD this August.

The stress level in this work can be very high at times, but the adrenaline and the experience you get when the concert is finally over are worth it. "The coolest moment is when the concert begins and I send photographers right to the front of the stage to shoot, and I can spend the first songs right at the stage myself. The energy that arises when the artist comes on stage always gives me chills," Tammepõld said.

"The choice of artist mainly comes down to logistics and dates, not so much thinking about the audience reaction. When we do something in Estonia, Latvians and Lithuanians also come," said Tammepõld, who works at a Latvian agency. "For very big artists, we treat Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania as one region."

Tammepõld works in a small company with four Latvians, one Estonian and one Lithuanian. "We talk a lot about artists among ourselves, and the final decision is made by the company's director, who also carries the risk."

It can also happen that an artist's tour is cancelled. "I gave my husband Neil Young concert tickets in Italy as a gift. We also bought flights and accommodation, but already in spring he cancelled the entire tour. Thanks to the fact that I had a credit card from a bank that included travel insurance, the insurance covered the costs because the purpose of the trip was the concert. It's worth checking these things," Tammepõld noted.

Moby had no surprising requests. "Moby's personal assistant on this tour is an Estonian, with whom we have been in close contact to make sure the artist feels very comfortable in Estonia," Tammepõld said. "Artists want to feel as much at home as possible while on tour. This week we have at both concerts a backstage helper who works with Andrea Bocelli. Estonians are capable people," she smiled.

American multi‑instrumentalist, producer and singer Moby released an album earlier this year that includes a track titled "Tallinn." "I did a bit of research and found that the song is a tribute to Arvo Pärt," Tammepõld said.

Tammepõld also organizes community concerts and wants to help Estonian artists reach big stages.

"I feel that a big part of my heart belongs to Estonian artists and Estonian music. Working at Tallinn Music Week is very close to my heart, and contributing to helping Estonian musicians reach big stages. In my hometown Elva, I organize a couple of concerts myself. At the end of July, Mikk Tammepõld and Lauri Räpp performed in the garden of the Verevi Motel. At the end of August, Mari Jürjens will perform," Tammepõld said.
