World.title: The rise in One Nation popularity is scary
World.content:
Letters NationalVictoriaLetters The rise in One Nation popularity is scary August 5, 2026 — 8:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Photo: Megan Herbert To submit a letter to The Age, email letters@theage.com.au. Please include your home address and telephone number. No attachments, please include your letter in the body of the email. See here for our rules and tips on getting your letter published. The rise of One Nation’s popularity in the polls is scary. One of the many reasons for the party’s popularity is the Labor Party and the Coalition have little on offer to encourage potential voters to look at them. One Nation has shown that it is a party that is against everything and has no real tangible and achievable policies. It is racist and anti-immigration, and people are falling for it. There are no policies on health, housing, defence, education and the many other platforms the major parties are promoting that Australians are concerned about. One Nation is a party based on fear, putting suggestions out there to scare the nation if they don’t get elected.

Alan Leitch, Austins Ferry, Tas Ignoring the party not the answer

Your correspondent proposes that The Age, ABC and The Guardian should retaliate against One Nation by ignoring it (Letters, 5/8). This wouldn’t work because a) it would make those media outlets look narrow-minded by not reporting the activities of a legitimate political party (and in the process reduce them to the same level of pettiness as One Nation), b) irresponsible, by not holding One Nation to account where necessary, and c) make them look like they were ganging up on One Nation, which would only support Pauline Hanson’s argument anyway. It would also be ineffective, because most One Nation voters are highly unlikely to read or follow any of those media organisations.

Greg Hardy, Upper Ferntree Gully The horror. The horror

The article ″⁣Victorian pick a self-described conspiracy theorist″⁣ (5/8) reminded me of The Age article by Michael Bachelard in which he wrote that the November election was shaping as ″⁣a classic pox-on-both-your-houses election″⁣, but if that pox were to kill off all our governing options, ″⁣what kind of zombies will be left holding power for the next four years″⁣. Bachelard said it was this prospect that caused him ″⁣to wake up in fright″⁣. Me too.

Neil Hudson, East Melbourne



Another worldwide conspiracy at work

Like One Nation’s new Victorian leader, Warren Pickering, I, too, am a conspiracy theorist. However, my theory differs significantly from his. Given that all the right-wing populist parties throughout the world of which One Nation is one are all fiercely pro-fossil fuel, anti-renewable climate change deniers I would theorise that their policies are controlled by a cabal of the powerful global fossil-fuel industry.

Phil Alexander, Eltham No surprises in Pickering selection

Should we really be surprised Pauline Hanson has appointed a conspiracy theorist as One Nation’s leader in Victoria? In truth, Warren Pickering, like Malcolm Roberts, is the perfect candidate for those at the fringe. As with Donald Trump, Hanson pushes an anti-intellectual, anti-establishment rhetoric that demonises the media and the minorities and has boogeymen lurking behind every shadowy corner.

Matt Dunn, Leongatha Death knell or clarion call?

The selection of Warren Pickering should, for any thinking Victorian, sound the death knell of the party’s chances. He is a self-confessed conspiracy theorist. This could make recent One Nation converts nervous, but will suit the die-hards.

Greg Cooper, Mount Martha The importance of money in politics

Clinton Fernandes (Comment, 5/8) includes the quote from 19th century Republican businessman and senator Mark Hanna, ″⁣There are two things that are important in politics. The first is money, and I can’t remember what the second is.” This sounds like a policy statement from the Rinehart One Nation coalition.

Barry Doyle, Portarlington THE FORUM



Whither our suburbs?

The state government’s new discretionary height limits around so-called activity centres will result in sunless, soulless wind tunnels along our high street shopping strips, characterless concrete towers with no trees or permeable spaces, overlooking of existing dwellings, and additional parking and traffic management problems. What will happen to our previously high-scoring liveable city? Where is the community and council consultation and right of appeal against inappropriate developments that threaten to ruin our suburbs?

Vikki O’Neil, Ashburton Numeracy needs work

The NAPLAN reports (″⁣Victoria shines as national test scores falter″⁣, 5/8) show one very disturbing result. The results for numeracy from 2023-26 show those who “need additional support” or are “developing” are reasonably consistent across years 3, 5 and 7. There is also a consistent increase in underperformance from year 7 to year 9 in each year. For 2026, that increase for those needing support or developing is 23.9 per cent in year 7 to 29 per cent in year 9. Think about nearly a third of Victorian year 9s underperforming in mathematics. And what that means for their future and for Victoria.

There is clearly something going seriously wrong in the early years of secondary schooling. It is likely that a majority of year 7s are being taught mathematics by an out-of-field teacher. Teacher shortages may mean that the teacher also changes during the year. The resulting year 9 results are appalling. No wonder so many students are disengaged. Fixing the teacher problems may also be a good way to address youth crime.

Let’s begin by paying Victorian teachers properly and giving them working conditions that give them time to work with students who need extra help. Especially in year 7.

Jan Thomas, North Melbourne Difference a year makes

There is some useful information to be found in NAPLAN test results, but my biggest concern has always been between comparing one calendar year with the previous year, such as 2025 with 2026. The cohorts of students are different. For example, the year 5 students in 2025 do not sit a test in 2026. As a senior mathematics teacher for many years, I always accepted that one particular year 12 mathematics class may be gifted and highly competitive, whereas, the following year students may be less able.

Alan Inchley, Frankston Sun shines on Sunshine

Congratulations to Sunshine Primary School for its ongoing success in literacy and numeracy as shown in their NAPLAN results (″⁣Little ray of sunshine″⁣, 5/8). The whole school community must be proud. However, as indicated by the principal, this achievement is no fluke.

Victoria has been on an improvement path for many years utilising a strong evidence base (national and international) to inform teaching and learning. The focus has been on the quality of the teaching and learning in every classroom and leadership of and within schools. It has not been a quick fix, of phonics or any other ″⁣off the shelf″⁣ panacea as often reported in the media (although the teaching and learning of phonics has always been part of literacy learning). The challenge has been to stay the course and to reach and support every school and leader. We now know the impact and skill of the teacher is powerful and profound.

The work has involved enormous ongoing learning for all teachers, in professional development and collaboration and teamwork (whether they are new grads or old hands). And ongoing monitoring of students’ learning and development, using all manner of assessments and data collection.

Yes the job of teacher has changed to be an extremely demanding one, but after seeing these NAPLAN results in Victoria they should be very proud of their hard work paying off.

Julie Chandler, Blairgowrie No Marx for this

Any time you see the toddler-level accusation ″⁣communist″⁣ by a politician, in the words of the immortal John Clarke, “turn away and do the crossword”.

Greg Champion, Montmorency



Old tropes die hard

Both sides of our family hailed from the Eolian Islands, north of Sicily. They arrived in Melbourne more than 100 years ago. I presumed our DNA would have identified us as “Italian”.

In fact, it identified us as Greek, Sardinian, Iberian, Sephardic Jew, West Asian, Ashkenazi Jewish, but zero per cent Italian!

So much for the monoculture. We are all boat people.

During WWII, our family’s “odyssey”, despite having lived and worked here for multiple decades, included racial abuse, disruption of the family fruit business by violent thugs, intimidation by authorities and accusations of stealing jobs from “real Australians”.

This was par for the course in those days.

But old tropes die hard. Opponents of cultural and religious diversity are now renewed and morphing into potential future political leaders.

To look forward however we must look back, to learn from past lessons of fear, xenophobia and questionable conspiracies.

Peter Russo, West Brunswick Climate strategy

Some would have us believe that, when the sun doesn’t shine and the wind doesn’t blow, we can’t rely on renewable energy so we need nuclear power as a back-up.

However, as the heatwave in Europe is showing, nuclear generation requires a lot of water for cooling and when that’s in short supply, generation must be scaled back as is happening now.

Logically, therefore, we need a more strategic approach like reducing the catastrophic warming of the planet before all options are exhausted.

Perhaps the answer is to burn more coal and gas to supply the energy we need. But wait, that’s how we got in this situation in the first place.

John Annison, Lilydale Come to Surrey Hills

Repurposing and developing the former St Joseph’s Home for Boys in Surrey Hills should be welcome news (″⁣Anger over push to turn one of nation’s oldest orphanages into apartments″⁣, 4/8).

This site of our significant history has been sadly vacant for a very long time. Let’s welcome more people into Surrey Hills, which is so well-endowed with all types of public transport, shops, schools and parks. We may not be in an ″⁣activity centre area″⁣ as such, but there is an abundance of services here for more people to share.

Jane Hudson, Surrey Hills Torpedo sub-portfolios

Although Premier Ben Carroll has acted commendably to reduce his new ministry down to 20, there remains a need for rationalisation of the excessive 63 different sub-portfolios now crammed into those 20 ministries.

Some arrangements are sound – for example, the combination of energy and resources, environment and climate action in one portfolio makes sense as these are related areas.

However, that contrasts with the jumbled portfolio arrangements for jobs, industry and advanced manufacturing, and trade, tourism and investment, which are split between two portfolios, yet are just different outcomes of or areas needing action as elements of economic development, which itself is shown in a third portfolio, when maybe two portfolios would have sufficed.

And why is prevention of family violence not included in the portfolio with police and crime prevention, and why is community sport split off from sport?

Thomas Hogg, East Melbourne Potholes everywhere ...

Please can people stop banging on about potholes.

Having just returned from a road trip that took us through Victoria and parts of NSW and Queensland, it is apparent that these states all have issues with the ubiquitous pothole.

We even saw a sign in NSW that read “potholes trialling” – we weren’t sure if they were trialling new shapes for potholes or working on a method of successfully repairing the wretched things.

Some suggested causes of potholes range from heavy trucks to extreme weather conditions. There have certainly been plenty of the latter in recent times.

After working on our own remedy, we have decided there is a very simple solution for this ongoing problem – bring back the Country Roads Board.

Graham and Louise Bell, Blackburn



... Even in Brisbane

Victoria’s Liberal promises to fix potholes could be treated with scepticism. Brisbane has had 20 years of Liberal government. Yet in inner Brisbane some potholes seem to reach to the centre of the Earth.

Glenn Wood, Bardon, Qld An election possibility

Why has no one been honest about the possibility of a hung parliament after the November state election? I was living in Tasmania in 1989 when the ALP and the Tasmanian Greens had to form a government because that is what the voting public determined in their voting at the election.

The reality is that if Pauline Hanson’s party gains the relevant numbers then they will have to govern with one of the major parties. That is our democracy at work. That is why voters need to understand this possibility when they vote on November 28.

Maree Williams, Kew In whose interests?

I agree with your correspondent (Letters, 5/8). Just because someone is super wealthy does not mean they have the best interests of the community at heart. In fact, they often get rich by self-interest. Not the best quality for politics.

Kim Abrahams, Fairhaven



Photo: Matt Golding AND ANOTHER THING Politics

Should One Nation be known as One News?

George Reed, Wheelers Hill There are conspiracy theorists galore for One Nation party opponents to explore. Warren Pickering is one such person.

Eric Palm, Gympie, Qld The contrast between the One Nation candidates and what they believe in and the exemplary work of independent senator David Pocock, in regard to wagering and taxation, is extraordinary.

Peter Baddeley, Portland



If Pauline Hanson is moderately successful at the Victorian and next federal election, all the major parties have only themselves to blame.

David Cayzer, Clifton Hill Furthermore

New Zealand has shown us the way on greyhound racing. How long will it be before the industry is shut down in Australia?

John Walsh, Watsonia Gambling advertising in any form should be banned, and we need a powerful federal industry regulator. Full stop.

Caroline Leslie, Hawthorn With children struggling with the basics of learning, let’s help them by stopping confusing fads like using “learning” as a noun.

Bernd Rieve, Brighton Re potholes, the only way to fix the problem is to run annual Tour de Victoria bicycle races.

Keith Robinson, Glen Waverley



If all Jetstar passengers paid for overhead luggage storage there would be no improvement in boarding and in punctual departures.

Virginia Heller, St Kilda Not sure the world could cope if Donald Trump won the mid-terms as Clinton Fernandes (Comment, 5/8) suggests.

Marie Nash, Balwyn Finally

It is the little things in life that matter. Every morning, rain or shine, a kindly neighbour picks up our delivered newspapers and puts them on top of our letter box.

Susan Munday, Bentleigh East

World.title: Man veered into teenage cyclists, allegedly killed dog in violent rampage in Auckland's Epsom
World.content:
A man has been arrested after allegedly hitting a group of teenage cyclists in a stolen car and strangling a dog to death on a busy street in Auckland's Epsom.

The 49-year-old would be facing 14 charges, police said, and was under police guard at Auckland City Hospital.

The charges included assault with a weapon, ill treatment of an animal, dangerous driving and aggravated assault.

Three Auckland Grammar School students were taken to hospital, one with life-threatening injuries.

Auckland City District Commander Superintendent Sunny Patel said there was no ongoing risk to the community, but one of the teenage boys was in a critical condition in hospital and had undergone surgery.

The two other boys were in a serious and moderate condition in hospital.

The teenagers had been training as part of a cycling club, he said.

Patel said the parents of the boys had been advised and were at their sides in hospital.

"I know all of us will have them in our thoughts today. These boys were part of a cycling club, doing something they enjoyed.

"This will be a life-altering event."

Auckland City District Commander Superintendent Sunny Patel. RNZ / Marika Khabazi

The school's headmaster, Tim O'Connor, said in a letter to parents of the school's students his immediate priority was the health, safety, and well-being of the affected students and their families.

"We are also ensuring that counselling and support services are made available to members of our wider school community who have been impacted by this incident.

"Our thoughts are with the boys and families affected, and out of respect for their privacy, we will not be making any further comment at this time."

O'Connor advised parents concerned about how the incident had affected their sons or their friends to contact school counsellors.

He said the school was cooperating with the police investigation.

A smashed windscreen on one of the damaged cars. RNZ / Marika Khabazi

What happened, according to police

Police said they were called to reports of a serious assault at the intersection of Ranfurly Rd and Manukau Rd about 7am.

What followed were described by Patel as six separate incidents.

Acting Detective Inspector Craig Bolton said a man without warning had assaulted a woman, causing bruising to her face, head and upper body.

"A member of the public stopped to assist the victim, before this offender has stolen the good Samaritan's vehicle," he said.

Police on Manukau Rd. RNZ / Marika Khabazi

Patel confirmed the woman was jogging when she was assaulted by the man who was not wearing any pants, and three our four members of the public came to help her.

"The offender then fled in the stolen vehicle, hitting several vehicles before striking three cyclists who were riding on Manukau Road."

After crashing the vehicle, the offender approached a woman walking her dogs.

"The offender has subjected one of the dogs to a violent assault, and sadly the dog has died at the scene," acting Detective Inspector Bolton said.

Patel said police attempted to taser the man once and then were able to taser him and pull him off the dog which had been killed.

"It is a random event that has occurred," he said.

Jessica Hopkins reports from scene of police incident in Epsom Midday Report Download MP3 2m

"This has all taken place in full view of the public going about their morning commute."

During the police standup, Patel confirmed the dog had been strangled.

Five patients were at the scene when Hato Hone St John arrived, a spokesperson confirmed.

Three cyclists were taken to hospital and two other people were treated at the scene.

Patel said the man was known to police, but had not been on bail he was expected to appear in court on Thursday.

Police were assisting the dog walker, Patel said, who was "very, very upset".

Anyone with information was urged to contact police on 105, referencing file number 260805/2349.

Do you know more? Email iwitness@rnz.co.nz

'It was like a warzone' - witness

Several smashed vehicles could be seen inside the cordon, along with a crumpled bicycle next to a red puffer jacket.

Petrol station worker Manthan Patel said he heard a "crazy" sound before he witnessed a man driving a car into another vehicle.

He said the man then got out of the car and attacked a dog.

Tasman Epsom Employee Manthan Patel RNZ / Marika Khabazi

Morning commuter Andre Lipa had pulled into the Tasman service station on Manukau Road when he heard yelling.

"The guy bolted across Manukau Road to the other side, and as he was going down the footpath he saw a couple of police cars coming so he started running... And there was a lady walking two dogs coming the other way towards him."

He said the man grabbed one of the dogs, which police later confirmed had died.

"One of the cops got behind him and tasered him and he went down but he was still fighting, and it took three of them in the end to subdue him," Lipa recounted.

It was not until he left the scene that Lipa discovered the series of events leading up to the arrest.

"I saw the five bikes absolutely buckled and smashed on the side of the road with an ambulance and one person being attended to, and then further down there were two or three cars just in the middle of the road that had been hit. It just looked like a warzone," he said.

Police moving one of the bikes. RNZ / Marika Khabazi

"I was shocked, what had happened at the service station was bad enough... I had never seen anything like that before."

"I just feel for the lady who got assaulted and the young boys, and of course the lady whose dog... I mean, she must have been absolutely terrified because she was within metres of this guy for quite some time."

A staff member at Forbes Homemade Gourmet on Ranfurly Rd told RNZ she had seen the incident unfold early this morning.

"There was a guy shouting in the streets next to where I'm working.

"It seemed as though he had no pants on."

She was worried that he could come into her workplace, so decided to call the police.

Police putting a bike into the back of a car. RNZ / Marika Khabazi

Soon after, customers told cafe staff that the man had crashed a car and punched a woman, she said.

A cordon put in place around the area had caused "bumper to bumper traffic" in the area, but it was now clearing, she said.

A worker at Steam Wand cafe just outside the Manukau Rd cordon heard a man screaming about 7am, followed by the screams of a woman. Police sped past the cafe soon after.

"This was an incredibly violent event which has unfolded very quickly. We acknowledge it has impacted many innocent people who were just going about their mornings," police said.

"Police are aware many people witnessed this incident, and we are appealing to the public for information and dashcam footage."

Debris inside the cordon. RNZ / Marika Khabazi

Offender 'known to police' - Seymour

Deputy Prime Minister and MP for Epsom, David Seymour, said the incident will shock people.

"People may be worried that this was some sort of premeditated terror-type attack, it was not that," Seymour said.

"It was a person known to police for mental health illness who has done something absolutely awful but not premeditated the way some people may fear."

He said Epsom was a tight-knit community.

"We don't expect things like this to happen here, or anywhere for that matter.

"Our thoughts will be with people affected by the incident, hoping they recover well and quickly."

World.title: Jetstar to charge new fees for using overhead lockers for carry-on
World.content:
Jetstar will soon charge customers money for using overhead lockers on its aircraft, with prices starting from $23.

The Qantas-owned budget carrier said it was part of a change in its carry-on model, which included removing its 7-kilogram carry-on weight limit.

It would instead move to a size-based carry-on baggage model and a fee to use the overhead bins.

From 2 February 2027, all Jetstar bookings would include one underseat bag such as a backpack, handbag or laptop.

Those who needed more carry-on baggage would have to pre-purchase what the airline called Priority Carry-on.

The add-on would allow for a second larger bag for the overhead locker, and those passengers would be among the first to board.

Jetstar said the availability of Priority Carry-on would be limited, and would start at $23 one-way on selected flights and vary.

For example, Dunedin to Auckland one-way would start at $23, Christchurch to Wellington one-way would be from $28, and Auckland to Brisbane from $34.

"We know that weighing carry-on bags at the gate can be frustrating for our customers and for our crew," Jetstar chief executive Stephanie Tully said.

"To make packing easier we've decided to remove the 7kg weight limit, so from February, the main thing customers will need to think about is the size of their carry-on."

Jetstar also detailed its size limits for underseat and overhead bags.

Underseat bags would have to be up to 40 x 30 x 20cm, and overhead bags with Priority Carry-on would have to be up to 56 x 36 x 23cm.

"By giving customers an underseat bag with the option to add Priority Carry-on, we can make better use of overhead locker space, streamline boarding and help more flights depart on time," Tully said.

"Our new carry-on baggage model provides more choice to customers while helping to keep our fares low. You only pay for what you need - travelling with less means paying less, and you can always add more if you need."

Jetstar said there were no changes to its checked baggage allowance.

It said customers with existing bookings for travel after 2 February 2027 would be upgraded to include Priority Carry-on at no cost.

Consumer watchdog, Consumer New Zealand, said Jetstar's plan to make passengers pay to use the overhead locker, reflects a lack of competition in the domestic aviation market.

Jon Duffy said more industries are charging more for something that was previously free.

"Really, it's a form of shrinkflation, so what Jetstar's done here is reduce what it's offering you and is now charging you more for something that was free before. So you're getting less for the same or more money."

He said New Zealand's limited choice of airlines flying domestic routes is also a factor.

"In our domestic airline market, there isn't a lot of competition, there's really just Jetstar and Air New Zealand.

"Jetstar probably knows that Air New Zealand is quite a lot more expensive so they can pull a move like this - charge you more for the same service and not worry too much about people leaving for the competitor because the competitor is that much more expensive".

Duffy said given Jetstar fares are usually a little bit lower, $23 could be up to 25 percent of a good fare.

"That's a decent increase. And most people would probably be taking a carry on piece of luggage for a domestic flight, because they're overnighting. Most people are not going to be able to avoid this extra charge."

Duffy said it would be difficult to find a hard-case bag that would fit under the seat, where the charge would not apply.

He said Consumer NZ has reviewed bags and could not find anything with wheels that would fit within the dimensions of an underseat bag.

World.title: Green MP Lawrence Xu-Nan grills Winston Peters on 'racist' comments that were directed at him
World.content:
The Green MP who Winston Peters told to "go back to your own country" has challenged the Foreign Minister in Parliament over his comments.

Peters says his comments were not racist, and he disagrees with the prime minister's statement condemning them.

The MP, Lawrence Xu-Nan, tried about a dozen times to pin Peters down.

The pair clashed repeatedly, with Peters using Parliament's rules to avoid answering directly whether he stood by his previous comments and Parliament's Speaker Gerry Brownlee stepping in to require Peters to answer.

In the end, on the interpretation taken by Brownlee, it seems a misquote on the Green MP's part may have let Peters avoid reopening the wound.

Peters last week during a general debate speech had responded to heckling from Lawrence Xu-Nan by saying "go back to your own country ... that's where they lie like a flatfish, but they don't lie like that here, all right?"

"This is called a democracy, unlike what you're used to," Peters said.

Xu-Nan grilled Peters during Question Time on Wednesday to ask whether he stood by his statements.

"I stand by all of my statements as Minister of Foreign Affairs including those made during two visits this term to China and my numerous engagements with my Chinese counterpart," Peters responded.

Xu-Nan repeatedly put Peters own comments to him directly, but Peters repeatedly quibbled that Xu-Nan's questions to him were about his comments made as leader of the party.

"If the member would like to question my statements made as leader of the New Zealand First party, he should understand the correct place to do that is during the general debate, not during oral questions," Peters claimed.

Labour leader Chris Hipkins challenged this, saying that when a minister was making a statement relevant to a portfolio they hold, "they cannot be doing that as a party leader ... the key point here is, is it portfolio related".

"Him saying that 'I made that statement in the general debate as New Zealand First leader' cannot be allowed to stand ... when he is in this House, he is the Minister of Foreign Affairs."

RNZ / Baz Macdonald

Peters and Seymour both raised points of order challenging that, Seymour pointing out that Hipkins had earlier challenged Prime Minister Christopher Luxon for using the defence force plane to fly home after a National Party event by claiming he was not acting as prime minister at the time.

Speaker of the House Gerry Brownlee said he did not have the previous rulings to hand about the matter, but it would be dealt with "at some point".

Xu-Nan asked if Peters agreed with Prime Minister Christopher Luxon that he had a "long track record of inappropriate attention-seeking comments designed to get the media and other politicians to talk about him instead of the issues Kiwis are facing".

Peters said the answer was "undoubtedly no", before also rejecting the suggestion his comments from last week had been racist.

He tried to refer to comments previously made by other MPs, but Brownlee disallowed it.

Peters eventually said what he agreed with was that "somebody who's been in this Parliament five minutes has wasted so much of Parliament's time".

Brownlee said that answer "doesn't help the order of the House" and his answer "doesn't need to be an insult to someone duly elected to the Parliament".

Xu-Nan tried again, but Peters again claimed the phrasing and forum was not correct.

Green MP Ricardo Menendez March challenged that with the Speaker, but Brownlee was having none of it.

"I know what the statement was, I know it very well, I've spent quite a bit of time on it ... it wasn't accurately given. Words matter."

When Labour's Kieran McAnulty raised a point of order about Peters' comments about Xu-Nan, Brownlee said he had given Xu-Nan licence to ask more questions, and people could "draw their own conclusions about what's happening here".

He did not think it appropriate at the time to have the person being questioned removed from the House.

However, he said he would review the Hansard - the official record of Parliament - and stood by his view that all members of Parliament "regardless of how long they've been here, are elected equally".

Xu-Nan was born in China, but migrated to New Zealand as a child and is a citizen.

Speaking to reporters afterwards, Menendez March said it showed the prime minister "would rather stay and keep the baubles of office instead of actually clamp down on behaviour that he himself has acknowledged is harming our communities".

"We're here to keep Winston Peters away from power this election, and we'll make sure that he doesn't get another go of government."

He said he could not see the Greens "credibly forming a government that included New Zealand First".

Xu-nan said the pair were taking that position as MPs, and could not rule out the party working with New Zealand First because "we do have a democratic process".

He said the system had allowed Peters to get away with racist comments for decades, and he was not fit for purpose to be a Minister of Foreign Affairs.

"For me, the most important issue... is the impact it will have on the Chinese communities. So, my concern has been the ability for a minister to continue - or a political party in general to continue - having racist comments and getting away with it under this government and what that would mean for migrant communities."

The Chinese Embassy has criticised Peters' comments, saying it had made "solemn representations" to the Foreign Ministry over the "negative" remarks.

Prime Minister Christopher Luxon himself criticised the comments as racist, but has refused calls to sack Peters as Foreign Minister.

World.title: What will cold snap mean for your power bill?
World.content:
If the cold snap has you turning on your heater more often, you might be wondering what awaits you in your next power bill.

New Zealand hit record levels of power consumption on Wednesday as temperatures dropped across the country, and the same is expected on Thursday.

But what does that mean for what households are paying?

Gareth Gretton, lead adviser at the Energy Efficiency and Conservation Authority, said normal heating would add about $150 a month to a power bill, when a household relied on electric heaters.

He calculated that using the example of Christchurch, because it does not have natural gas. "There's roughly a $150 difference between August, which is the coldest month, and February, which tends to be one of the warmest. So that's roughly $150 for heating in August."

He said a cold snap, with temperatures at least 5C lower than normal, would add another 50 percent to heating bills.

"Bearing in mind that it's cold in August anyway, that's kind of what a cold snap looks like.

Do I have to buy that extended warranty? No Stupid Questions with Susan Edmunds Download MP3 12m

"As a really rough guide you'd maybe be talking $15 or $20 extra heating costs a week for the unseasonably cold or particularly cold winter weather."

He said people who were worried about the cost of heating could focus on only heating the rooms they were in.

"All being in the main living room and using the heat pump, which is probably in the main living room and is the most efficient form of heating as well.

"A common setup is you've got a heat pump in your main living room but you've maybe got just electric panel heaters or something in the bedrooms … we're certainly still encouraging people to heat bedrooms when they're in them but if you really are trying to shave your costs then just heating the rooms that you're actually in at the time you're in them is kind of the best way to go."

Powerswitch general manager Paul Fuge said people needed to remember that electricity bills were not driven solely by how much power a household used.

"While colder weather typically increases electricity consumption, the relationship between usage and bills isn't one-to-one. Around 35 percent to 40 percent of a typical household power bill is made up of fixed or largely fixed charges, such as transmission, local lines, and metering costs. These costs remain the same regardless of how much electricity a household consumes..

"The impact can be larger or smaller depending on the household's pricing plan and how much electricity they use during peak demand periods."

He said other things were also a factor. Houses with solar panels would often have less electricity generation in winter because the days were shorter.

"For households on time-of-use plans, winter can also make it harder to shift some electricity use for space heating away from peak periods. Heating demand is often concentrated in the morning and evening when people need it most, and these are typically the times when electricity is most expensive. As a result, households can end up consuming more power during peak pricing periods than they typically would, which can magnify the impact on their bills."

He said households that had people home for much of the day, such as those where people worked from home or were looking after young children, would often see bigger winter bill increases because they had to heat all day long.

"It's also worth noting that there's usually a lag between cold weather and the bill arriving. Most households are on post-pay plans, so higher usage during August won't typically show up until the September bill, by which time the weather may have already improved. In general, it's not uncommon for a household's power costs in the coldest months to be around 60 percent higher than in the warmest summer month."

Fuge said while recent demand had pushed wholesale electricity prices up at times, most households were insulated from short-term fluctuations.

"Retailers typically manage this risk through hedging arrangements and long-term electricity purchases, allowing them to offer consumers fixed or predictable pricing. While sustained high wholesale prices eventually flow through to retail prices, the recent wholesale spikes were brief, so I wouldn't expect them to have a material impact on longer-term retail electricity price trends."

World.title: Steps the Tauranga hospital cat goes missing, community launches search
World.content:
A much-loved "community cat" who has spent years greeting staff and visitors at Tauranga Hospital is missing.

Steps, a 12-year-old tabby, affectionately known as the hospital's "patient support officer" was last seen in the hospital carpark on Monday night.

He had been curled up beside his bed by the hospital steps on Clarke St. His house near the carpark lift was also missing.

His disappearance was shared on a Facebook group set up to share posts about Steps with more than 4000 followers.

Owner Quinn Pratt said while Steps was "technically" his cat, he was much more of a community cat.

"He's more famous than I'll ever be," Pratt said.

A work ID for "Dr Steps" at Tauranga Hospital. STEPS THE TAURANGA HOSPITAL CAT / SUPPLIED

Pratt had brought Steps and his brother home as kittens after a hunting trip to Murupara about 12 years ago. He and his wife Emily had lived right across from the hospital, until about a year ago.

He said right away Steps began hanging out on the hospital steps, which led to his name.

Since then he'd become a common sight at the hospital and when Pratt's family decided to move they arranged for a neighbour, Karla Horn to watch over him.

He said Steps was loved by hospital staff and visitors and could often be found hanging out in the emergency department or taking the lift up and down.

Over the years Pratt said he had disappeared a handful of times, he was microchipped, and Pratt would normally get a call from a local vets within a few days.

People had also tried to take him home, Pratt said, but now he had his own house and signage in the carpark this happened less.

Steps in his house. STEPS THE TAURANGA HOSPITAL CAT / SUPPLIED

Pratt said what made this time different was the fact his little white plastic house was missing too.

"He's probably too friendly... I'm hoping it's someone who has taken him with good intentions.

"Unfortunately, he's the most generic looking cat on the planet."

Both Tauranga MP Sam Uffindell and Bay of Plenty MP Tom Rutherford both have appealed for Steps to be returned on social media.

Uffindell said Steps was a "friendly companion to all that come for treatment or to visit loved ones" at the hospital.

Rutherford said Steps was not a stray and was well-cared for by the community.

"He plays an important role around the hospital, bringing comfort to patients and staff.

"If you've seen him or know anything, please get in touch... let's help get him home safely."

World.title: More cold weather on the way: 'There's going to be plenty of negative temperatures'
World.content:
A cold snap gripping the country will intensify tonight and tomorrow, forecasters warn, with double-digit negative temperatures on the way for part of the central South Island.

Support agencies are seeing more demand for blankets and hot food, and Transpower is warning high demand could lead to energy shortfalls.

MetService meteorologist Alwyn Bakker said the southerly fronts that brought snow to Christchurch, Dunedin and Wellington on Tuesday had given way to a ridge of high pressure bringing still, clear and icy cold conditions across the motu.

"What that's doing is keeping clouds away overnight, letting all of that heat that's come up from the southern ocean - and there wasn't really a lot of it to start with - escape... so that means that we're getting even colder on top of what we've already had," he said.

"There's going to be plenty of negative temperatures around for the next couple of nights."

Cold snap set to intensify, concerns for vulnerable people Checkpoint Download MP3 3m

Mount Cook Village was forecast to drop to -10°C on Thursday morning, while Christchurch was expected to reach -5°C, he said.

In the North Island, Hamilton and Taumarunui could see lows of -4°C and -6°C respectively.

"It's definitely colder than average in a lot of places. We have some places that are reasonably close to getting into their top-five coldest for the month records," Bakker said.

Snow in Christchurch on Tuesday. RNZ / Nate McKinnon

Helping with the cold

Support agencies in main centres told RNZ they were seeing more people in need of help.

Christchurch City Mission missioner Corinne Haines said outreach workers had been checking on rough sleepers and delivering blankets, hygiene supplies, socks, gloves, sleeping bags and mats to sleep on.

There were as many as 300 people either couch-surfing or living on the streets in Christchurch, and this week the weather had shifted from wet to freezing cold, she said.

"The cold alone is not so bad in some ways, because you can put on a jacket and sleeping bag and socks and gloves and you can be relatively warm. But once you get wet that is a big problem. Once their clothing or their sleeping bags get wet, it's very difficult for them to get it dry," Haines said.

In Auckland, where overnight temperatures had been hovering near zero, Lifewise's Merge Cafe on Karangahape Road said it was welcoming about 30 homeless people each morning to thaw out.

Service manager Paula Bold-Wilson said the cafe served subsidised and pay-it-forward meals and had also been giving out donated blankets, thermal wear and shelter bags.

"We provide a hot meal in the morning and lately we're seeing a lot of whānau coming in for breakfast - in particular porridge, hot drinks. [They're] cold and damp as well. Where we can we try and respond with warm clothing," she said.

Grey Power Central Otago president Lorraine McKeown said she was worried elderly people were having to choose between staying warm or having enough to eat.

"The winter subsidy - that is now being used for essentials. It's being used for groceries, for petrol and necessities and then there may be nothing left over for the actual power... what it's supposed to be used for," she said.

McKeown - who lived in Alexandra - said it was definitely the coldest winter in recent memory.

"I've been here 10 years and for me this has been one of the longest winters with fog and frost all day," she said.

Snow on Remutaka Hill Road on Wednesday. Supplied / NZTA

Power concerns

The cold snap drove the country's electricity consumption to an all-time record of more than 7200 megawatts on Wednesday morning.

Major Electricity Users Group executive director Karen Boyes said industrial users were being asked to prevent a potential power shortfall on Friday morning, which had been flagged by Transpower.

That could mean shifting production away from peak times or generating more of their own power, she said.

"The key thing for most customers is it's not signaling an outage. It's saying things are tight. So the sector's taking all the steps that it should, and can, take to make sure that when we get to that [Friday] morning peak that we're the best prepared," Boyes said.

Electricity demand soars during cold snap Checkpoint Download MP3 5m

Transpower executive general manager operations Chantelle Bramley told Checkpoint there could be another record demand for electricity tomorrow morning, "and we do expect similar levels on Friday morning, as well."

Bramley said one of the challenges of the cold weather was that while it drove electricity demand higher, it also came with quite stable weather.

"That means that a lot of the wind generation that we usually have available in our power system isn't available. So that's why we need to co-ordinate a response with industry to make sure that other generation is made available to the system.

"And what we often find in times like this, where we have lots of hydro in the system - our hydro lakes are really full, they're sitting at above average now - that means that our thermal units may not be running as frequently, due to that abundant renewable supply, so we need this time with industry to co-ordinate a response."

She said the alerts were not common, and the last previous one had been issued by Transpower in May 2024.

World.title: English 'didn't have to compete' for official status - Māori Language Commissioner
World.content:
Te reo Māori has had to fight for recognition after generations of suppression, while English has long dominated life in Aotearoa, professor Rawinia Higgins says.

Last week, Parliament passed the English Language Bill, formally recognising English as an official language alongside te reo Māori and New Zealand Sign Language.

The bill is part of New Zealand First's coalition agreement, and party leader Winston Peters said at the bills first reading it would help solve a "virtue signalling narrative," and that the country should be using English as the primary language.

Te Taura Whiri i te Reo Māori - Māori language commission chair, professor Rawinia Higgins told RNZ te reo Māori, NZSL and English have not had the same journey to recognition. She uses a Commonwealth Games analogy to help articulate her whakaaro.

"The English language is the athlete that didn't have to compete. Like they just qualified anyway," she said.

"They got automatically selected for the team without having to be on the same kind of journey as te reo and as for sign language.

"There has been a lot of challenges for te reo and getting recognition. And we've seen attitudes towards te reo kind of wax and wane through successive governments."

Māori Language petition newspaper clippings. SUPPLIED

Higgins said she is holding on to wording in the new legislation that states recognising English as an official language will not affect the status or use of te reo Māori or New Zealand Sign Language.

"I think I'm holding on to that phrasing and hopefully the legislation lives up to that, that there will continue to be support for te reo and for sign language," she said.

"I struggled to see at the time when it was being proposed, what is the problem we're trying to solve here?"

Her whakaaro is grounded in the history of te reo Māori, which she said has been shaped by generations of government policy favouring English.

"If we go back, of course, we have 1840 as a good kind of marker for everybody in terms of the signing of Te Tiriti o Waitangi, but come 1847, you have the Education Ordinance Act, which essentially starts the journey of assimilation," Higgins said.

"And so that is the dominance of the English language in schools."

The Native Schools Act 1867 further entrenched English in education, with Māori children in many schools punished for speaking their first language.

Māori flag at Parliament: Phil Smith

"That, of course, totally eradicates te reo from the education system. And then consequently, you kind of have these different kinds of policies that shape the way Māori value their own language. Because there's a kind of conditioning to believe that the language of the day is clearly English in society. And so in order to support their children, they stop speaking te reo at home."

She said urban migration after the Second World War also accelerated language loss, as Māori families moved into towns and cities and were dispersed through government housing policies.

"Come World War II, where you also have a lot of men who don't come home from the war, that has a huge impact on whānau. And post-World War II is also when you get the urban migration. And so with that, moving into the towns, you have housing policies, that are pepper pot policies to ensure that Māori were being integrated into society so they didn't cluster together and regain their language and as such."

By the 1970s, a new generation of Māori university students were confronting the consequences.

Higgins said the Māori language petition delivered to Parliament in 1972 was driven by young Māori who were increasingly aware of what had been lost.

Rawina Higgins. Te Rawhitiroa Bosch / Supplied: Te Taura Whiri i te reo Māori

"They're also the first generation urban migration. And they are often the first ones to go to university," she said.

"And it's also around the same period where you have heightened awareness of civil rights movements overseas, that kind of global understanding of race relations. And these, this generation, don't have the language.

"So they understand that loss of the language, it really affects them, that their core part of their identity they don't have."

That activism helped spark the Māori language revitalisation movement, leading to institutions including kōhanga reo, kura kaupapa Māori, wānanga and Māori broadcasting.

Higgins said the progress made since the 1970s is significant, but language revitalisation is a multi-generational kaupapa.

"It takes one generation to lose a language. It takes three generations to restore that language. And often if you're that first generation to try and turn the tide, it feels like you're fully on an uphill battle, that you're trying to gain the language, you're trying to learn the language. That in and of itself to become bilingual is, it takes time."

She said the emergence of new generations of first-language speakers is one of the most encouraging signs for the future of te reo Māori.

"For some whānau they have restored the language as a first language in their whānau. And, you know, they're doing amazing things.

"I'm always heartened by that generation who are first language speakers today because they're more creative. They don't have any inhibitions because they don't actually understand what it means to not have the language.

World.title: Christopher Luxon defends using Air Force flight after attending National Party fundraiser
World.content:
Christopher Luxon is defending his use of an Air Force flight after attending a National Party fundraiser, saying he has a "busy job" and "full schedule".

Labour on Wednesday accused the prime minister of using the Defence Force as a "personal taxi service" for campaigning purposes.

Luxon flew from Whanganui to Auckland on a six-seater NZDF King Air plane on the evening of 23 July after attending a National Party fundraising dinner.

Speaking to reporters at Parliament, Luxon said he needed to get back to Auckland for a meeting the next morning and no Air New Zealand or Jetstar flights were available.

He said he had brought the meeting forward to 7am that he could also attend the funeral of former National MP Bill Birch that day.

"I needed to get back to that meeting... I couldn't catch a commercial flight to get there after a full day in Feilding and Whanganui," he said.

"Those planes need to be flying, and the pilots need the hours and the training anyway. It's not costing the taxpayer any additional money."

Labour leader Chris Hipkins said Luxon could have easily skipped the National fundraisier and caught an earlier commercial flight from Whanganui in order to make the next meeting.

He said instead Luxon appeared to be using the Defence Force like a "personal taxi service".

"It's absolutely unjustifiable. Attending a party fundraising event is a bright line," he said. "Air force planes should not be used to support that."

Hipkins said only a select group of people, including the prime minister, had access to those planes.

"It's really important for the political neutrality of the Defence Force that they are not used by those people for campaigning purposes."

Luxon has come under pressure in the past week over his use of NZDF flights. Previous prime ministers also made use of such facilities, though Hipkins argued that was never for party purposes.

Luxon said his job as prime minister was a busy one and so he used military assets "if and when it's appropriate".

"It's an extreme job. It has a lot of commitments. They're long hours. Commercial flights don't always work from different parts of New Zealand.

"You want to use my time efficiently, so I can do as much as I possibly can."

World.title: 'Gone down like a lead balloon': Ex-FA boss on FIFA's World Cup backflip
World.content:
"It's gone down like a lead balloon."

This is David Gallop's view of FIFA president Gianni Infantino's now-infamous World Cup privatisation proposal.

"It's so far off passing the pub test that I think it's like he let off a stink bomb in the middle of the pub and people ran screaming, leaving half a schooner behind," Mr Gallop told 7.30.

"That's how poorly it's been received."

Mr Gallop has been one of Australia's foremost sport's administrators. He was CEO of the NRL from 2002-2012 before jumping ship to become the boss of Football Federation Australia for seven years until his tenure ended in 2019.

He has watched on this past week as Mr Infantino's failed sell-off plan has evolved into a full-blown crisis over his leadership.

"He's definitely under pressure now … to throw out an idea like this that's gone down so badly," he said.

Mr Infantino's proposal, dubbed the FIFA Forward Enterprise, would have seen the commercial rights of FIFA's most popular tournaments, including the World Cup, transferred to a private company, and a 20 per cent stake sold to investors, valued at $20 billion.

It's been reported Joshua Kushner, the brother of Jared Kushner, Donald Trump's son-in-law, was one of the private equity figures behind the plan.

FIFA President Gianni Infantino's relationship with US President Donald Trump was under scrutiny at the World Cup. (Reuters: Dylan Martinez)

"Anytime you sell anything, you need to have good, compelling reasons, but particularly so when it comes to something like the World Cup and ... sport in general," Mr Gallop told 7.30.

"You've got to know that you really need to do it. You really need the money. What are you getting for the slice of the asset and what are you giving up?

"Clearly people have not liked the idea that private investment, and therefore, a profit motive that comes away from the game to those private investors would be something that FIFA would contemplate."

'One-off sugar hit'

Mr Gallop said privatisation was not inherently wrong but required an overwhelming strategic and financial case to be valid.

"It will be a mistake to burn the furniture to heat the house," he said.

"You need to be setting up your sport and the business of your sport for sustainability, not for a one-off sugar hit of capital.

"These are the questions that have to be answered when one is looking at private sale of these effectively community assets that people feel strongly about."

FIFA President Gianni Infantino's plan to privatise has been met with derision by many football bodies. (AP: Eduardo Verdugo, File)

The proposal offered FIFA's 211 member federations one-off payments of $20 million each, but Mr Gallop said FIFA's financial position only heightened questions about why such a proposal had been pursued.

"FIFA has $5 billion in cash now after the World Cup," he said.

" I think that's one of the reasons why a proposal to sell an equity stake has fallen so flat. They're not desperate for money. "

Within three days of the proposal, Mr Infantino and FIFA scrapped the plans.

Europe's UEFA, North America's CONCACAF and Asia's AFC, which Australia is member of, all opposed the plan.

UEFA, CONCACAF, as well as a growing number of national federations have taken it further by withdrawing their support of Mr Infantino's leadership.

Football Australia's chair Anter Isaac and CEO Martin Kugeler both declined an interview with 7.30.

The organisation has welcomed the decision by FIFA to scrap the privatisation proposal but is yet to weigh-in on Mr Infantino's, now under siege, leadership.

Mr Gallop said Australia's influence on the world game came less through political power than integrity.

Infantino's 'blotted copybook'

The integrity of Mr Infantino, like that of his predecessor Sepp Blatter has now been called into question.

Former FIFA President Sepp Blatter's tenure ended due to corruption. (Reuters: Stefan Wermuth)

Mr Infantino was elected in 2016 promising to restore confidence in FIFA, following a number of corruption scandals that occurred under Mr Blatter's 17-year reign as president.

Mr Gallop's time at FA straddled the terms of both men. He was also CEO in 2010, when Australia's bid to host the 2022 World Cup was beaten by Qatar, a decision that was mired in controversy and allegations of corruption.

"There was a bit of a stench around FIFA and Gianni came in with a pitch of transparency, accountability, consultation and putting football first," Mr Gallop said.

" I think it's fair to say this proposal, albeit backflipped on, has blotted his copybook in respect to what people expected from him and from his presidency. "

"[Especially} coming hot off the heels of a number of other contentious decisions, including the lifting of the red card on the USA player during the tournament."

United States' Folarin Balogun's red card was rescinded during the World Cup after a call from Trump to Infantino. (AP: Jeff Chiu)

Despite calls for Mr Infantino's resignation growing louder, Mr Gallop said his tenure at the top of world football might not be over just yet.

"I don't think it's necessarily so that he won't get re-elected. He has some big confederations against him at the moment, but he has others where FIFA has carefully funded development in a lot of smaller nations," he said.

Mr Gallop remembers representing Australia at FIFA congresses, sitting next to the small Caribbean nation of Aruba — "a population of a hundred thousand people."

"Behind us would be Brazil … millions of people, an absolute icon of world football … but everyone gets one vote; that's where your confederation structure comes into play," he said.

Mr Gallop believes the president's political future will depend on whether member associations believe the successes achieved under his leadership outweigh the damage caused by the failed privatisation proposal.

" Whether there's enough credit in the bank for all the good things that FIFA have produced … or whether this has blown them up will remain to be seen. "

Fan outrage

Patrick Clancy, head of the Football Supporters Association in Australia, told 7.30 many fans felt betrayed by the proposal.

Football's governing body has long been at the centre of controversy and corruption allegations. (REUTERS: Arnd Wiegmann )

"He's tried to privatise football at the expense of the game of football," he said.

"It's something that came out of nowhere and is not in line with what anyone has thought of before. And so I think that's the concern; where's it all going?"

His organisation is now very keen to understand where Football Australia stands on Mr Infantino and his leadership.

"These are very troubling times in world football and Football Australia needs to make its position very clear," he said.

Mr Clancy says football supporters want to see the game run properly.

"They want to feel that there is a degree of integrity and they don't want a money-hungry organisation that seems to be interfering with that organic nature of the game," he said.

"Within 24 hours, Infantino and FIFA completely changed the shape of world football.

" They blindsided almost everyone in the game, so goodness knows what's going to happen in the next seven days. "

World.title: Australia's coach says no tour match ahead of India Test series
World.content:
Australia will again opt for a training camp ahead of the five-Test tour of India rather than play ​a traditional warm-up match before attempting to end a 22-year wait for a Test series victory on the subcontinent.

Australia also chose not to play a tour match before ​the 2023 series, ‌instead training on specially prepared, spin-friendly pitches in Bengaluru before the opening Test.

The decision drew scrutiny after India won the Nagpur opener by an innings ‌and 132 runs, setting the tone for a 2-1 series ⁠victory that allowed the hosts to retain the Border-Gavaskar ‌Trophy.

Ifs, buts and maybes for Australia in India The record books will show that Australia left India without the Border-Gavaskar Trophy, but the series defeat offers plenty of opportunity for introspection ahead of the Ashes.

Head coach Andrew McDonald ​said Australia would scout ‌a location to immerse themselves in conditions similar to India before the series opener in Nagpur starting on January 21.

"We've got a couple of options there," he told Cricket Australia website Cricket.com.au ​on ‌Wednesday.

"We have gone to the UAE previously and we have also gone into India last time into Bengaluru, so we're ⁠just working through what that ‌would look like in terms ‌of how we then manage the individuals."

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

Australia has not won a Test ‌series in India since 2004 when Adam Gilchrist's side triumphed 2-1.

Australia have a gruelling schedule before they ‌arrive in ​India, with a ⁠two-Test home series starting against Bangladesh in Darwin next week followed by a three-Test tour of South Africa in October and another four-Test home series against New Zealand from December ⁠9.

Fast bowler Michael Neser has been ruled out of the Bengaluru series with a ‌calf strain suffered ‌at training in Brisbane but McDonald said wicketkeeper-batter ​Josh Inglis was expected to be available after recovering from a back spasm.

Reuters

World.title: Tony Modra medical record probe expands to extra staffer
World.content:
Another staff member is being investigated for allegedly inappropriately accessing the private medical records of AFL legend Tony Modra, SA Health has confirmed.

Modra was seriously injured in a truck crash at Back Valley, near Victor Harbor on South Australia's Fleurieu Peninsula, in June, and later underwent facial surgery.

Last month, SA Health said three staff were being investigated for allegedly inappropriately accessing the private medical records of the former Crow, while a further five employees were also being "assessed" to determine whether their access was "always appropriate".

In a statement, SA Health today said the investigation was ongoing.

Police were called to the scene of the truck crash, near Victor Harbor. (Supplied: SA Police)

"One additional SA Health staff member is under investigation for potential inappropriate access of a patient record, following an audit that identified eight staff members who remain under investigation," the statement said.

"In total, nine staff members are part of the current investigation, which is ongoing."

The alleged breaches are not the first time that concerns have been raised about SA Health staff inappropriately accessing patient records in cases involving high-profile individuals.

In 2016, 13 hospital staff were sanctioned after being caught snooping on the medical records of Cy Walsh, who was charged with the stabbing murder of his father — Crows coach Phil Walsh — before being found not guilty by reason of mental incompetence.

In 2024, ABC News revealed an SA Health investigation had found 18 staff engaged in misconduct or inappropriately accessed the medical records of a patient understood to be Charlie Stevens, the late son of SA Police Commissioner Grant Stevens.

Tony Modra was injured while driving a truck at Back Valley in June. (Supplied: 9News Adelaide)

SA Health has previously apologised to Modra's family.

The department has also previously said it regularly conducted audits "to ensure that staff are accessing appropriate information".

"Any staff member who has accessed information inappropriately may be subject to disciplinary processes, which may include termination of their employment," SA Health said previously.

Last month, Modra posted an update on his progress on social media, saying he was "getting out and about" and praising the medical staff involved in his recovery.

World.title: Hawks' Wizard looking to pull off Coleman medal shock
World.content:
Hawthorn coach Sam Mitchell has sung the praises of Nick Watson as the 170cm "Wizard" attempts to snare what would be one of the most unlikely and magical Coleman medals in VFL/AFL history.

Watson's five-goal haul in last week's 16-point win over North Melbourne lifted his season tally to 52 goals.

It means Watson became the first player since Syd Dyer and Lou Richards in 1946 to kick 50-plus goals in a season despite being 170cm or shorter.

Sydney's 194cm forward Charlie Curnow leads this year's Coleman medal count with 57 goals, with Gold Coast's 202cm spearhead Ben King (53 goals) in second and Watson lurking in third.

AFL round 21 Saturday live updates Josh Fraser's bid to become Carlton's next full-time coach receives a massive boost as the Blues record a thumping win over the Brisbane Lions.

Hawthorn face Brisbane at the Gabba on Friday night before rounding out their home-and-away campaign against Collingwood and West Coast.

A big finish from Watson could be enough to snare him the Coleman, and although Mitchell says the Hawks won't go out of their way to target him in the next three weeks, they would celebrate his achievement if he gets there.

"It'd be great if it happened," Mitchell said.

"But he's young and he's got plenty of opportunities in front of him.

"I certainly hope that's not the focus of the lads going into a game like this. But I won't be shying away from it if he gets that opportunity, of course."

Watson, fondly dubbed "The Wizard", is already a superstar of the competition despite being just 21 years old and 61 games into his AFL career.

"The level of consistency is probably the best thing that we've got from Wizard this year," Mitchell said.

"And it's probably one season earlier than most. He's certainly maturing. Like, he's 21 years old and he's quite popular, and how he handles that is really impressive."

Third-placed Hawthorn (14-5-1) haven't won at the Gabba since 2016, but they have only played three games at the venue since then.

Mitchell wants his team to use Friday's blockbuster against two-time defending premiers Brisbane (13-7) as an interstate finals rehearsal.

"I think if you look at the ladder most Victorian teams are going to have to win interstate at some point, and this is a start for us," said Mitchell, who earlier this week re-signed with Hawthorn until the end of 2030.

The Hawks have a number of selection queries heading into the crunch clash with Ned Reeves (knee), Karl Amon (knee), Mitch Lewis (concussion) and Henry Hustwaite (face) all under injury clouds.

Meanwhile, an American court has formally dismissed charges against Hawthorn player Connor Macdonald for his off-season misadventure.

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

Macdonald and teammate Dylan Moore spent a night in a US jail after being charged with trespassing for climbing onto a cherry picker.

Moore's case was wrapped up last month, while Macdonald's case has also now been concluded with the pair having previously agreed to complete a substance abuse counselling program.

"It's probably nice for them to have it off their back," Mitchell said.

"They're both having really good seasons and really pleased with their performances. Sometimes dealing with adversity can make you grow, and I think they've both done that this year."

AAP

World.title: Pay war on ice as Australia's netball stars sign truce
World.content:
A pay war has been averted — for now — after Australia's Super Netball players agreed to an updated collective player agreement for 2027.

Under the new collective player agreement (CPA), Super Netball players will receive improved pay and conditions, more time off and greater ability to sign individual sponsorship deals.

The 12-month bridging agreement to the CPA has been agreed between Netball Australia, the Super Netball clubs and the Australian Netball Players' Association (ANPA).

It means Super Netball clubs can start contracting players and preparing for the 2027 campaign.

Before this week's agreement went through, players had been in contract limbo.

Netball agents frustrated as pay talks roll into Glasgow 2026 Messy and drawn-out pay negotiations are once again overshadowing a major tournament for the Aussie Diamonds.

The protracted pay dispute also meant plans to expand Super Netball had been placed on hold until at least 2028, despite a new five-year broadcast deal with the Nine Network starting in 2027.

With the CPA now locked in for 2027, attention will turn to a longer-term deal for 2028 and beyond in coming months, with Netball Australia hoping to avoid a repeat of a drawn-out pay dispute.

The ANPA want a revenue-share model, as well as better pregnancy and parental leave policies as part of a longer-term deal.

Netball Australia interim chief executive Mark Falvo said the 12-month bridging agreement struck the right balance between delivering immediate benefits for players, while also positioning the sport for future growth.

"We are at a pivotal moment for our sport," Falvo said in a statement.

"This agreement gives our players, clubs and the league certainty while we enter a period of significant commercial opportunity for netball.

"There is more work to do on meeting some of the asks for the athletes and the clubs, but this agreement delivers meaningful outcomes for players today while demonstrating our responsibility to balance the long-term sustainability of the league."

The news of the fresh CPA comes on the back of Sports Entertainment Group (SEG), headed by Craig Hutchison, putting the final touches on their takeover of the licence of the Giants Super Netball club.

SEG already owns the Melbourne Mavericks as well as multiple basketball clubs, with the Giants set to become the latest franchise to go under their SEN Teams banner.

The flurry of netball news comes just days after the Australian Diamonds suffered a shock 46-45 semi-final loss to Jamaica at the Commonwealth Games in Glasgow.

The Diamonds were hot favourites to snare gold, but had to settle for bronze with a 80-65 win over England in the third-versus-fourth play-off match.

Although New Zealand walked away with the gold medal, their domestic competition faces an uncertain future after losing around $3.7 million in 2026.

With no broadcast deal in place, rumours are bubbling the Premiership in New Zealand could be placed on hold for 2027, or downgraded to amateur status.

It means a flurry of Kiwi players could seek out Super Netball deals for next year as they seek financial security.

New CPA deal:

Increase to the total player payment pool (minimum and maximum amounts) by greater than the Consumer Price Index (CPI)

Players to receive a one-off payment upon the signing of a commercial partner for the Super Netball league

Additional time off through condensing hours for club commitments that will free up an additional two weeks of time off per year

Option for athletes to enter into multi-year contracts

Greater ability for athletes to secure their own individual sponsorship deals

Increased health insurance and meal allowances

AAP

World.title: De Minaur wins all-Australian clash as Popyrin gets through in Montreal
World.content:
Fallen star Alexei Popyrin has dug deep for a morale-boosting victory to join Alex de Minaur in the second round of the Canadian Open in Montreal.

Two years after upstaging the great Novak Djokovic in a seismic US Open triumph, Popyrin has slumped to number 139 in the world as he battles a crisis of confidence.

But after toiling through qualifying just to make the main draw, Popyrin toiled for another two hours and 12 minutes to see off Argentine Roman Andres Burruchaga 4-6, 7-5, 6-3 to notch his first ATP-level win since May in the Masters event.

The breakthrough was only Popyrin's ninth win of a lean 2026 campaign and vaulted the one-time world number 19 into a second-round contest with US seventh seed Taylor Fritz or another Argentine, Thiago Agustin Tirante.

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

De Minaur, meanwhile, looked to be cruising before fellow Sydneysider James Duckworth put the world number seven through the wringer late on.

Runner-up in 2023, de Minaur was a set and 3-1 up before Duckworth fought back hard seeking a first win over his countryman in three meetings.

But de Minaur held firm to fend off six set points and progress 6-2, 7-6 (6) and book a third-round date with either Britain's Cameron Norrie or Peru's Ignacio Buse.

"In the first set everything was flowing," de Minaur said after the one-hour, 46-minute dogfight.

"I was up a break, had a couple more chances to go up by a double break and all of a sudden it slips away.

"Then all of a sudden momentum shifts and we got into a battle. So I am glad I was able to sneak through. There are a couple of things I need to tighten up on, but we live to fight another day."

While de Minaur and Popyrin move on, fellow Australian Adam Walton crashed out with a 6-3, 6-4 loss to American Jenson Brooksby.

In the women's WTA event in Toronto, Tahlia Gibson continued her stellar 2026 season with an upset 7-5, 6-1 second-round win over Polish 18th seed Maja Chwalinska.

Gibson's 28th win of a breakout year earned her a crack at Russian 16th seed Ekaterina Alexandrova.

World.title: NRL club claims player Keith Titmuss contributed to training death
World.content:
A rugby league player who died of heat exhaustion at pre-season training contributed to his own death by not managing his weight and diet in the off-season, his former club says.

The family of Keith Titmuss, who died in November 2020 after collapsing during pre-season training, is suing the Manly Warringah Sea Eagles for damages owing from negligence in his death, including failing to implement the NRL heat policy.

In a defence filed in the NSW Supreme Court the club has claimed it was not responsible for the death of the young man because he did not inform coaching and medical staff of his worsened physical state through the off-season.

"NRL training is inherently dangerous," the club wrote in its defence.

"Any injury, loss and damage suffered by [Titmuss's family] … was caused or contributed to by the deceased's own negligence."

Former NRL player's mother speaks on lawsuit The mother of Manly player Keith Titmuss, who died of exertional heat stroke following a 2020 Sea Eagles training session, breaks her silence on her family's multi-million-dollar lawsuit against the NRL club.

Manly Warringah alleged Titmuss failed to properly train or diet during the off-season and put himself in danger by not stopping training when he felt sick.

"Players were instructed … if they were feeling ill or feeling like they were not coping with the physical demands [that] they were to inform coaching staff," the club said.

The club also filed in its defence that it conducted a fitness test on the 20-year-old four days before he died and found "no red flags".

The session at the Sydney Academy of Sport at Narrabeen involved outdoor sprint tests before moving inside for an intense cardio session.

A 100-passes drill and a cardio circuit involving up-downs/burpees, bear crawls and "fireman carries" was conducted inside the facility's dojo, the parties agree.

The temperature was about 21 degrees Celsius during the session but the humidity was 92 per cent, court documents state.

Manly Warringah admitted the dojo was not fitted with air-conditioning but said there were multiple floor-standing fans, the back doors were open and hydration breaks were enforced.

The player's family alleged the fans were not switched on during the session.

There were 10 staff to monitor the 15 players inside, the club said.

NRL player Keith Titmuss died after 'inappropriate' training session, magistrate finds A magistrate who oversaw the inquest into the death of a young Manly Sea Eagles player recommends the NRL consider mandating a two-week period of controlled training acclimatisation after off-season breaks as part of an existing review.

A 2024 coronial inquest into his death concluded the budding NRL player died of exertion heat stroke, with a pre-existing heart condition unlikely to have played a part.

The work-out at the club's Narrabeen gym, which followed an outdoor session, was "more likely than not inappropriate", the coroner found.

Evidence at the inquest was that paramedics at the scene noted Titmuss's temperature at 41.9C, while his heart rate was more than 140 beats per minute.

Titmuss's family claimed the precautions instituted by Manly Warringah were not sufficient to meet its own heat policy guidelines, alleging the club is liable for the young man's death.

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

"[Manly Warringah] owed a duty of care to the deceased as an employee and … breached the duty of care owed," the statement of claim said.

Titmuss's family alleged the player started to struggle physically after an outdoor sprint test three days prior, which the club denied.

The club instituted a heat policy after former prop Lloyd Perrett said he was planning to sue the club over a training session in late 2017 which left him hospitalised with heat stroke after suffering a seizure.

Manly Warringah and the NRL were contacted for comment.
